paragraphs: Reproductive rights / Access to housing / Strong workforce & economy / Quality childcare & education / Environmental justice & climate action / LGBTQIA+ / Gun responsibility

It’s important to note that issues affecting large portions of our district are disproportionately felt by natives and communities of color. I am committed to analyzing all legislation with a lens of equity to move our society to a point where race and ethnicity can no longer be used to predict a person’s outcomes in life.

Reproductive rights are not just a woman’s issue. I am a firm believer that men must consider the shared responsibility of sexual and reproductive health and protect a woman’s ability to make her own choices.
Cosponsored the My Data My Health bill, using my expertise with technology to protect the PRIVACY of patients so their data cannot be used against them
Voted to direct the state government to stockpile the abortion pill in case the Supreme Court limited its availability.
Voted to establish an abortion savings program to provide long-term, consistent, stable funding for abortion services
If elected to the Senate, I will continue protecting reproductive rights for all women and help win the fight for gender equality. I commit to:
Protect the access to REPRODUCTIVE HEALTH CARE , including ABORTION and CONTRACEPTION
Increase the SAFETY and security of all patients, providers, and clinics

Our neighbors are often pushed out due to the rising cost of living in our community, elders are forced to sell their homes due to increasing property taxes, and renters have few protections. I have firsthand experiences with the problems in the housing market and power imbalance between owners and renters. We must protect tenants while we rebalance the housing market.
Championed the passage of RENT STABALIZATION so that tenants have predictable housing costs and are their finances are not decimated by the rental market
Sponsored a bill to expand the supply of housing by allowing residential development in commercial zones.
Voted to pass the MISSING MIDDLE HOUSING bill which ended exclusionary zoning in transit rich areas
Voted for the largest ever investment in the HOUSING TRUST FUND so that that we can fund affordable housing
If elected to the Senate, I will continue fighting to:
Strengthen TENANT PROTECTIONS , like rent stabilization , so that landlords can’t exploit renters and can be held accountable if they do
Support RENTAL ASSISTANCE to help families navigate temporary life hardships
Continue state investment in AFFORDABLE HOUSING
Provide housing VOUCHERS so that working people can afford to live in existing market rate housing

Too many people are struggling to make ends meet. As a professional soccer referee, I stood with our union to win fair compensation by using a work stoppage. I understand the value of the labor movement and support improved compensation, conditions, and benefits for all working people.
During my time in the House I have maintained a 100% labor voting record .
If elected to the Senate, I will continue fighting to:

Support WORKER RIGHTS and LIVABLE WAGES , promoting UNIONS and the ability for workers to organize for quality wages, benefits, and safety protections contribute to increased community purchasing power and a healthy economy.
Protect and invest in small businesses by increasing ACCESS TO CAPITAL and INCUBATION PROGRAMS for micro-entrepreneurs

Address the barriers to ECONOMIC OPPORTUNITIES and GENERATION WEALTH for communities of color, communities with low incomes, and immigrants who may lack the necessary capital to start a small business

The costs to care for and educate our children continue to climb for families in Washington and force them to make sacrifices. My parents felt those sacrifices as they camped out overnight to get me into the best public schools. When we ensure all our schools and students have the resources they need, we will see incredible results.

During my time in the House, I’ve worked to grow the state’s capacity for training the next generation of computer scientists and engineers while also closing the digital divide. I’m proud to have become the legislative champion for UW’s Pathways for Inclusive Excellence. Expanding opportunities, and providing them closer to our diverse communities, will help to engage folks who have been traditionally underrepresented.
If elected to the Senate, I will continue fighting for families in the 37th District and across the state to:
Expand access to quality EARLY EDUCATION and CHILDCARE
Ensure Washington schools lead the nation in STEM offerings
Expand investments in TRADE , certificate, and APPRENTICE programs to prepare young people for jobs in high demand fields
Increase access to collegiate education by first funding FREE 2 YEAR COLLEGE

Climate change and pollution are an immediate threat to our existence. The 37th District disproportionately experience air and water pollution due to the proximity to pollution and hazardous water. Washington faces serious impacts to its ecosystem, infrastructure, and water supplies as the climate changes and temperatures increase.
During my time in the House, I served on the Environment & Energy committee and got to work on the many environmental bills we passed. I personally sponsored bills to:
Update our state’s 10 year old climate resiliency plan
Establish the nation’s most effective BATTERY RECYCLING program in Washington state
Fight for ENVIRONMENTAL JUSTICE disproportionately in BIPOC and lower income communities adjacent to transportation infrastructure and hazardous sites
Use the best SCIENTIFIC EVIDENCE to create sound policy decisions
Support efforts to replace aging systems with CLEAN ENERGY and expanding adoption and accessibility of rooftop solar
Lead strong ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTIONS for our state’s valuable forests, waterways, and unique ecosystems

Everyone deserves equal treatment under the law, regardless of sexual orientation or gender identity and expression. I will advocate for, and elevate the voices of, the LGBTQIA+ community to ensure equity in all aspects of state government.
Voted to pass the “shield law” to protect people in Washington from civil and criminal actions in other states that restrict or criminalize reproductive gender-affirming care.
Reaffirm the RIGHT TO MARRY the partner of your choice
Expand access to high-quality health care for LGBTQIA+ individuals, including removing barriers to medications like PrEP
PROTECT LGBTQIA+ individuals from violence, particularly transgender women of color
Ensure FAIR TREATMENT of LGBTQIA+ individuals in the criminal justice system

A person is killed in Washington State with a gun every 14 hours. Gun violence is all too common now in our society, and the debates that have followed have been predictable. I have lost many friends and community members to gun violence. This is the horrible reality for me and America. Although gun violence is preventable, we all know someone affected by it. I will fight to:

Protect “red flag” laws that empower families and law enforcement to prevent gun tragedies by temporarily RESTRICTING ACCESS to guns for individuals at an elevated risk of harming themselves or others
RAISE THE AGE to buy a semi-automatic rifle
RESTRICT GUNS at city and county council meetings, school board meetings and ballot counting centers
BAN GHOST GUNS that people can buy online and assemble at home to evade background checks

pages.title: Meet Chipalo – Chipalo Street
paragraphs: Street is a leader with a proven track record creating change. He’s used his experience to improve the systems that shape our state in the House and is excited to continue the work in the Senate.

He grew up in a working class African American community with a sister and two loving parents during the tumultuous decades of the ‘80s and ‘90s. As a product of the public school system, he was lucky to discover a love for technology during high school. This focus helped keep him engaged in his studies and prepared him to excel. He earned a Bachelors and Masters in Computer Science at Brown University where he also cofounded a start-up in remote cardiac rehabilitation before graduation.

Street entered the workforce at Microsoft and has created continuous innovation which kept Microsoft as a leader in the industry. This includes starting the Azure IoT Edge product which spearheaded Microsoft’s approach to edge computing, had four of his pending patents granted.

Street realized his education provided him opportunities to which many other black and brown kids didn’t have access. He improved this deficit by cofounding the Teacher Scientist Partnership at Technology Access Foundation Academy where he developed and taught computer science curriculum in south Seattle.

His work to improve our community goes well beyond a dedication to digital equity. Street served on the board for the Institute for Democratic Future which trains the next generation of Democratic civic leaders. He also served on the Public Policy Impact Council at United Way of King County, and was co-president for Brown University’s chapter of the National Society of Black Engineers.

Street fed his entrepreneurial spirit by starting a small real estate company which views rental homes as a partnership between the owner and tenants. Determined to live his morals, he managed to keep all of his tenants housed throughout the pandemic despite 30% of them losing work.

Performing at the highest levels does not intimidate Street. He retired from a successful “nights and weekends” career refereeing international, professional, and collegiate soccer matches and gives back by mentoring young referees.

pages.title: The Plan | Tatiana Brown for WA State Senate LD 37 — Tatiana for Washington
paragraphs: Tatiana will bring the power of this Senate seat directly to the people of the 37th.

Our Platform is built by community leaders and in collaboration with our neighbors. The policy memos and priorities below are a reflection of Tatiana’s commitment to collaboration across the 37th and Washington State.
We need a real community-driven economy. One that puts the people of the 37th first.
Champion family owned, small businesses—respect and protect the culture
Fund community wealth building models and scale them up
Uphold community-centered organizations and cultural pillars
Click HERE for Tatiana’s full policy memo on Education & Youth.
I will defend crucial state-funded programs like Running Start, Washington College Grant, and the Washington Education Legacy Trust account
I will champion progressive revenue sources such as HB 2100 , the Well Washington Fund to continue investing in the College Grant
I will commit to championing bills such as SB 5906 (SAFE Act), to create the strongest protections to ICE-proof our schools, and community spaces

I will ensure free K-12 meals are healthy, nutritious, and grown locally by supporting Statewide Food Security Strategy ( HB 2238 ) and commit to further building on the 2008 Local Farms - Healthy Kids Act

I will invest in CTE (Career and Technical Education) partnerships with local public schools, CTCs (Community Technical Colleges), and local unions to ensure students have access to high-quality, hands-on training that ensures access to a well-paying job
I will work to pass legislation that bans exclusionary discipline (suspension, expulsion, arrests) for vague and subjective behaviors
I will work to restore funding for the Outdoor Education for All Act ( HB 2078) so our fifth and sixth graders can enjoy multi-day, outdoor learning
I will fight to fully fund counselors, social workers, and community-based providers like Healthpoint so that students are easily able to access necessary care
Click HERE for Tatiana’s full policy memo on Data Centers & AI Regulation
I will work with colleagues in the Legislature to pass a statewide moratorium on new hyper-scale AI data centers.
I will pursue a Senate version of HB 2515 , requiring data center developers to pay for their energy use, lower usage during peak hours, and comply with existing energy laws.

I will introduce a State accountability mechanism for communities to report violations to established regulations, and work with the Washington State Attorney General’s Office to absorb resident litigation costs and ensure corporate accountability.
I will fight to preserve and restore funding for HEAL and the de-funded community capacity grants that support the 37th.
Cultivate a nutritious and culturally diverse food system.
Weatherize housing to withstand rising temperatures.
Protect community health from major polluters.
Click HERE for Tatiana’s full policy memo on Affordable Housing and anti-displacement.
How well a government serves its people is measured in the health of those most vulnerable.
Care for our elders with robust community infrastructure
Keep our kids safe, and expand after school programs
Increase access to affordable and culturally informed healthcare
Prioritize public safety by delivering community what they need
Design fast, reliable, and relevant transit throughout our district
House our community and combat displacement

Hacks & Wonks is a podcast and radio show hosted by Crystal Fincher, who talks with Policy Wonks and Political Hacks to gather insight into local politics and policy in Washington state through the lens of those doing the work, with behind-the-scenes perspectives on what's happening, why it's happening and what you can about it.

pages.title: About Tatiana | Tatiana Brown for WA State Senate LD 37 — Tatiana for Washington
paragraphs: Tatiana was raised in the multicultural community of Tysons Corner, VA. She was taught the beauty and necessity of cultural exchange, and the strength in celebrating our differences. Brought up among an intergenerational network of organizers in Richmond, VA, Tatiana was trained to deliver results on the question: how do we serve our community?
More importantly, how do we bring decision making power back to our community leaders—and create the change we need?

In Richmond, Tatiana worked alongside a community coalition to secure greater access to healthcare for her refugee and immigrant neighbors. She joined a crew of visionaries who believed we didn’t have to live in a food desert. Together, they got their hands into urban farming and built a robust network of community-run fridges, which are still feeding neighbors to this day.
In 2021, Tatiana came to Seattle with the mission to learn from the community leaders setting the standard–on the $15 minimum wage, the HEAL Act, and holding polluters accountable.
She found her academic home at University of Washington-Seattle, and her organizing home in South Seattle and CID.

Pursuing a dual Masters in Public Health and Public Administration, Tatiana studied the consequences of a government that does not serve its people—whether in the form of wealth inequality, health disparities, environmental injustice, or disenfranchisement of communities who deserve better.
Since moving to Seattle, Tatiana has worked to learn from those around her, and to answer the questions that matter to her home.

She develops collaborative governance tools with the People’s Economy Lab, and has piloted the first examples of government-funded community assemblies in the country. She organizes with local leaders in environmental justice, community wealth building, and education.
At 24, she was appointed as the youth representative by Governor Inslee to serve with 15 leaders across the state on the Washington Environmental Justice Council.

She was elected by her peers as the youngest co-chair in council history. Three years later, she continues to fight alongside communities hit first and worst by the climate crisis: in the 37th and across Washington.
She is a proud graduate of Sage Leaders, member of Standing for Democracy, paddler for Wakinikona Outrigger Canoeing Club, and enthusiastic patron of the amazing food in the 37th.

Tatiana believes in a future that allows communities to plan long-term, escape a constant state of survival, and build within our community’s vision. This future will be hard fought, and she is ready to work.
Together, united, and grounded in the communities of the 37th LD.

pages.title: Kelabe Tewolde for State Representative | Washington's 37th Legislative District
paragraphs: “Kelabe is an educator and housing advocate who has spent his career investing in the community he's from. He's a fierce champion for fully funding early education for our kids, for housing working families can afford, and for safety built on community investment. Vote Kelabe as your next State Representative.”
The safest and healthiest communities are those that are well-invested in and well-resourced. For far too long South Seattle and Skyway have not been prioritized by our local leaders.
I support policies that will center community solutions that protect working class families, our children, and our most vulnerable populations.
Now more than ever the 37th needs a strong local leader that has lived experience and shared values of our community.

As a lifelong Seattleite and educator, Kelabe has watched his students and their families face the same issues he and his mother faced over 20 years ago: being priced out of their own neighborhoods, losing a loved one and watching medical debt bankrupt the family left behind, and seeing young people lost to gun violence because no one invested in them first. These aren't policy talking points: they're the daily realities of the 37th. It is long overdue for our communities to have the proper safety nets in place so that families can stop surviving and start thriving.

This is a movement that will take ALL of us. Whether you’re most comfortable contributing time to make calls, the energy to get out and canvass with your neighbors, or want to host a house party to share the priorities of this campaign with your friends and family we need you on our team!

"Kelabe is an educator and housing advocate who has spent his career investing in the community he's from. He's a fierce champion for fully funding early education for our kids, for housing working families can afford, and for safety built on community investment."

"I'm excited to endorse Kelabe for State House. His hands-on education experience is important as we seek to improve outcomes and meet the needs of kids statewide. He's a thoughtful, engaged leader, with perspectives and ideas we need in Olympia."

"As a lifelong educator, Kelabe understands firsthand what students need and the struggles they face in the 37th. He’s a champion for fully funding early education because he knows firsthand how much investing early can change a child’s future. The 37th deserves an advocate that will meet the moment with the urgency needed to make tangible change. Vote Kelabe as your next State Representative."

The cost to rent or purchase a home has more than doubled over the last 25 years. Kelabe's experience serving on the Seattle Planning Commission is what we need in Olympia to craft policies that will prevent displacement and help make South Seattle more affordable for working families.

pages.title: Priorities — Kelabe Tewolde for State Representative
paragraphs: Fund the first chapter, not the last resort

As a first-generation college student, I understand firsthand that access to quality education can change the entire trajectory of a life. We need to fully fund our transition to kindergarten programs, early literacy supports, and behavioral health resources like social workers in schools to meet the needs of our students.

Every child deserves a strong start. That means fully funding transition to kindergarten programs and early literacy supports, because reading resources shouldn't be a privilege reserved for families who can afford the support. And I will work to establish the youth development fund account to increase access to positive youth development programs.

I will work to bring back funding for the education legacy trust fund, which includes resources for K-12 education, childcare, class size reductions, and support for teachers. Ensuring better outcomes for our kids.
We need to provide pathways to employment for our youth. That means funding pathways to 2 year and 4 year degrees, as well as workforce training.
My mother went bankrupt because of the mountain of medical debt left behind when my grandmother passed away after a long battle with lymphoma. Families shouldn’t be punished for seeking medical care.
I will work to create limits on interest incurred on medical debt. We shouldn’t punish families that are seeking care.
Healthcare is a human right. Washington state should take steps to establish Universal Healthcare. I will be a champion in Olympia for healthcare for all.

I will support the establishment of the Washington Health Trust funded by progressive revenue. The Washington Health Trust could amount to saving the state an estimated $5-13 billion annually in total healthcare spending by eliminating administrative waste, fraud, and cost-inflation incentivized within the for-profit insurance industry.
Priced out is not a plan when it comes to housing

As a kid, I moved around all over Seattle because no matter how hard my mother worked as a CNA, a single mother’s wages could not meet the high costs of rent, food, and healthcare. And as an adult, the rising cost of living and the housing landscape the dream of owning a home has become out of reach. We need to prioritize pathways to homeownership for those historically left out.

I will fight for legislation that protects renters. We need a ban on junk fees and regulations on Ratio Utility Billing Systems (RUBS), which inflate basic utilities on many renters. These protections would ensure people do not end up overpaying for the basics while living in one of the most expensive cities in the country.

The racist history of redlining in Washington state has made it difficult for marginalized communities to own their own homes. We must prioritize pathways towards homeownership for those historically left out of the process. Through partnerships from the state, counties, cities, and local community land trusts.

I will be an advocate for investing in social housing developers all across the state. The social housing model is a self-sustaining and publicly-funded affordable housing development that allows families to stay in place.
Safety starts with investment, not incarceration

I have friends that were recruited to join gangs in middle school, and if they didn’t have programs like Rainier Scholars, they would have gone down that path. Keeping young people engaged in learning isn't just an education issue, it's a public safety solution.

Invest in a multi-pronged approach to violence prevention. Providing mental health services to youth, case management that keeps kids in school, and provides training for youth to develop and build job skills.

Fund activations in our communities along targeted blocks and corridors. This means infrastructure investments like lighting and safe sidewalks, as well as legislation that incentivizes small businesses to open in empty store fronts. This not only makes our neighborhoods feel safer, but community bonds are built between community members.
Expand investments in non-violent services like the CAREs team across the state. We need to create legislation that allows them to do their jobs in a safe and effective manner.

pages.title: About — Kelabe Tewolde for State Representative
paragraphs: Kelabe was raised in a working class union family by his single mother who came to this country as a refugee. She had dreams that were put on hold because of the barriers that come with raising a child on your own. They were priced out of neighborhood after neighborhood because no matter how hard she worked, rising costs always moved faster than her wages. They dealt with housing insecurity, but they were supported by their tight knit community. When they lost his grandma to lymphoma, Kelabe and his mother were not only grieving, they were buried under medical debt that drove his mother to bankruptcy. Parents shouldn’t be worried about eviction or where their next meal is going to come from because our legislators are unwilling to create safety nets for those in need. That’s why Kelabe is running to represent the 37th LD because our families deserve better.

Growing up, Kelabe’s education was made the number one priority by his mother. At an early age Kelabe saw his mother advocate for his education at every turn. She saw education as a way to keep her son safe. She saw Kelabe’s older cousin become a victim of gun violence and made sure Kelabe was on a positive pathway, with education as her north star. His mother’s values stuck with him as he went on to become an educator.

She enrolled him in Rainier Scholars, a decision that changed the trajectory of his life. That program kept Kelabe engaged, challenged, and on a positive path. He watched friends in the program who were recruited to join gangs in middle school stay the course. They were too invested in the work to fall into it. That experience showed Kelabe firsthand what happens when you invest in young people early. It's where he learned that the best prevention isn't punishment, it's opportunity.

Over the past 8 years Kelabe has been an educator at Rainier Scholars, working with students routinely left behind by our school system as a teacher, an advocate, and a mentor. He has spent his entire career working with kids all over this district. In his time as an educator he has done what he can to support students as they face hardships and become leaders in their communities. The issues he faced as a kid growing up in Seattle continue to impact the students he serves. Families continue to be displaced from their long-time homes in the Central District. Parents have to make difficult decisions between going into medical debt or keeping food on the table. Students fear for their safety in their neighborhoods losing classmates to gun violence. Kelabe has done everything he can inside the classroom. Now it's time to lead outside of it. The 37th deserves a representative that will do all he can to ease the burden on families from the Central District all the way to Skyway.

pages.title: Reelect Sharon Tomiko Santos for State Representative | 37LD | Democrat
paragraphs: In 1998, Representative Santos was elected to the Washington State House of Representatives, becoming the first Japanese American woman elected to a mainland state legislature.
For more than two decades, she has represented the 37th Legislative District with a focus on:
Protecting longtime communities from displacement and helping more people stay housed in the neighborhoods they call home.
Strengthening public education and expanding opportunity for students and families.
Protecting civil rights and immigrant communities.
Advancing economic, criminal, and environmental justice.
Housing, Anti-Displacement, & Community Preservation
Prevent displacement, expand affordable housing near transit, and help more people get and stay housed.
Invest in students, educators, and families through stronger schools, affordable childcare, and workforce development.
Public Safety & Behavioral Health Response
Investing in community-led violence prevention, behavioral health response, and long-term mental health and substance use disorder treatment.
Public Transit & Pedestrian Street Safety
Build safer, more connected neighborhoods through reliable public transit, pedestrian safety, and transit-first housing growth.
Protecting Workers & Supporting Small Business
Protect workers, support small businesses, and expand pathways to economic opportunity.

pages.title: About | Sharon Tomiko Santos Representative for Washington State's 37th Legislative District — Sharon Tomiko Santos for State Representative 37LD
paragraphs: Growing up, Sharon Tomiko witnessed both the pain that injustice leaves behind and the determination of a community that refused to disappear.
Her mother and grandparents were among the Japanese American families forcibly removed from their homes and incarcerated during World War II.
In the years that followed, Sharon Tomiko witnessed elders, organizers, churches, families, and small business owners slowly piece neighborhoods and community life back together.

Kenneth Miyake 三宅 富子 (left) born in Kurashiki, Japan moved to the United States for seminary school. While living in Berkeley, CA., he met Joyce Ishizaka 石坂 (right) a California born Nisei. In 1961 they welcomed their daughter Sharon Tomiko Miyake.

As a student at Franklin High School, Sharon Tomiko became part of that work herself, organizing youth participation in Seattle’s first Day of Remembrance , galvanizing fellow students to join a caravan from Seattle to Puyallup, where Japanese American families had first been assembled before mass incarceration in 1942.

As a student at The Evergreen State College, Santos was inspired by Seattle civil rights figure Gordon Hirabayashi’s work exposing the federal government’s corruption used to justify Japanese American incarceration.
After graduating in 1988, Sharon Tomiko continued her studies in public policy, leadership, and community-centered public service at Northeastern University, where she earned her Master’s Degree.
While working on Mike Lowry’s campaign for U.S. Senate, she met Bob Santos , the beloved Chinatown International District organizer known to many as “Uncle Bob.”
The two married in 1992 and shared a deep commitment to civil rights, community preservation, and opportunity for working families until his passing in 2016.
Before serving in the Legislature, Sharon Tomiko worked in banking, for local elected officials, and in nonprofit leadership.
She also became active in international women’s issues and served as a delegate to the 1995 Fourth World Conference on Women in Beijing.
Sharon Tomiko Santos has earned recognition from educators, civil rights organizations, community advocates, and public service institutions across Washington.

Honors and awards include the Franklin High School Hall of Fame, The Evergreen State College Joseph Albert Dear Distinguished Alumna Award, the Children’s Alliance Champions for Children Award, the Northwest Asian Weekly Foundation Lifetime Achievement Award, and more.

pages.title: Jaelynn Scott for State Representative
paragraphs: The 37th is a vibrant, diverse district with a powerful legacy of Black & Brown community-driven leadership.
Send me to Olympia and I will not only protect that legacy, but build on it.
I’m running for Washington State House of Representatives 37th District, Pos 2 to strengthen our communities, provide opportunity, deliver increased public safety, and safeguard our civil rights.

As Executive Director of the Lavender Rights Project, Jaelynn has built a nationally recognized model for broadening social safety nets and advancing justice for Black gender diverse communities in Washington State.
Her first project after stepping into leadership?

Building a coalition that redirected $16 million public dollars from jail expansion into alternative solutions and permanent supportive housing for QT2BIPOC residents in partnership with the Chief Seattle Club.
That’s what standing on business looks like.
Jaelynn Scott is a spiritual leader, community organizer, proud Democratic Socialist, the Executive Director of the Lavender Rights Project, and ready to deliver for our community on day one.
Washington state has one of the fastest growing economies and state GDP in the nation, but our investment in public goods do not reflect a deeper commitment to our progressive values.
Decommodify housing. Land and housing belong in public, cooperative, and community-stewarded hands — not on the speculative private market in the hands of private equity.

Community Safety and Prevention, Not Criminalization: Community-based crisis response, independent police oversight, and an end to mass surveillance and mass incarceration — not slogans, but a fully funded alternative system.

pages.title: Jaelynn Scott’s Policy Priorities | Public Safety, Housing & Democracy Reform — Jaelynn Scott for State Representative
paragraphs: Jaelynn’s platform is a community-informed declaration of what is possible when we hold corporations accountable and invest in universal care. Healthcare, childcare, housing, these are not radical ideas, but common needs were. And we’re ready to fight alongside a broad multi-racial working class.
Meanwhile the billionaire class, private equity, and corporate profits are breaking records. Let’s fight back together because we share more needs than differences.
We CAN pass the wealth tax and the high earner payroll tax
We CAN tax the billionaire class avoiding taxes
We CAN tax AI and advanced computing corporations and data centers
We CAN tax private prisons and close tax loopholes carved out for corporations that are costing our state billions of dollars in potential progressive revenue.
We CAN fight displacement and gentrification with community stewardship of the land.
We CAN limit how much your landlord can raise rent from 10% down to 5%.
We CAN reform the housing trust fund investment priorities
We CAN open a public bank and decommodify housing, and reclaim the profits going to private equity
We CAN build more social housing and permanent supportive housing.
We CAN build permanent supportive housing with public partnerships with communities.
We CAN ban junk fees and enforce tenants rights
We CAN give tenants the opportunity to purchase (TOPA/COPA) and give community first rights when residential and public land go up for sale before the private market.
We CAN expand and align a statewide behavior health crisis response system
We CAN hold police accountable and subjected to independent oversight
We CAN pass common sense gun responsibility legislation by investing in community-led solutions
Healthcare is a Human Right, that means universal coverage, no deductibles, no debt — and defending abortion and gender-affirming care from federal attack.
We FIGHT because for universal healthcare coverage
We FIGHT for care and reinvestment in our Washington Health Trust
We FIGHT for a Healthcare system, not a commodity
We FIGHT to defend abortion and gender-affirming care from federal attacks by FIGHTING for expanded state programs and investments.

Billionaires and corporate PACs have hijacked our "Democratic" legislature, our campaigns, and ballot initiative process. It's time to give power back to the people who show up to the doors, not the people who write the checks.
We CAN win campaign finance reform to get big money out of politics.
We CAN tax the rich to pay for statewide democracy vouchers so all voters have spare money to spend on state races.
We CAN restore voting access to incarcerated and formerly incarcerated people.
We CAN expand voting rights and protect from federal attacks on our democracy
Rainier Ave S and MLK Way S are two of Seattle's most dangerous roads — in the most diverse district in the state. That is not a coincidence.
We SHOULD invest in just transition for our workforce as we build new infrastructure
We SHOULD keep air pollutants and toxic runoff out of our ecosystem
We SHOULD use CCA funds for what they are intended
We SHOULD ensure community oversight without the delaying process
We SHOULD ensure our world class public transportation serves the communities it passes through.
We SHOULD hold big oil accountable to the harm we’ve done to our environment
We SHOuLD regulate and tax data center centers energy, water, and utility use.
We SHOULD protect consumers and our climate and invest in our workers at the same time.
Working people share more than we disagree about. Our communities are too often divided and siloed into fighting against one another, when in reality working people make Washington state run.
We FIGHT to protect labor standards and workplace conditions.
We FIGHT to end racism and do more than study reparations
We FIGHT for a real sanctuary for Washington state
We FIGHT to build unity among working people through building collective identity, not siloing issues into individual identities
We FIGHT to end the school to prison pipeline by decriminalizing our students and meeting our paramount duty to fully fund our public schools.
We FIGHT for universal childcare so working families can afford to have families in our increasingly expensive state.

pages.title: About Jaelynn Scott | Candidate for Washington State House 37th District — Jaelynn Scott for State Representative
paragraphs: I am a spiritual leader, community organizer, Democratic Socialist, and the Executive Director of the Lavender Rights Project, a national black trans feminist advocacy organization advancing justice for gender diverse communities.
Guided by my faith and informed by my lived experiences, I have dedicated my life to building a community where all can live in freedom, dignity, and belonging.

As a Black trans woman, I’ve faced many of the same challenges others in QT2BIPOC and marginalized communities face — unstable housing, barriers to employment, addiction, and ideologically motivated violence and threats to our civil liberties.
Through that experience, I saw clearly that our so-called social safety nets were riddled with holes.
And, it didn’t just test me — it gave me the pragmatic expertise to repair the very systems that fail us.
So, when I say it’s difficult to survive in systems that were never designed for us, it is an embodied understanding.
And, that deep knowledge shapes how I design policy, with urgency, precision, and a focus on prevention.
While I was able to rebuild my life through faith, community, and a commitment to service, I know not everyone has that same access to support and that truth anchors my work.

Before stepping into my current role as Executive Director of the Lavender Rights Project, I spent years working in community, organizing, responding to crisis calls, helping people find sanctuary, and trying to help folks navigate the confusing, frustrating, broken system of social services. And it was clear, this alone would never be enough.

Inspired by the legacy of Black and Brown leadership in the 37th like the “ Gang of Four ,” as well as community leaders like Peggy Joan Maxie, Marjorie Pitter King, I brought together a coalition strong enough to demand real, structural level change.

T ogether, we redirected $16 million in public dollars from jail expansion into permanent supportive housing and services for queer and trans BIPOC communities, including gender-affirming care, community-led programming, fresh food access, safe space for rest, and care grounded in Black trans leadership.
And, we proved something powerful: when public investment follows community wisdom, real system level support is possible.
That’s what standing on business looks like and I am ready to bring that same discipline, clarity, and results-driven leadership to Olympia.

Jaelynn is a proven coalition-builder across nonprofit, government, and community sectors, delivering measurable public policy outcomes that strengthen housing stability, public safety, and civil rights.
Executive Director, Lavender Rights Project — Leads a nationally recognized model advancing Permanent Supportive Housing and civil rights protections for Black gender diverse communities.
Coalition Leadership — Helped redirect $16 million from jail expansion into Permanent Supportive Housing and wraparound services in partnership with Chief Seattle Club.
Housing & Public Safety Policy — Advanced Housing First solutions and prevention-based public safety strategies that reduce crisis and strengthen community stability.
Care-Based Crisis Response — Championed upstream investments in behavioral health and community violence prevention.
Progressive Revenue & Civil Liberties Advocacy — Supported and protected the Millionaires Tax, Capital Gains Tax, and Keep Washington Working protections.
Ordained Minister & Community Leader — Reimagined and led inclusive worship and education spaces centered on multigenerational, LGBTQIA+, and communities of color perspectives.
Master of Divinity, Naropa University — Studied Black theology, engaged Buddhism, and social activism, and the role of spiritual leadership in structural reform.
Arts Corps — Led organizational restructuring and strengthened operational systems during a period of transition.

Nonprofit Organizational Leadership, Public Policy, and Equity & Inclusion Consulting — Advising nonprofit and social justice leaders on policy strategy, organizational effectiveness, and intersectional governance.
Jaelynn Scott is a housing and civil rights leader running for Washington State House of Representatives in the 37th Legislative District, Position 2.
She is also the Executive Director of the Lavender Rights Project and an ordained minister with a Master’s of Divinity (MDiv) from Naropa University.
The Washington State 37th Legislative District includes the Central District, Rainier Valley, the Chinatown-International District, Columbia City, Beacon Hill, and Skyway.

Washington’s 37th Legislative District has a powerful history of Black political leadership and grassroots organizing playing a critical role in the Pacific Northwest civil rights movement and helped shape statewide conversations around housing equity, voting rights, and police accountability.
The district has produced trailblazing elected officials and community leaders who have advanced policies on education funding, labor protections, criminal justice reform, and housing justice.
Just as important as its elected leadership is its deep tradition of community-based organizing — from faith institutions and tenant unions to immigrant rights coalitions and youth advocates.

The 37th remains the most diverse legislative district in Washington State and continues to lead with a legacy rooted in accountability, resilience, and the belief that government should serve the people.

pages.title: Vote Evon McCorkle
paragraphs: My name is Evon McCorkle. I'm a Seattle college student studying physics, and like many people in this community, my path hasn’t been easy.

I’ve experienced housing instability, relied on public assistance, and worked to stay in school while navigating real-life challenges. Those experiences didn’t hold me back they shaped how I see the world and why I care about the issues that affect everyday people.

I believe in education as a pathway forward, in stable housing as a basic foundation, and in making sure people especially, those who feel unheard, have a voice in the decisions that impact their lives.
I’m not coming into this with decades of political experience. I’m coming in with lived experience, a willingness to learn, and a commitment to serve my community with honesty and focus.
This is about building something better, together.

pages.title: ‍ ‍ Priorities | Get Involved Today — Evon Mccorkle's page
paragraphs: As a state, we have a responsibility to invest in education, ensure housing stability, and create real opportunity for the people who live here

I have seen firsthand how funding decisions impact schools at every level. In Olympia, I stood alongside teachers advocating to keep schools open and secure the resources their students deserve. I saw young children holding signs in support of their schools.

Education funding is not an abstract budget line. It determines class sizes, support staff availability, program access, and whether institutions can remain open at all. From early childhood education to community colleges and higher education, consistent and responsible funding is essential.
Our state must treat education as an investment in long-term stability and opportunity, not an expense to be negotiated away.

Housing instability takes many forms. It is not limited to rising rent. It includes families living in vehicles, individuals staying in shelters, and people relying on extended family simply to avoid sleeping outside.

I have seen this firsthand. I have volunteered in outreach efforts and spent time with individuals navigating homelessness. These experiences shaped my understanding of how housing insecurity affects stability, education, employment, and overall well-being.

Effective housing policy must address both affordability and access to safe, reliable shelter. Expanding capacity, improving shelter conditions, and creating pathways toward long-term stability should be central priorities.
Housing is not only about property, it is about dignity and security.
Representation means more than occupying a seat. It means listening to communities that often feel unheard, especially minority and working-class residents.

As someone who comes from these communities, I understand firsthand the gaps between policy and lived reality. Representation is not about identity alone; it is about perspective, accountability, and ensuring that decisions reflect the full diversity of our district.
When leadership reflects the people it serves, trust grows, participation increases, and policy becomes more grounded in real experience.
We all want better housing opportunities, stronger homelessness response systems, and greater stability for our communities. But meaningful progress requires financial responsibility.

Washington residents already shoulder some of the highest combined gas and sales tax burdens in the country, yet we continue to struggle with housing instability and visible homelessness at alarming rates. This signals not just a revenue question, but a prioritization and allocation challenge.

When our district and the City of Seattle operate under significant budget pressures, long-term planning becomes difficult. Sustainable reform requires balance understanding the tradeoffs between investment and constraint, between sacrifice and measurable gain.
True progress means aligning our financial decisions with our stated priorities. If we expect change, we must ensure our budgeting reflects it.

As a student who depends on access to affordable care, I understand how critical it is to have reliable coverage. You can’t focus on school, work, or building a future if you’re worried about whether you can afford to take care of your health.
Access to healthcare should not depend on income or circumstance. It should be something people can rely on when they need it.
If we want stronger communities, we have to treat healthcare as a basic foundation not something people have to struggle to access

pages.title: Elle Nguyen for Washington State Representative — LD-41 | Make It Make Sense
paragraphs: Common-sense leadership for Legislative District 41

Elle Nguyen is not running for name recognition; she is running to serve. As a widowed mother, small-business owner, real estate investor with college degrees, and dedicated community advocate; Elle understands the value of hard work, the reality of everyday challenges, and the importance of standing up for what matters. Elle is running for Washington State Representative in Legislative District 41 to give our community an independent, accountable, and transparent voice in Olympia—one grounded in common sense and responsive to the people she seeks to represent.
Elle Nguyen doesn't just talk about civic engagement — she has put herself on the line for this community, twice.

Elle ran for the Mercer Island School District School Board and advanced all the way to the final two candidates — a testament to the trust and confidence Mercer Island families placed in her vision for education.

Elle challenged incumbent My-Linh Thai for Washington State Representative in Legislative District 41, Position 2 — taking on an entrenched incumbent and proving she is willing to fight for the people of this district.

pages.title: Issues — Elle Nguyen for Washington State Representative LD-41
paragraphs: Below are Elle Nguyen's priorities vs. Janice Zahn's legislative record.
Zahn First Bill Signed Into Law: HB 2228

My opponent's first bill signed into law was not about lowering your taxes, housing costs, reducing your utility bills, lowering your gas costs, or making groceries more affordable. House Bill 2228 began changing building rules to allow consideration of scissor stair designs in multi-family housing. These designs can reduce the amount of floor space devoted to separate stairwells, leaving developers with more usable, and more profitable space for additional units. As someone with experience in real estate, I understand that every square footage has economic value to a Developer. Who was this bill really designed to help? Washington families are struggling with affordability. We have much bigger problems than making apartment-building layouts more efficient for developers.

My opponent voted for House Bill 2266, giving Olympia more control and local communities less control over where shelters and supportive housing are located. Helping people experiencing homelessness is crucial; however, statewide officials should not impose one-size-fits-all decisions on every community. Parents, neighborhoods, schools, police, and local leaders deserve a meaningful voice because they live with the consequences. Communities understand their own roads, schools, public-safety needs, infrastructure, and available services better than legislators in Olympia. We need solutions that expand housing and services while preserving transparency, accountability, and local participation. Olympia should support communities not override them, and local families should not be left to deal with the consequences of decisions made without their meaningful input.

My opponent sponsored HB 1870, which would give counties the authority to impose a new property-tax levy for public-health clinics. Elle supports access to public-health services, but homeowners should not automatically become the next source of revenue whenever government identifies another funding need. Washington already spends billions of dollars across its health-care and public-health systems. Before creating additional property-tax authority, government should identify efficiencies, eliminate waste, prioritize existing revenues, and demonstrate why current resources are insufficient. Homeowners should not be treated as an unlimited source of funding.

While ordinary drivers sit in traffic, my opponent proposed HB 1980, a bill that would allow private employer shuttles to pay for access to certain transit-only lanes. Washington families already pay taxes, fuel costs, registration fees, and tolls to use our roads. Large employers should not receive preferred access while everyday commuters remain stuck in congestion. This is not about opposing employer transportation, it is about fairness and accountability. Before granting private companies access to public transportation facilities, the state should demonstrate that the policy will reduce congestion rather than create another advantage for those with the resources to pay for preferential access. Any such arrangement should be transparent, narrowly limited, and structured to benefit the public not simply private employers.

My opponent sponsors HB 2566, which would allow counties to bypass normal competitive-bidding requirements for certain taxpayer-funded contracts. Taxpayer-funded contracts should be open to competition whenever practical, not quietly handed to a preferred contractor. My concern is not that a county can never use a company it has worked with before; it can. The concern is that competition helps prevent favoritism, inflated prices, and friends-and-family contracting by giving other companies an opportunity to compete.

My opponent is endorsed by Democratic organizations actively campaigning against IL26-638, the 2026 initiative addressing participation in K-12 athletics, and Zahn has publicly aligned herself with House Democrats' transgender-policy agenda. I believe girls deserve fair competition based on biological sex. Female athletes should not lose roster spots, records, scholarships, or championships to biological males, who, by nature, are physically stronger than females.

My opponent supports Washington policies on House Bill 2332 and its companion Senate Bill 6002 that restrict the use and sharing of automated license-plate-reader data for federal immigration enforcement. The law prohibits Washington agencies from using these systems for immigration investigations or enforcement and requires safeguards preventing federal civil immigration authorities from accessing the data. I support immigration and it must be legal. America cannot maintain secure borders or the rule of law if government makes lawful immigration enforcement more difficult. Families who waited, applied, and followed the legal process deserve fairness. Secure the border, enforce the law, and welcome those who come through the front door.

My opponent voted Yes on SB 6182, creating Washington's Abortion Savings Program to provide funding for abortion services. While Washington families are struggling with health-care costs, housing, groceries, and basic necessities, Zahn voted to create a state program specifically designed to help fund abortions. I believe government should protect unborn life and invest in mothers, prenatal care, adoption resources, and families — not abortion. Zahn co-sponsored HB 2182, whose official title is Improving Access to Abortion Medications. If any of my constituents have ever watched an abortion being performed, it is heartbreaking. Limbs and skulls are crushed. I believe abortion is the taking of an innocent human life, and I oppose government funding for abortion.

My opponent sponsored HB 2571, which would limit the medical-cost evidence an injured person can use when seeking damages from a local government. If someone is injured because of the actions of a city, county, school district, or other public entity, government should not receive special rules that make it harder for the injured person to establish the full extent of their damages. The law should be fair to the injured citizen not tilted in favor of the government being sued. If government causes harm, it should be held to the same standard of accountability expected of everyone else. Injured people should not face additional barriers simply because the responsible party is a public entity. Government accountability means protecting the rights of citizens, not creating legal advantages for the government itself.

My opponent co-sponsored House Bill 1805, which would allow counties to impose an additional sales tax to fund services that include children's mental-health programs. Zahn also co-sponsored House Bill 2038, which proposed another business tax to fund youth behavioral health. I strongly support mental-health treatment, particularly for children and families who need help; however, mental health must be treated as an essential government priority, not another reason to reach into taxpayers' pockets. Before creating another tax, Olympia should identify waste, reprioritize existing spending, and put mental-health treatment ahead of non-essential programs. Mental health deserves funding because it is a priority, not because government found another tax to impose.
The Constitution Is the Supreme Law — No Exceptions

Washington State has a Trojan horse problem. Foreign legal codes — including Sharia law — are quietly being introduced into our communities through private arbitration panels, family courts, and institutional accommodations that bypass the protections guaranteed to every American by the U.S. Constitution. Sharia law, in its political and legal form, is incompatible with the First Amendment, the Equal Protection Clause, and the fundamental rights of women and children. No foreign legal system — religious or otherwise — supersedes the Constitution of the United States. As your State Representative, I will oppose any effort to allow foreign legal codes to govern disputes, influence public institutions, or erode the constitutional rights of Washington residents. Every person in LD-41 — regardless of faith, background, or origin — deserves the full protection of American law. One nation. One Constitution. No exceptions.
Join Elle's campaign and help bring these priorities to Olympia.

pages.title: About - Re-Elect My-Linh Thai
paragraphs: State Representative My-Linh Thai (D, LD 41, Position 2) is a former Bellevue School District President, a healthcare professional, and an award-winning PTSA parent who is committed to improving education, opportunity, and quality of life for all Washingtonians.

My-Linh Thai is the first refugee elected to serve in the Washington State House of Representatives. She immigrated to Washington state at the age of 15 with her family as a Vietnamese refugee. After graduating from the University of Washington School of Pharmacy, she worked as a King County patient health advocate and medical interpreter. My-Linh and her husband Don built a successful pediatric neurology practice in Casper, Wyoming from the ground up. She later worked as a practicing pharmacist and co-taught Vietnam’s first nursing graduate program. She has lived in the district with her family for over a decade. Her two children have recently graduated college and her husband, Don, is a neurologist at Valley Medical Center.

In her role as Director and Board President of Bellevue Schools, My-Linh utilized her skills in listening, consensus-building, and goal achievement to ensure all children could reach their full potential. She prioritized parent and community engagement, established rigorous curricula, aimed to close the Opportunity Gap, and improved services for students with special needs. My-Linh also served as Vice President of the Washington State School Board Directors Association. On the Association’s Legislative and Equity Committees, she championed statewide education investments and reforms for equitable access to educational opportunities.
As State Representative, My-Linh has championed and sponsored legislation to:
Guarantee access to quality local schools, prioritize food access and stability for students
Expand abortion rights focus to include people of all genders
Establish state level civil cause of action (accountability) for unlawful use of force by law enforcement
Protect renters from landlords unjustly withholding their security deposits
Ensure that courts are accessible for all regardless of immigration status
Require clinical trials to adopt a policy of recruiting participants from underrepresented demographics to widen the lived experiences of participants
Recognize Lunar New Year as a legislative holiday in Washington State
Notably, she was the prime sponsor of the Working Families Tax Exemption, a tax refund that puts money back into the pockets of Washington families who need it most.

pages.title: Financial Responsibility & Accountability | Michael Rosen for WA
paragraphs: Financial Responsibility & Accountability
The money is here. What is missing is the discipline to manage it, protect it, and prove to taxpayers that every dollar is being spent wisely.
Even Democratic leaders are sounding the alarm.
This isn't a partisan argument. The people raising it are the ones who have run Olympia for years.
Former Governor Christine Gregoire (D): “We don't really have an income problem, we have a spending problem.”
Former Governor Gary Locke (D): Olympia “simply needs budget discipline” — and hasn't shown it in years.
State Treasurer Mike Pellicciotti (D): calls it a “check engine light” moment for our finances.
When leaders from the party in charge are the ones warning about the spending, it's time to listen.
Washington has a strong economy, productive industries, and the capacity to generate revenue over time.
Dead last in the country for keeping enough cash on hand to pay bills and balance the budget right now.
U.S. News Best States, 2026. Washington's only last-place ranking among the report's 71 measures.

Washington is a great place to headquarter a company and a punishing place to operate one. Employers are facing rising costs, and nearly one in four said in a spring 2026 survey that they were considering moving out of state.

Strong economic fundamentals do not excuse weak stewardship. When spending rises faster than revenue and job creators are treated as a bottomless source of new money, the result is predictable: less investment, fewer opportunities, and higher costs for families.
A budget that grows by raiding its own safeguards

Over the last decade, Washington's budget more than doubled—from roughly $30 billion to more than $80 billion. Instead of controlling spending, Olympia has repeatedly used money dedicated to one purpose to cover another.
Withdrawn from the fund that protects Washington during the next downturn, leaving reserves among the lowest in the country.
Pulled from a surplus built through decades of disciplined stewardship. Retiree benefits are not cut, but the cushion was used for current spending.
Swept away from accounts created for climate and environmental work and redirected to general uses.
Redirected from local roads, water, and sewer projects to day-to-day operations.
Moved from capital projects into operating expenses instead of building for Washington's future.
Capital-gains revenue intended by law for school construction was redirected to operations.

Dedicated funds are protected by ordinary statute, not the state constitution. That means the same majority that makes a promise can break it with a simple budget vote. A promise is only as good as the next vote.

In April 2026, two of the three major credit-rating agencies placed Washington on a formal negative outlook. Moody's pointed to spending outpacing revenue year after year despite solid economic and revenue conditions.
A downgrade could cost taxpayers an estimated $60 million a year in higher borrowing costs—money that should help families, not pay interest.
We pay to find waste. Fixing it should not be optional.

Voters created an independent performance-audit program to identify savings in state government. Olympia has swept money from the very fund created to fund those audits, and lawmakers are only required to consider the findings—not act on them.
Financial responsibility is not complicated.
It is the same discipline families and businesses already practice every day.
Do not create permanent spending commitments that cannot be sustainably funded. Families and businesses have to make tradeoffs; Olympia should too.
When the state auditor identifies waste or inefficiency, Olympia should formally respond: implement the recommendation, modify it, or reject it publicly with a reason.
Money set aside for reserves, pensions, schools, and public works should be used for those purposes—not treated as a plug for unrelated budget holes.
Restore the cushion that protects families from the next recession, so the next downturn does not become the next round of tax increases.
Before Olympia asks for more, it should prove it is spending what you already gave wisely.
Washington is not a revenue problem. It is a responsibility problem. When we genuinely cannot afford something, Michael will vote no.

I believe that stable, affordable housing is essential for healthy communities. I led efforts to provide $770 million in new funding for housing. pages.title: About — Jamie Pedersen for Re-election
paragraphs: Democratic Senator Jamie Pedersen serves as the Senate Majority Leader, the highest ranking Democrat in the State Senate.

The son of two teachers, Jamie worked his way through college at McDonald's before attending law school. An activist and advocate for marriage equality and LGBTQ+ civil rights before joining the legislature, he led the successful six-year effort to win marriage equality in the legislature, making Washington State one of the first states in the nation to have full marriage rights for same-sex couples.

As the most progressive Senate leader in Washington's history, Pedersen secured historic investments in public schools, affordable housing, transportation, and paid family medical leave. He led passage of stronger prohibitions against police misconduct, life-saving gun violence prevention measures, and significant climate action to reduce emissions and lower energy costs.

This year, Jamie led the legislature to pass Washington's Millionaires Tax that applies to household incomes above $1 million per year to support public schools, health care, human services, and higher education, and make the tax code fairer. It will also eliminate sales tax on personal care products, diapers, and over-the-counter medicine, provide free school breakfast and lunch to all public-school students, expand eligibility for the Working Families Tax Credit to 460,000 additional households, and help small businesses.

Jamie’s also made sure our state stood up against Trump’s brutality and attacks on our democracy. Under Jamie’s leadership, the legislature protected abortion rights and women's healthcare with historic investments in Planned Parenthood across the state so everyone could get the healthcare access they need, protected sensitive voter information, banned ICE agents and law enforcement from hiding their identities behind masks, stopped the use of cameras for surveillance and immigration enforcement, and banned local law enforcement from sharing data from FLOCK cameras with ICE officials and the Trump Administration, one of the first states to do so.

paragraphs: Reducing rent and putting homeownership within reach by…
Ending apartment bans statewide and ensuring more housing can be built everywhere, especially near transit centers.
Cutting bureaucratic red tape that slows housing development, including lengthy permitting processes and outdated requirements that make housing outrageously expensive to build.
Investing in social housing developers at the local level, which are innovative models for more self-sustaining and publicly-funded affordable housing development.
Winning transformative safety net programs like universal childcare by…
Expanding our Paid Parental Leave program by providing at least full-time minimum-wage compensation to every new parent.
Building a universal pre-K program statewide and establishing a flexible home-care cash benefit for families seeking care for 2- and 3-year-olds.
Restoring enrollment in Washington’s Working Connections Childcare program, which provides access to affordable childcare for tens of thousands of low-income families.
Preventing school closures, improving student outcomes, and investing in our youth by...
Reducing barriers and requirements to approve bonds for local school districts that support new facilities and repair aging, dilapidated classrooms.

Undoing recently passed tax cuts for ultra-wealthy people that reduce funding for the education legacy trust fund, which includes critical resources for K-12 education, childcare, class size reductions, and support for teachers.
Increasing pay, workplace standards, and safety for paraeducators and teachers that provide high-quality care for our kids but currently receive sub-living wages.
Protecting immigrant and trans communities’ right to safety, opportunity, and freedom by…
Regulating and restricting the use of AI and surveillance by law enforcement, including the expansion of data centers that drive up utility costs and impact our environment.

Taxing the ultra-wealthy corporations in our state to right our broken tax code and invest in the services we need by…

Ending tax loopholes for corporations and undoing recently-passed tax cuts for the ultra-wealthy.

Funding the new caseload standards for public defenders mandated by the Washington Supreme Court, which both protect people’s civil rights and, if left unaddressed, will lead to cases being dismissed and potentially dangerous individuals on our streets.
Investing in community-based programs that mentor youth, provide alternatives to incarceration, and are proven to reduce gun violence in our neighborhoods.
Establishing programs that send social workers and mental health professionals to non-violent emergency calls.
