What a beautiful celebration of Recovery, Perseverance, Achievement, and Hope. I was honored to attend the most recent graduation ceremony for participants in the King County Drug Court graduation. What I witnessed was more than a ceremony. It was an entire community coming together to rescue and rebuild lives. Judges, court staff, health care professionals, law enforcement, families, and peers all working together to create new beginnings and new leases on life. As one mother tearfully told her son, “you’ve been blessed with a crown of beauty instead of ashes.” I also attended part of the Seattle Police Department’s “Before the Badge” Program and saw how new recruits were introduced to the Drug Court program. They met with the Drug Court Judge and professional staff, including peers who themselves are graduates and in recovery, to learn about the policies, best practices, and behavioral science that make the program so effective. As a police veteran explained to the recruits, it’s one of the few areas where police officers get to see how their work is changing lives. I am so grateful to see how the Drug Court and BTB programs are both working to save and rebuild lives. ... See More See Less

It’s been 25 years since the horrific terror attacks changed our world. Back then I was working in Washington, D.C. and on that morning was part of a national tribal leaders summit in downtown D.C. when the attacks happened. There was such a suffocating sense of dread as hundreds of us gathered around the Hyatt hotel’s coffee shop TV to watch what was happening live in NY and DC. But then, even through the panic there was also a growing sense of calmness and determination to make sure we all would be OK. I remember that night feeling so amazed at how ￼everyone joined together in spirit that day: there was unity, pride, love and compassion. Our nation’s resolve was put to the test, and we passed the test with flying colors. That is the America I love and still love. ... See More See Less

pages.title: Ted Cooke - Home
paragraphs: Government has been overreaching in taxation, regulation, and mandates. It has failed in areas like the economy, education, election security, road maintenance, and allowing the police to do their jobs. The other party did this. I want to fix it. -Ted Cooke ​

pages.title: Priorities - Ted Cooke
paragraphs: Stop mandates and over-regulation on businesses.
Lower gasoline prices by lowering or eliminating the states' nearly 50 cents per gallon gasoline tax.
Improve transportation by realigning DOT spending to match up with the types of transportation people choose to use, not what DOT wants people to use.
Help fill store shelves by removing blockages to the economy- No quarantine, lockdown nor masking of the healthy, there should be medical right to refuse, and no vax mandates.
Lower energy costs by ending cap and trade.
Stop making it more rewarding to stay home than work.
Parents should always have oversight of children and education.
Schools should not define by skin color, present sexually encouraging material nor seek to replace parents’ values.
Make all current school curricula publicly available online for review by parents.
Schools should proficiently teach reading, writing, arithmetic, objective sciences, and American civics.
Implement cost-effective shelters which are sober, sanitary, have public safety and offer job counseling.
Fix and expand state mental health services.
Ease the Growth Management Act, streamline permitting & inspection, lower excise and B&O taxes and eliminate the capital gains tax to encourage building affordable new houses.
Your vote should be as secure as your pocket book.
Ballots should be stored according to precinct.
Tabulation machines should be domestically manufactured and tamper-proof.
Require full independent audits, and represent both major parties in elections staffing at all levels.
Return the option of in-person voting with ID check to protect everyone's vote.
When you call 911, the police should show up and be allowed enforce the law.
Allow police to act on reasonable suspicion once again, not be held to the unworkable standard of probable cause.
Stop putting police in peril for doing their jobs- No individuals on police use of force review boards who have shown anti-police bias.
The law should be universal and applied the same to everyone.

pages.title: Vandana Slatter for State Senate
paragraphs: State Senator Vandana Slatter (D, 48th District) is a former Bellevue City Councilmember, community leader, public school parent, and biotech and healthcare professional.

A Doctor of Pharmacy (UW), Vandana worked for over twenty years at leading biotechnology companies, including Amgen and Genentech, bringing multiple parties together, making sense of complex information, and achieving safe and efficient solutions to best serve patients. She is a licensed pharmacist in the State of Washington.
Working Hard for the 48th Every Day. Learn more about Vandana’s Accomplishments
Endorsed by Leaders across Washington Read Vandana’s List of Endorsements

pages.title: Priorities – Vandana Slatter for State Senate
paragraphs: Education is the cornerstone of opportunity. Pursuing higher education should unlock opportunity, not come with a debt sentence or financial hardship. Families across the state face rising costs from daycare to college while many students skip meals just to make ends meet. Vandana has worked alongside OSPI and local school districts to craft funding models that meet diverse needs across the state.
Equitable funding K–12 public schools with equitable, statewide resources
Investing in mental health supports, inclusive curriculum, and teacher pay
Uplifting career-connected learning and apprenticeships
Expanding access to early learning and special education services

Healthcare is a human right. Healthcare access is under threat—Medicaid and Medicare cuts loom, and too many families forgo necessary care to remain financially stable. If federal programs shrink or insurance costs rise, millions could lose coverage, especially vulnerable populations. Protecting healthcare access to all is our duty as public servants, and Vandana brings her background as a clinical pharmacist and public health professional to shape policy that puts people first. As the only licensed healthcare professional in the Senate, she is committed to protecting and fighting for healthcare for all. She has championed mental and behavioral health access, rural nursing workforce programs, reproductive freedom, and culturally competent care particularly for underserved communities.
Health data privacy and consumer protections
Expansion of maternal care and the behavioral health workforce
Increased access to telehealth and community-based care

Everyone deserves a safe, stable place to call home. Housing costs continue to spike, pushing seniors and families out of their communities. Every Washingtonian deserves the dignity of aging in place and the stability of a permanent home near transit and jobs. Vandana is leading with urgency and compassion to increase affordable housing near jobs, transit, and schools while ensuring we don’t leave behind low-income and working families.
State investments in permanent supportive housing and emergency shelters
Data-informed anti-displacement tools and rental stabilization policies
Early, transparent community engagement around new housing developments
Smart planning to allow for growth while protecting the character of our communities

True public safety comes from mutual trust, respect, accountability, and prevention. In many marginalized neighborhoods, the lack of crisis response and consistent support undermines both trust and safety. Vandana has worked closely with law enforcement, community leaders, and public health professionals to advance policies that prioritize safety, healing, justice, and equity. She has helped provide resources for law enforcement and community safety—while ensuring local jurisdictions have the flexibility to respond with the tools they need. With organizations like the Alliance for Gun Responsibility backing her, it’s clear Vandana is committed to a thoughtful, community-centered approach to public safety.
Violence prevention and behavioral health crisis response
Strengthening mutual trust and respect between law enforcement and the communities they serve
Advancing accountability, transparency, and collaboration in public safety
Centering impacted communities in public safety policy
Resources for community-based and locally driven public safety programs
Support for law enforcement and first responders with the resources and training they need

Climate action is urgent—and it must be equitable. As we fight to reduce emissions, expand clean energy, and protect our natural resources, we must also ensure that no community is left behind. The reality is that air and water pollution, extreme heat, and climate-related disasters hit low-income and historically marginalized communities first and worst. Our climate economy is also at risk. Without strong investment in clean water systems, climate resilience, and green job creation, we risk leaving entire communities without the tools to thrive. Vandana has championed bold climate policies—from emissions reductions and clean transportation to protections for environmental health.
Environmental health protections in historically overburdened communities
Clean transportation and equitable transit access
Urban forestry, green infrastructure, and climate resilience planning
A just transition to clean energy and good, green jobs

As an immigrant and long-time advocate for inclusive communities, Vandana is committed to ensuring Washington is a place where everyone, regardless of immigration status, can feel safe, respected, and able to thrive. A thriving Washington depends on protecting immigrant safety, mobility, and participation.
Legal aid, healthcare, and education access for undocumented Washingtonians
Protections against workplace exploitation and discrimination
Leadership pathways for immigrant youth and communities
Washington as a safe haven for asylum seekers and immigrant families

pages.title: Accomplishments – Vandana Slatter for State Senate
paragraphs: Vandana’s work in the Legislature has focused on access to postsecondary education, affordability of housing and healthcare, efforts to address climate change, equitable transportation access, women’s reproductive health, health data privacy, pathways to success for youth and workers, science and technology policy, and economic development.

Viewing issues through the lens of a scientist and healthcare professional, Vandana brings an evidence-based approach to legislating, with an eye toward the future and a focus on growing equity and ensuring representation for all.

Vandana is the founder and Co-Chair of the Science, Technology and Innovation Caucus. She also serves as the Chair, Postsecondary Education and Workforce Committee and sits on the Appropriations Committee and the Environment & Energy Committee.

Expanding Healthcare Access and Lowering Healthcare Costs : Using her decades of experience in the healthcare field, Vandana authored legislation creating the Washington Health Corps, working to connect medical professionals to underserved communities in need of support, while also offering loan repayment assistance for healthcare workers who serve. A strong advocate for expanded telemedicine programs – she also successfully worked to improve telemedicine services for children’s mental health and grow the telebehavioral health video call center.

Vandana supported Washington’s first-in-the-nation Public Option , groundbreaking Long Term Care Act , and best-in-the-nation Paid Family and Medical Leave program , along with authorizing $200 million to address the coronavirus pandemic .

Fighting for a Healthy Environment: Named Washington Conservation Voters’ 2020 Legislator of the Year, Vandana is deeply committed to conserving our environment and taking on climate change. As a scientist with a deep understanding of the threat of climate change, Vandana championed one of the most important environmental bills of the 2020 session – aligning Washington’s emission reduction goals with the latest climate science. She also supported Washington’s landmark 100% Clean Energy Bill , clean building standards , a ban on hydrofluorocarbons , new funding for pollution clean up and to hold big polluters accountable , and laws to reduce and eliminate toxic chemicals .

Improving Jobs and Outcomes in a Changing Economy: With new challenges stemming from automation, a changing economy, and COVID-19 recovery, Vandana has focused on innovating and expanding workforce education and Future of Work initiatives. Vandana was a leader in enacting Career Connect Washington , which will help match students with rewarding and stable careers in a changing economy. This session, she passed a law mandating collection of critical workforce data – which will be necessary for COVID-19 economic recovery efforts. While Vandana has served as a legislator, Washington has consistently been ranked one of the best states in America for workers and for businesses .

Ensuring a Great Education for All Kids : Washington’s STEM Legislator of the Year , Vandana has been a tireless advocate for Washington’s K-12 and higher education students. She has supported robust investment in schools, teachers, and special education, and worked to ensure all students have access to innovative engineering, science, and robotics programs. A strong advocate for equity in education, she championed a law to increase accessibility of college transcripts, improving student’s ability to pursue new jobs and further education .

Vandana played a key role in passing Washington’s landmark free and reduced college tuition bill , making higher education affordable for all students, paid for progressively by large businesses. She also passed legislation promoting girls athletics and supporting sports for girls with disabilities.

pages.title: Meet Vandana – Vandana Slatter for State Senate
paragraphs: Washington State Senator Vandana Slatter (D, 48th District) currently serves as the Vice Chair of the Senate Environment, Energy & Technology Committee and is a member of the Health & Long-Term Care and Higher Education & Workforce Development Committees. Previously she served four terms in the State House and was chair of the House Post Secondary Education and Workforce (PEW) committee. She is a former Bellevue City Councilmember, community leader, public school parent, and a biotech and healthcare professional.

A Doctor of Pharmacy (UW), Vandana worked for twenty years at leading biotechnology companies, including Amgen and Genentech, bringing multiple parties together, making sense of complex information, and achieving safe and efficacious solutions to best serve patients. She is a licensed pharmacist in the State of Washington.

While obtaining her Master’s degree in Public Administration (MPA) from the University of Washington, Vandana served as an intern to U.S. Senator Maria Cantwell. She was appointed to a 4-year term on the Washington State Board of Pharmacy by Governor Christine Gregoire in 2007 and also served on the Foundation Board of NARAL Pro-Choice Washington.

In 2009, Vandana traveled with the Center for Women and Democracy (CWD) to Morocco, and in 2015, to Iceland as part of the organization’s mission to advance women’s leadership locally, nationally and globally. Since then, she has traveled to Washington DC, China, Belgium, Denmark, and Germany with delegations of NW political and business leaders.

On the Advisory Boards of local non-profits, Global Social Business Partners (GSBP) and Farmer Frog, she helped establish a Lake Hills Greenbelt urban farm, where healthy organic produce is provided to low-income households. In 2014, Vandana completed the first ever City of Bellevue Community Emergency Response Team (CERT) training course.

Vandana serves on the Ruckelshaus Center Advisory Board, the UW Evans School Dean’s Advisory Council, and the Hopelink Foundation Board of Directors. In the past she has served on the Overlake Hospital Foundation’s Board of Trustees and is a past board member of NARAL Pro-Choice Washington and the Children’s Institute for Learning Differences, a school serving children with special needs.
Vandana reflects on the importance of representation and being the first Indian-American elected to the Washington State House of Representatives.

Elected as a Bellevue City Councilmember in 2015, she served on multiple committees, helped pass a $1.5B city budget, and worked on issues including affordable housing, technology & innovation, public safety, and transportation.

Vandana was appointed in 2017 to be State House Representative #1 for the 48th Legislative District. Over her 4 terms as a State Representative she has sponsored and passed first in the nation legislation to help protect the privacy of sensitive health care data, set statewide greenhouse gas emissions targets, and secure funding for higher education for low income students. Her legislative efforts have helped homeless youth access government services, improved collection of educational data, and created a tax exemption for low-income housing. She also sponsored legislation to reduce Washington’s greenhouse gas emissions, and develop regional air travel through electric or hybrid-electric aircraft.

Vandana is co-chair of the House Science, Innovation and Technology (ScItech) Caucus, a member of the Members of Color Caucus (MOCC), and a member of the National Conference of State Legislators (NCSL) higher education task force and energy security working group.

Vandana immigrated to the US from Canada in 1988, and is a naturalized US citizen. She is a graduate of the University of British Columbia (B.Sc. Pharmaceutical Sciences). At UBC, she earned a varsity athletic letter in the sport of fencing, was captain of the UBC women’s varsity fencing team, and a gold medalist at the BC Junior Women’s foil championships.
Vandana and her family have lived in Northeast Bellevue since 2003. Her husband Greg is a research scientist.

pages.title: Elect Osman Salahuddin for State Rep
paragraphs: *If you've saved your information with ActBlue Express, your donation will go through immediately.
Committed to Community. Dedicated to Progress.

Like many in our community, I’ve navigated life as a renter, a user of public transit, and a graduate of our public education system in the Lake Washington School District.
I’ve brought new leadership and fresh ideas to the Legislature , and I am proud to represent the 48th Legislative District.
I am deeply committed to my community and to making ethical, equitable decisions that will help our district and the entire state thrive.”
“As your State Representative, I worked with my colleagues in the Legislature to advance policies that reflect our shared values, and I remain committed to working alongside you.”
We simply need more housing. Long-time residents are not able to remain in their homes while young families, working people, and new residents can’t attain affordable housing.

Having attended public schools, I know the strength of our community requires investing in our next generation. With my mother dedicating 20 years as a preschool paraeducator, I will always advocate for support for our teachers and staff.
In my healthcare experience, I’ve seen the struggles that folks face in dealing with unexpected physical & behavioral health crises. Healthcare is a human right, and I will fight for access.

Creating a safe community means ensuring a comprehensive community response that aligns with that of our first responders. It also means prioritizing prevention. Having served as a volunteer Fire Corp member, I know this requires key actions

We live in one of the most beautiful states in the country, and it’s up to us to fight climate change and protect our environment. This will involve a strong focus on a just transition to clean energy while we prioritize environmental justice in our reduction of carbon emissions.

As the child of an immigrant small-business owner, I’ve seen my dad navigating the complexities of the system just like so many others in the community. My mom is also a union-represented para-educator, and I will advocate for small businesses and workers alike.
Rep. Osman Salahuddin currently represents the 48th Legislative District .

A Redmond native and proud son of immigrants —a special education teacher and small business owner—he earned a B.S. in neurobiology from the University of Washington, where he served as Student Body President.
Before being elected, Osman worked as a researcher at Fred Hutch Cancer Research Center and UW Medicine.
He has served his community on the Redmond City Council , worked for the King County Council, and contributed to non-profit boards like the Transportation Choices Coalition.
Washington's 48th Legislative District is one of forty-nine districts in Washington state for representation in the state legislature.

It covers areas of Redmond, Bellevue (including West Lake Sammamish), and Kirkland, and it encompasses Clyde Hill, Yarrow Point, Hunts Point, and Medina. It also contains Bridle Trails State Park and Marymoor Park.
Interested in getting involved with Osman’s campaign for State House, want updates, or just have a question?
Feel free to reach out to Osman and the team! We’ll get back to you as soon as we can.

pages.title: Priorities — Elect Osman Salahuddin for State Rep
paragraphs: We simply need more housing. Long-time residents are not able to remain in their homes while young families, working people, and new residents can’t attain affordable housing. We need to ensure expedited permitting and expansion of missing middle awareness opportunities. We must also make stronger investments in affordable housing, permanent supportive housing and emergency housing.

Having attended local public schools in the Lake Washington School District, I know the strength of our community requires investing in our next generation. With my mother dedicating 20 years as a preschool paraeducator, I will always advocate for support for our teachers and staff. This includes building on the support for special education and materials for teachers to work effectively. I will also advocate for expanded workforce development opportunities and apprenticeship programs.
Public Safety and Gun Violence Prevention

Creating a safe community means ensuring a comprehensive community response that aligns with that of our first responders. It also means prioritizing prevention. Having served as a volunteer Fire Corp member, I know this requires key actions. I will prioritize investing in first responder resources and technology, such as body-worn cameras (for more transparency) and opioid detectors, and training & support, including mental health training. I will also advocate for programs that support survivors along with investing in youth intervention strategies to tackle behavioral health & substance use.

As the child of an immigrant small-business owner, I’ve seen my dad navigating the complexities of the system just like so many others in the community. My mom is also a union-represented paraeducator, and I will advocate for small businesses and workers alike through increased access to capital, microloan, training and incubation programs for entrepreneurs and support for streamlined processes for permits and licenses for small businesses. We must also work with local corporations leading in technology, biotech, and aerospace to expand small business partnerships and increased workforce development via Career Connect WA. Finally, I will support unions in the fight for worker rights and wages.

We live in one of the most beautiful states in the country, and it’s up to us to fight climate change and protect our environment. This will involve a strong focus on a just transition to clean energy while we prioritize environmental justice in our reduction of carbon emissions. I will promote a focus on environmental justice to directly support clean energy transition for disproportionately served residents, particularly in BIPOC and lower-income communities. I will also place an emphasis on environmental protections for our forests, waterways, and open space, especially as we see dramatic shifts in climate and severe weather, such as wildfires.

pages.title: About — Elect Osman Salahuddin for State Rep
paragraphs: Osman is currently a State Representative for the 48th Legislative District, representing the parts of Bellevue, Redmond, Kirkland, and all of Clyde Hill, Medina, Yarrow Point, and Hunts Point.
He was raised in Redmond, where he has spent nearly his entire life. He completed his K-12 education in the Lake Washington School District public schools.

His drive to serve his community is rooted in his parents’ journey immigrating to the United States in hopes of living out the American Dream. They taught him the importance of pursuing your dreams while inspiring and supporting others to do the same.

His mother has dedicated 20 years as a union-represented special education preschool paraeducator, while his father is a 35+ year small business owner. When hate surged during Trump’s first term, Osman was inspired by his parents’ resilience to stand up for the values that protect everyone.

After graduating from local public schools in the 48th LD, Osman attended the University of Washington, where he graduated with a BS in neurobiology while serving in his first foray in elected office as Student Body President.
He represented over 45,000 students, and led on student issues like equity, international student health insurance, and affordable housing.
Before being elected, Osman worked as a researcher at Fred Hutch Cancer Research Center as well as the UW Medical Center in the Emergency Department.

He has served his community on the Redmond City Council , worked for the King County Council , and contributed to non-profit boards and committees, including the Transportation Choices Coalition Board, LWSD Career and Technical Education Committee, and Asian Pacific Islander Americans for Civic Empowerment Board.

Osman found his passion to be the health of entire communities, and was elected with over 70% of the vote to serve as a City Councilmember in his hometown of Redmond, where he chairs the Public Safety & Human Services Committee and serves on the Eastside Transportation Partnership Committee among others.
He is a strong youth advocate, serving as Advisor for the WA High School Democrats, hosting annual Young Leaders Summits, and having a Youth Board focused on policy creation

pages.title: Jeff Poppe for State Representative — 48th LD
paragraphs: Jeff Poppe is a retired independent CPA and financial consultant with 40 years of experience. He audited a billion-dollar bank fraud for the FDIC, conducted audits for the Los Angeles County Grand Jury, and consulted on financial systems with five Fortune 500 companies, the federal government, the State of California, and California's largest counties. He has also owned and operated a Greek restaurant.

A Christian and devoted family man, Jeff has been married for 48 years and is the father of three children and two adopted adults, with four grandchildren. He has called the 48th Legislative District home for 16 years.
Now Jeff is running for State Representative to bring real financial responsibility, transparency, and accountability to Olympia.
40 Years as a CPA & financial consultant
BS, University of Cincinnati — magna cum laude
MBA in Finance, San Diego State University
Post-graduate instructor of Accounting Information Systems
Director, San Diego Taxpayers Association
Led his church's donation program for the homeless
Washington has a spending problem, not an income problem. My opponent voted for six new taxes — I will reject any new or unnecessary ones.
I will spearhead fraud audits to stop the squandering of your money and push to make our government truly effective and efficient.
My opponent took 72% of his campaign money from PACs and unions. I will accept only individual contributions and work hard for you.
I will make state spending and performance metrics open and transparent, so you can see exactly where your tax dollars go.
Jeff has earned the backing of Republican leaders across the 48th District and King County.
There are three easy ways to help Jeff win on November 3, 2026.
Every dollar fuels door-knocking, mailers, and field staff. Chip in any amount.
Knock doors, make calls, host a meet-and-greet — every hour matters.
Get campaign updates, event invites, and ways to help — straight to your inbox.

pages.title: Jessica Forsythe for WA State House of Representatives
paragraphs: "I am excited to take this next step in my public service journey and run for the Washington State House of Representatives in a people-powered campaign."

Jessica Forsythe is a small business owner, proud union member, and former Executive Director of Emerge WA, a non-profit that focuses on uplifting women and non-binary future leaders. With a Bachelor of Fine Arts from Kent State University, Forsythe has a diverse background in environmental graphic design, non-profit arts, and politics.

No stranger to volunteerism, Jessica entered the pro-democracy space in 2016 through joining the boards of the League of Women Voters and the 48th Legislative District Democrats. She also volunteered her creative skills on numerous voting rights initiatives and King County’s Access for All.

Jessica was elected to the Redmond City Council in 2019 and served as the Council President in her first term. As a Councilmember she has served on numerous regional committees, passed multiple $1B budgets, proposed policy that became state law, and worked on issues including affordable housing, climate change, public safety, transportation, and infrastructure. She is incredibly proud of the many accomplishments the City Council achieved together.

Being elected as the world entered a global pandemic meant facing unprecedented challenges and that the government had to make tough decisions, be more collaborative and nimble. This made Jessica a stronger and more resilient leader and advocate. It also provided her with the experience and a solid foundation that she looks forward to taking to Olympia as we face a whole new set of complex challenges.

Prior to entering the political arena, Jessica has been an award-winning creative director and small business owner. Her work has ranged from LEED-certified mixed-use architecture projects — like the ones popping up across our district — to establishing the brand for the Seattle Symphony’s Grammy Award-winning record label. Her background as a creative thinker means taking a holistic approach to every problem and putting people at the forefront of all decisions. Jessica brings this kind of design-thinking to the legislature.

Inspired by her Baba’s (grandmother) stories of being a Riveter, her Papa’s (grandfather) fight against fascism serving WWII, and her upbringing centered on volunteering, curiosity, and continual learning, Jessica honors her family's legacy through her work and commitment to public service.

It’s imperative that we take steps today to secure a healthy environment for future generations. Between the bomb cyclone and catastrophic flooding, we’re seeing the direct impacts of climate change right now. We need policy focused on tangible large and small scale actions that can be taken at all levels. In my first few months as a Councilmember, I co-wrote the city’s Climate Emergency Declaration and shaped our Environmental Sustainability Action Plan that serves as the roadmap to an environmentally sustainable community and achieve net zero carbon emissions. I will bring the insights needed to shift the conversations on climate change legislation from the price tag of immediate costs to the price we are already paying.

Everyone deserves to have housing where they feel stable and connected. I’ve heard from families and working people in our district who struggle with remaining in their homes or finding affordable housing. These are people who serve and have deep roots in our community. We need more housing options that provide affordable housing at all levels of affordability so that they can remain a part of the community they call home. As a Redmond City Councilmember, I have advocated for increased levels of deeply affordable housing and renter protections, and I will continue that fight in Olympia.
Investment in Education & Future Generations

Investment in education is an investment in the long-term prosperity of our district. Washington ranks 40th in the Nation for investment in K–12 education as a percentage of our State's Total Economy. With a properly adjusted funding plan we could have avoided staff cuts, school closures, and service reductions. We must actively seek sustainable and equitable funding models that fully-fund education and reduce reliance on local levies to address the growing inequities. I will continue to advocate for sustainable and equitable funding for K-12 schools, expansion of access to early learning and special education, and an deeper investments in career-connected and post-secondary programs.

A healthy community is a thriving community. Far-reaching actions at the Federal level are having direct impacts on our daily lives. As a state, we must safeguard reproductive rights, expand mental, behavioral, and disability services and ensure that we respond with evidence-based practices. I am committed to ensuring that every Washingtonian has the opportunity to live a healthy life, regardless of income, identity, or circumstance.

No one is above the law. In order for our government to work for the people, everyone’s voice must be considered — especially those less frequently heard. We must examine issues from all perspectives and develop thoughtful, inclusive solutions that ask whose voices are not being represented and why. My experience in design-thinking framework has guided my work in office and will continue to inform my commitment for responsive solutions. I will continue being a voice fighting to maintain your constitutional and civil rights.

Small businesses provide ingenuity and opportunity while playing a critical role in our vibrant and healthy economy. Too many of our small and local businesses are being squeezed out and over burdened. As a small business owner and union member, I’ve worked closely to understand the complexities of these issues and advocate for increased small business support in the form of financial support programs, rent relief, and employee stability. I will continue to lead with curiosity and fight for solutions that uplift economic opportunities for all.
Yes! I'd like to donate to help elect Jessica as State Rep!
Your donation will go a long way to support Jessica's campaign for WA State Representative! Thank you so much for your support our vision for LD48!
Thank you for contacting the Friends of Forsythe campaign.
We will get back to you as soon as possible.

pages.title: AMY WALEN FOR STATE HOUSE
paragraphs: Rep. Amy Walen was ranked the most effective Democrat in the Washington House of Representatives for the 2023-2024 session by the Center for Effective Lawmaking, with a score of 2.70.
She introduced 42 bills, 34 of which received action in committee, and 11 became law!
Your voice matters. Join me in creating the community we all deserve.

Our families are feeling pinched with increased housing prices, the lingering effects of Trump Tariffs, increased gas prices due to Trump’s adventures in the Middle East and inflation that continues to hit working families.

In Olympia, I have fought predatory loan sharks, passed trailblazing legislation to increase housing supply and lower costs, and demanded tax relief for our most vulnerable. My affordability agenda includes tax relief to the working class and small businesses, increased investments in housing, and pushing for quality childcare and early education through state funding and reform.

There is an “arc” of housing for all of the people of our state as I see it, and that starts with the creation of lots of units. High interest rates and development costs mean we need to repurpose existing buildings to create housing for families, and we need to do everything we can to ensure we have a competitive environment for home builders.

State Government has a huge role to play in managing and spurring housing growth. Housing has been one of my biggest priorities, and my work has helped turn the Seattle metropolitan area into the largest builder of affordable apartments in the country from 2020-2024.

I’ve funded many affordable housing projects in the 48th District, appropriating $2M for the Illahee Affordable Housing project in Bellevue, $260K for the New Ground Young Adult Affordable Housing project in Kirkland and $3.2M for the Redmond Supportive Housing project
In the 2026 legislative session, I was the prime sponsor of permitting and zoning reform bills that unleashed conversion of unused commercial spaces to residential units.
I also supported the passage of a bill that allowed religious organizations to build affordable housing in residential neighborhoods, and redundant obstacles to housing construction.

In the 2026 legislative session, I also voted for increased incentives and permitting reform to build dense housing near public transit corridors, like the Light Rail. Developing housing along transit corridors helps our seniors age in their home towns, letting them downsize without leaving their neighborhood. It also gives our young people the opportunity to own homes without having to own a car.

Condos are the gateway to home ownership, because they allow for individual units to be bought or rented. I will fight for the creation of a warranty system which allows condo owners to get repairs done quickly and fairly, as well as incentivizing the apartments we have built to be converted to condos.

Once we establish this reliable revenue-producing development pipeline, we can build on our successes and spread the wealth to state programs and public-private partnerships that stabilize housing for low income families, immigrants, IDD, sober, and behavioral health communities

Owning a home makes THE difference in closing the generational wealth gap. Increasing supply, lowering costs, and incentivizing condo growth will all make home ownership for young people an achievable goal rather than a pipe dream.

Our district is heavily populated by tech workers, and recent layoffs, furloughs, and buyouts at Microsoft, Amazon, Oracle, Expedia, Zillow, Meta and other tech companies, along with the rise of AI, means that we need focus on expanding the economy with an eye towards AI-resilient work, entrepreneurship, and job growth.

Throughout history, communities that responded to economic hard times with investments in their people and their communities have thrived. The innovation and entrepreneurship of the 48th District is one of our greatest strengths, and we should work with all our stakeholders, from community groups to corporations, to ensure we will be the home of the next generation of groundbreaking companies and startups. Entrepreneurship leads to innovation, venture capital investment, and high-paying jobs in our area.
In the midst of intense economic instability we have the opportunity to lead by investing in "AI-proof" jobs which require human ingenuity and craftsmanship.
Expanding our education and vocational training system is essential in the face of job displacement due to AI.

As the manager of a car dealership, I make sure our master certified technicians are always teaching new techs so that the next generation of auto technicians have a real-world foundation of skills and experience. I will fight to apply this practice as much as possible across industries in our state.
I will advocate to give tax incentives to those who train workers, and allow for Business & Occupation tax credits for money invested in training both for the trainer and the trainee.

I will fight to make sure that small businesses get the same or more opportunities for partnership and growth assistance from the state as big companies. I will ensure our grants and lending programs for small businesses continue to be robust.

I will work to institute "Business in a box" programs to facilitate entrepreneurship through the State Department of Commerce. This support would streamline licensing, bookkeeping, and tax returns, allowing innovators to innovate and service providers to provide service, rather than being bogged down by administrative tasks.

Apprenticeship, entrepreneurship, and vocational programs give our community the flexibility to adapt to changing economic conditions, and they should be an integral part of how we approach job growth, not an afterthought.
In the last session, I took the lead in demanding a progressive tax code and tax relief for working families now, rather than years down the road.

I believe in the promise of a high-earners income tax, but I am fighting to ensure that the income threshold isn’t lowered as a crutch for future budgeting shortfalls. I proposed two amendments to the state income tax passed in the 2026 legislative session:
My amendment 2596 would have changed the bill's $1 million standard deduction so that it applied per individual, rather than $1 million per household.

This amendment would have restricted the millionaire’s tax to true millionaires, rather than allowing a couple making $500,000 each to be required to pay half of their marginal income in state and federal income tax.

My Amendment 2598 would have given the majority of the projected $3.9B in revenue from the high-earners income tax back to everyday Washingtonians by reducing the state retail sales tax rate from 6.5% to 5.75%.

Since our State Supreme Court ruled against the constitutionality of a state income tax all the way back in 1933, I also proposed the passage of a state constitutional amendment authorizing a state income tax, and limiting the deduction at $1M for single earners.

These amendments would have made sure the new income tax was not open to court challenges, future expansion to middle class earners, and made our tax code more progressive, rather than just raising taxes to fill budget gaps.
I voted against the millionaire’s tax because it was unconstitutional, not progressive enough, and raised the possibility of broad middle class tax hikes in the near future.

In Olympia, I will continue to fight for a progressive income tax structure that actually relieves the tax burden for everyday people and working families—not 5 five years later pending a court challenge and ballot initiative, but in the present day, closing loopholes and righting wrongs that already exist in our code.

My top tax priority next session is reforming the Business and Occupation (corporate revenue) tax so that the industry giants that call WA and the 48th LD home pay back their fair share to the communities that help them thrive.

Our current corporate revenue tax structure allows WA-based businesses to declare their revenue in tax-haven states like Wyoming. This is unacceptable—we cannot allow corporations to benefit from our district’s highly-skilled workforce and friendly business climate without keeping them honest and spreading the wealth.
Hardworking small business owners do not have the benefit of fancy accounting and pay their Business & Occupation taxes here.

I support the replacement of the B&O tax with a corporate income tax, as we have at a federal level, which only levies taxes on profitable businesses, and allows deductions for operating costs, reducing the relative tax burden for low-margin businesses like mom-and-pop grocery, retail, or restaurants compared to the giants with billion-dollar profits.
As a small business owner, I understand the challenges of entrepreneurship, and I will fight to level the playing field and reform the corporate revenue tax code in WA.
A huge part of the gender pay gap comes from the fact that women are still the primary caregivers for children, often leaving them behind in the job market.

We can’t wait for the Federal Government to act to make progress in our state. We need action on ensuring that quality childcare and early education are plentiful throughout our state for working families to be able to thrive. This is an essential need for moms, dads, and kids.
In my next term, I will fight for comprehensive childcare reform.
My comprehensive childcare reform plan includes:
Robust state funding for childcare and tax relief for the provision of childcare services

A licensed and accredited childcare profession, with training in our technical colleges and an early career pathway to becoming a professional childcare provider in high school. So many talented young people in our state want a career helping kids, but the pathway to that career is not clear.
Business incentives for benefit plans that include childcare, for on-site childcare services, and for paying tuition for employees who want to become certified childcare providers.
Tax subsidies for tenant spaces with childcare providers, making rent for providers affordable.
The creation of a cooperative model for insurance to make insurance more affordable for childcare providers.
State Government-provided services to childcare providers to help them navigate the regulatory environment at the state, county and city level.
Minimum pay and workplace standards for workers, project labor agreements, and transparency on wages and working conditions.

These reforms will make this profession attractive to young people and will bring many retirees back to work doing what they love, which is teaching children. It’s not solely the responsibility of parents and their workplaces to support a robust childcare environment. We are all responsible for raising the next generation.
Fighting Gun Violence and Protecting Public Safety

I believe that fighting gun violence and protecting public safety are inextricable issues. That is why in my time in the legislature, I have passed an assault rifle ban, a high-capacity magazine ban, and a permit-to-purchase policy, while continuing to be endorsed by our local police departments. There is no either/or—public safety is about prevention, trust, and accountability.

I believe in a serious, realistic, and compassionate approach to public safety and gun safety that invests in well-trained, community-focused law enforcement while also expanding mental health and crisis response services.

I was lucky enough to spend much of my childhood in Australia. On a recent visit, it was remarkable and noticeable that I had a certain relief in my heart that there were no guns in the audience. People were having fun, and there were the usual concert shenanigans, but I was not concerned that a gun would be drawn and my children would be harmed.

We have more guns than people in the United States and firearm ownership is a very important part of being an American. However, rights come with responsibilities and protecting our communities is nonnegotiable.

I come from a family of hunters and fishermen and all weapons were stored safely. Young people were trained properly. Guns were treated seriously, handled carefully and were placed in safes when they were not in use.

I drafted the “safe storage” bill introduced in 2025 to require secure storage of firearms in vehicles, to address the persistent problem of firearms being stolen from vehicles, then used in crimes or intimate partner and family violence and suicide.

I passed HB 1562 in the 2023-2024 session, which adds safeguards to firearm purchases through firearm dealers. These restrictions and safeguards are appropriate as firearms are often stolen from licensed firearm dealers and also straw purchasers, or illegal conduits for those who are not qualified to own a firearm to acquire them through deception.

I will continue to fight for reasonable firearm violence prevention such as education around suicide risks, permits to purchase, and other measures so that very permanent decisions are not made in the heat of the moment.

We must have a robust mental health system and a community where we care enough about each other to pause rushed decisions so that we cannot harm ourselves or others when we are at our weakest and most vulnerable point.

Animals are an integral part of many families in our district, and I have led the way on animal welfare in Olympia for my entire time in office. I founded the “Fur Fighter” caucus, which convenes a bipartisan group of legislators to address the needs of our wildlife and companion animals and created a first-in-the-nation “Animal Welfare Plan” for Washington to roadmap statewide standards for animal welfare.
I spearheaded the passage of HB 1424, requiring that pet dealers only source from rescue operations, rather than puppy mills.
My HB 1097 prohibited the sale of cosmetics tested on animals in Washington state.

In 2027, my top priority on animal welfare is reforming pet insurance—applying the same Obamacare-mandated coverage of those with pre-existing conditions to our companion animals. These reforms will lower costs for pet-owners and protect animal welfare.
I will continue to make sure that pets, pet-owners, and animal welfare are not afterthoughts in Olympia.

Healthy communities are built on trust, dignity, and the freedom to make personal healthcare decisions. I believe those decisions belong to individuals, not the government. I’m focused on expanding access to care broadly, so that everyone in our community can get the services they need, when they need them.

I’m also committed to protecting and strengthening access to reproductive healthcare in Washington, including safeguarding the right to choose. That means ensuring people can make deeply personal decisions with the guidance of their healthcare providers, with privacy, respect, and without political interference.

We all must have the power to make our own decisions about if and when to carry a baby, to determine our own gender identity, and to express our sexuality as we wish. This freedom to express ourselves gives us the strength and resources to be a fulfilled person, to thrive and to contribute our unique selves to our communities.

Reproductive options and gender affirming care are health care, and decisions made between ourselves and our physicians are private and must be affordable, accessible, and covered by all kinds of health insurance.
State and Federal funding must be in place to secure these rights. These are human rights and must be available to every person in our communities.
Our school system has an essential role in providing comprehensive sexual health education, and all of our systems must provide a safety net to protect children from unhealthy or abusive families.
Old systems of control over women, children and vulnerable members of our community must be dismantled.

Crumbling infrastructure costs us all time and money. Every minute lost to a bridge closure, road repair, or bus shortage is time we could have spent with loved ones, working, or relaxing after a long day. We know that our roads, bridges, and transport systems can be better, and should be state of the art. I’ve passed over $4B for the construction and transit improvements in the 48th Legislative District. I will continue to fight for necessary infrastructure improvements when I return to Olympia.

This is a time to forgo our usual conservatism around local borrowing and recognize that what we build will pay dividends (and generate tax revenue) to make us globally competitive, drawing new jobs, industries, and people to our state and the 48th District. Borrow now and put people to work.
As a legislator and steward of your tax dollars, affordability also means getting our tax revenue from the right pathways, staying on budget, and holding State Government accountable when we misstep.

I’m very troubled by the recent downgrading of the credit rating of the state, and spending down of the rainy day fund, which will result in more public money being spent on interest, not on programs that help people thrive.

Recent revelations about $16 million going missing from the Regional Homelessness Authority are a striking example of funds being misspent without sufficient oversight. As chair of the House Consumer Protection & Business Committee, I'm committed to ensuring that public money does what it should—benefitting the public.

In Olympia, I will continue to insist that designated impact fees are required to ONLY go to their earmarked purposes. We cannot lose public trust by manipulating dedicated funding sources to fill gaps caused by project mismanagement. Families of the 48th District want their tax dollars to go to projects and services that help them, not administrative overhead and bloat.

Protecting our environment is essential to the health, quality of life, and future of our community. From cleaner air to preserved green spaces, these are the things that make our region a place people are proud to call home.

I’ve been working on these issues for years. I advocated for Washington’s plastic bag ban during my time on the Kirkland City Council. In Olympia, I have strongly supported efforts to transition to clean energy, reduce carbon emissions, and protect our natural resources.

In 2021, I voted for the Climate Commitment Act, which helped make Washington a national leader in environmental protections, emissions controls, and renewable energy. I firmly believe that we should weave environmental stewardship into our infrastructure and housing construction. We can and should support the environment by re-creating salmon habitat not just with culverts but with waterway and forest restoration.

In Olympia, I will fight to improve our resilience for climate-related emergencies by building out shelters for extreme cold and heat that can house families including children and companion animals. Our healthcare facilities, public buildings, libraries and schools need to be improved and modernized with energy efficiency in mind.

I continue to work to create a virtuous cycle where as much of our waste as possible is diverted and converted into compost, which can then be used in our own communities, in parks, in construction and transportation projects. We can make sure that each community is able to recycle its own energy and waste by improving compost and wastewater collection and processing.

On the House Consumer Safety Committee in Olympia, I have led the fight against high quantities of substances like sodium nitrite. Toxic chemicals and plastics are still ubiquitous in our lives. We must remain vigilant in not repeating the mistakes of history as we tolerated lead and asbestos. Dangerous chemicals in food, water, household products and cosmetics must be prohibited as a matter of urgency.

I will fight for increased transparency in who owns our utilities—some of our utilities are not community owned but rather owned by overseas pension funds or Wall Street. I will not allow utilities to pass their lobbying costs onto low income families.

I will fight to use objective criteria to locate energy facilities, rather than taking advantage of underrepresented communities. We cannot continue to place energy generation facilities in the poorest of neighborhoods, exposing already vulnerable people to more harm.

I will continue to advocate for bills that incentivize the development of hydrogen, nuclear, solar, wind and geo-thermal alternatives, working with large utilities and corporations, as well as with private citizens and innovative startups.

I am also passionate about supporting new energy initiatives like Community Solar, an opportunity to build solar and share the energy it creates. We need to expand our ability to collaborate neighbor-to-neighbor, creating connections and lowering costs.
Protecting our home, conserving our resources, and building our energy future requires bold action now.

The 48th Legislative District is a majority-minority district, and the ingenuity and work ethic of thousands of immigrants is instrumental in our communities—economically, socially, and culturally. As your representative, I will continue to stand up for immigrant rights, so that their dreams can come to fruition and to continue to make the 48th District a land of opportunity.

I was a strong supporter of the latest session’s HB 2173, which barred ICE agents from wearing face coverings while interacting with the public. I also voted to prevent ICE from entering sensitive areas like schools, hospitals, and daycares without a judicial warrant.

As prime sponsor of HB 1889, I helped immigrants use their skills to enrich our communities. My bill established that professional licenses in our state shall not require US citizenship (with a few exceptions). The bill broadly expanded licensing pathways for qualified applicants. If one can pass our testing, they can and should work and participate in our economy.
In Olympia, I will continue to fight ICE’s scare tactics, and provide resources and assistance for all the immigrant communities that make the 48th District their home.
Leveling the playing field for Public Housing Authorities:

Amy was the prime sponsor of HB 1075, which enables public housing authorities to access financing tools available to private developers. Access to capital and the costs of financing are one of the major barriers to housing development for public and private entities and this bill expands their bond and financing capacity.
Rep. Walen was also the prime sponsor of HB 1046, which cut red tape and freed public housing authorities to construct more “mixed middle” or working family housing.
Sustainable development and permitting and zoning reform:

As prime sponsor on HB 1757 and HB 1042, Amy has enabled the large-scale conversion of existing constructions into housing. Existing buildings are embedded carbon, and rather than tearing them down and filling our landfills with waste, getting in a long and costly line for permit approval and finding financing, they can be quickly modified and turned into housing for families. From churches to office parks and strip malls these bills streamline and give tax exemptions for entities that do conversions.

Rep. Walen was also prime sponsor of HB 1576, which prevents the abuse of the “historic designation” process by requiring owner consent and for a building to have to be at least 40 years old to be “historic”—except for specific exemptions in historic districts such as Pioneer Square and the International District. This bill is being used right now to develop housing that would otherwise have been blocked.

Arbitrary occupancy limits obstruct the ability of multi-generational families and students, or other cooperative housing situations, to settle in a neighborhood. As prime sponsor on HB 1054, Rep. Walen prohibited this practice for cities and counties in condos, townhomes, and retirement communities. When housing is scarce, we should get out of the way of people finding ways to affordably house themselves.

Amy has consistently supported missing middle and transit-oriented development, carrying concerns from the cities I represent and ensuring that their voices and our particular geography were allowed for.
Her work on a multi-family tax exemption program rewards communities who increase density in designated zoned areas.

In the last session, I advanced my colleague’s Representative McBride’s bill to allow religious organizations who develop dense affordable housing as long as that housing fits with the neighborhood character. I carried this charge and handed this bill (HB 1859) to my seatmate, who completed it in 2026.

As prime sponsor of HB 1094, Rep. Walen expanded the nonprofit property tax exemption exemption to cover nonprofit-like operations which benefit the public good. If the school district or a city is providing services, those should not have to pay property taxes. HB 1094 is also known as the Together Center bill.

Amy’s amendment to restore the exemption from Business & Occupation tax for nonprofits provided a vital reprieve from the Supreme Court decision that threatened to put many nonprofits out of operation.

Rep. Walen continues to support a progressive tax code that does not unduly burden working families. However, her common sense amendments to the institution of a state income tax last session—requiring a Constitutional amendment, and enacting broad-based sales tax relief to offset this new revenue source—were rejected by the State Legislature.

Passed with Rep. Walen’s support, HB 1867 prevents the Department of Revenue from requiring filing of a return by a widow or widower if the value of the family home is the only asset that makes the estate over the filing threshold of 3.076m.

Rep. Walen was a strong supporter of the Climate Commitment Act, which established a carbon emissions market in WA and set a goal of reducing emissions by 95% by 2050 under a “cap-and-invest” system. The CCA additionally mandates low-carbon fuel standards as well as community engagement with tribal communities and job retraining programs for the new clean energy workforce.

Amy was prime sponsor of HB 1033, which requires food service materials to be compostable and for waste collection companies like Recology to bring compostable food service materials to high-pressure compost facilities and out of the landfill. This is emblematic of her work on composting – there’s a virtuous cycle in waste management, where organic material generated in our communities is recycled or reused and returned to us, to be used in our parks, stormwater and transportation projects. Compost filters water and helps salmon habitat. We all have a responsibility to allow compost facilities to operate here – sending our waste to other communities is not stewardship.

Amy passed HB 1730 to prevent debt collectors from taking advantage of consumers. Collectors can no longer go after “zombie debt” that is chased many years after proof of that debt may no longer even exist.
HB 1031 strikes the right balance in the case of a stillbirth – providing that families who lose a child by stillbirth can still obtain a birth certificate in Washington state.
Amy has been the “go-to” legislator to negotiate garnishment and collection procedure updates. HB 1447 was passed to protect more debt from garnishment during and after the COVID pandemic.

Rep. Walen is an integral part of the group of legislators working on firearm policy. We have passed an assault rifle ban, a high-capacity magazine ban, and a permit-to-purchase policy. I drafted the “safe storage” bill introduced in 2025 to require secure storage of firearms in vehicles, to address the persistent problem of firearms being stolen from vehicles, then used in crimes or intimate partner and family violence and suicide.

Amy’s HB 2118 requires more of firearms dealers—to have electronic monitoring and enhanced security around doors and windows. Point of Sale personnel should be required to recognize signs of a person in distress and tools to dissuade a purchase or reporting to law enforcement if signs designated by mental health professionals are present. Guns are fast—and suicide is the most prevalent form of gun violence.

An ongoing body of work started in her first term with HB 1095—restoration of firearms rights to those with criminal or domestic violence in their background. This bill standardized processes and ensured effective notice is given to DV survivors and crime victims.
Her HB 2623 expanded the crimes for which firearms can be taken to include animal cruelty and brandishing.
Her HB 1941 reformed “active shooter drills”, making active shooter drills “age-appropriate and trauma-informed”. This work is ongoing.

Amy came from a “modern family” and has life experience in divorce, child custody, conservatorship, guardianship and child support systems. Amy serves as the legislative designee on the Child Support Work Group.
Her HB 1088 allows for more families to use arbitration in child custody proceedings- making it easier and less expensive to settle these matters.

Employers are required to report to the child support collecting agency in our state, the Department of Children and Families, as their employees are onboarded, and ongoing for their wages. Amy is working on a policy that would cover contractors and gig workers.
Rep. Walen’s HB 1262 requires employers to report lump sum bonuses so that they can be intercepted for back child support due.
Rep. Walen’s HB 1171 covers insurance settlement proceeds—insurers must report lump sum payment to DCYF.

The recommendations of the Child Support work group were carried in a bill I co- sponsored with my colleague on the work group, and was passed in 2026, updating child support payment levels and streamlining processes.

Amy founded the “Fur Fighter” caucus, which convenes a bipartisan group of legislators who meet with community and animal welfare organizations and sponsor legislation to address the needs of our wildlife and companion animals. My budget proviso for $250,000 to the Department of Agriculture created a nationwide first “Animal Welfare Plan” for Washington to roadmap this work for us.
We can and should have animal welfare standards not county by county but statewide—subsidized spay/neuter, minimum number of veterinarians by community, shelter and boarding minimum standards.
The Fur Fighter caucus began with the passage of HB 1424, addressing the import of dogs and cats raised in puppy mill settings, by requiring that pet dealers only source from rescue operations.
Rep. Walen’s HB 1097 prohibits the sale of cosmetics tested on animals in Washington state.
Amy’s pet insurance bill—prohibiting the cancellation of policies on elderly companion animals by insurance companies advanced but did not pass in the last session but will return in 2027.

As a member of the Public Safety caucus, Amy reviews legislation moving through the process, and consults with cities and counties, police and prosecutors, firefighters and fire chiefs. She ensures that every policy we pass makes our communities more safe, does not impact people of color or those historically disproportionately impacted by police misconduct, and does not create unfunded mandates on our cities and counties.

I supported all of our work on police accountability and also supported expansion of slots in the Law Enforcement Academy. We must address mass incarceration, and should start with the elderly incarcerated who are no longer a danger to our communities. Prison is no place to be undergoing treatment for cancer or dementia, or to be using hospice services.

Amy was a strong supporter of the latest session’s HB 2173, which barred ICE agents from wearing face coverings while interacting with the public. She also voted to prevent ICE from entering sensitive areas like schools, hospitals, and daycares without a judicial warrant.

As prime sponsor of HB 1889, Amy helped immigrants use their skills to enrich our communities. Her bill established that professional licenses in our state shall not require US citizenship (with a few exceptions). The bill broadly expanded licensing pathways for qualified applicants. We have very strict licensing requirements in our state for all kinds of professions—from architecture to hair stylists, from medical assistants to auto dealers. If one can pass our testing, they should be able to work and participate in our economy. We have a district with a great many families coming from overseas, and their spouse or family member may have wonderful qualifications – this is win/win for employers and those who want to go to work in our state.
Here are just a few of the 48th District projects that Amy has passed funding for in Olympia:
Burke-Gilman Trail Transit Access, Safety & Efficiency Improvements
Eastrail Multi-Use Corridor through Bellevue
King County Metro Totem Lake/Kirkland to Bellevue/Eastgate Transit Implementation
King County Metro - Bike Share Expansion - Kirkland, Bellevue, Redmond
I-405/NE 8th St to SR 520 Braided Ramps - Interchange Improvements
I-405 South Downtown Access Study Support
I-405/NE 85th St Interchange - Toll Infrastructure
SR 520/Evergreen Point Floating Bridge R&R - Preservation
SR 520/124th St Interchange (Design and Right of Way)
SR 520/148th Ave NE Overlake Access Ramp
SR 520/Bellevue Corridor Improvements - East End
SR 520 Trail Grade Separation at 40th Street
SR 520/148th Ave NE Overlake Access Ramp
SR 520/148th Avenue NE Bicycle/Pedestrian Crossing
City of Kirkland - 108th Ave NE Transit Queue Jumps
Kirkland 132nd Ave NE & Slater Ave Crossing

City of Redmond-Parking Management & On-Demand Microtransit Plan

pages.title: ISSUES & PLATFORM - AMY WALEN FOR STATE HOUSE
paragraphs: Amy Walen is a dedicated advocate for the people of Washington’s 48th District, championing policies that support working families, small businesses, and a thriving local community.

Amy believes effective leadership is rooted in listening and acting with integrity—a philosophy she’s carried with her through every role, from the Kirkland City Council to the Washington State Legislature.

On the House Consumer Safety Committee in Olympia, I have led the fight against high quantities of substances like sodium nitrate. Toxic chemicals and plastics are still ubiquitous in our lives. We must remain vigilant in not repeating the mistakes of history as we tolerated lead and asbestos. Dangerous chemicals in food, water, household products and cosmetics must be prohibited as a matter of urgency.

pages.title: ABOUT - AMY WALEN FOR STATE HOUSE
paragraphs: My husband and I fell in love with the 48th District when we moved to Kirkland in 2005 and have been proud to call it home ever since.

Elected to the Kirkland City Council in 2009, I was selected by my colleagues to serve as Mayor in 2014. I was elected to the State Legislature in 2018, motivated by my belief that true leadership involves listening to diverse perspectives and creating policies that consider all viewpoints.

I grew up in Oregon and had the opportunity to study abroad in Australia, graduating from the University of Queensland Law School. My education gave me a strong foundation in problem-solving and public service, values that continue to guide my work today.

Family has always been at the center of my life. Jim and I are proud to have built a blended, growing family together, including Ryan, Rachel, and my nephew Josh, whom we’re raising and who attends Lake Washington High School and participates in Studio East. Like so many families in our community, we juggle work, school, and everyday responsibilities, and I understand firsthand the challenges people face trying to make it all work.

That perspective is what I bring to my work in the legislature. I’m focused on practical solutions that make a real difference in people’s lives by expanding affordable housing, supporting working families, protecting our environment, advancing public safety, and standing up for fundamental rights. I believe the government should work efficiently, be accountable to taxpayers, and deliver results that strengthen our communities.

Before serving in the legislature, I spent nearly 20 years working as a Chief Financial Officer for companies with more than $100 million in annual revenue. Jim and I also worked together to grow Ford of Kirkland into Ford–Hyundai of Kirkland, helping create jobs for more than 120 people in Totem Lake. That experience taught me how to manage budgets, support employees, and make tough decisions, skills I bring with me to Olympia every day.

In 2005, after breast cancer treatment, I became even more committed to giving back. I’ve been proud to support local organizations, organize community events like blood drives and cleanups, and stay actively involved in the place we call home.
I’m running for reelection because I believe in this community, and I’ll keep working to make sure it’s a place where everyone has the opportunity to thrive.
Amy welcomes conversations about what matters most to you. Feel free to reach out at Amy@AmyWalen.com.

pages.title: Melody For Justice | Support Fair Justice Today
paragraphs: Upholding the Rights of Washingtonians With Integrity and Fairness

Born and raised in Spokane County, Colleen grew up in a family of public servants. Her father was an elementary school teacher and principal, and her mother was a nurse who worked at the Department of Health. Colleen worked through college waiting tables, and then attended law school with a commitment to serving her community as a lawyer.

Colleen has dedicated her career to protecting the rights of Washingtonians. She built the Civil Rights Division of the Washington State Attorney General’s Office from the ground-up, turning it from a startup into a nationally recognized powerhouse that protects state residents from harassment, discrimination, and violence no matter their gender, race, age, or disability.

She has taken on Fortune 100 companies for unfair business practices and held the Federal Government accountable for violating the rights of Washingtonians. From trial courts in every corner of our state to the U.S. Supreme Court, Colleen has stood firm for the rule of law and all of our rights.
"I am very proud to pass the torch on to Justice Colleen Melody. She is smart, hardworking, and will uphold the rule of law. I wholeheartedly endorse Justice Melody."

“It was a privilege to witness Justice Colleen Melody's intellect, work ethic, and legal skills firsthand during her time at the Attorney General’s Office. I am honored to have had the opportunity to appoint her to the Supreme Court."

"When I first became Attorney General, it was immediately clear to me that Colleen Melody was the single best lawyer we had. No one else cares as much about justice or the people as her. I am thrilled she will continue her career of service on the Supreme Court."
Justice Melody is committed to protecting and upholding your rights. She believes:
Courts must safeguard Washington’s independence and longstanding protection of rights in the workplace, in healthcare, and other individual civil and constitutional rights.
Everyone deserves to be safe and free from violence, harassment, or discrimination. Crime victims and discrimination victims deserve dignity, respect, and safety
Our Courts are a cornerstone of our democracy and must be trusted and accessible to everyone
Judges are public servants. They must work hard, listen, and approach each case with impartiality and humility

pages.title: About | Support Civil Rights — Act Now — Melody For Justice
paragraphs: Born and raised in Spokane County, Colleen grew up in a family of public servants. Her father was a public school educator, and her mother was a nurse who worked at the Department of Health on improving our health care system.

In college at the University of Washington, Colleen waited tables full-time while earning double degrees in Law, Societies, and Justice and in Spanish. She volunteered throughout college at the Casa Latina Day Workers’ Center, helping immigrant workers find employment opportunities, access essential services, and safely integrate into our communities.

Colleen returned to the University of Washington for law school, where she was an inaugural recipient of the Gates Public Service Law Scholarship, a highly competitive scholarship for students dedicated to public-interest law. She interned at the National Immigrant Justice Center in Chicago, helping LGBTQ+ immigrants fleeing violence and torture from countries where it is illegal to be gay. She also interned as a public defender serving indigent adults and children in King County.

After law school, Colleen dedicated her career to protecting and defending civil rights. She worked at the U.S. Department of Justice in Washington, DC from 2010-2014, enforcing our nation’s bedrock civil rights laws in courtrooms across the country. Then in 2015, she returned home to Washington to serve as the first Chief of the Civil Rights Division in the Washington State Attorney General’s Office, where she developed a team of lawyers, investigators, and skilled professional staff that became a national model of civil rights enforcement.

In that role, she took on Fortune 100 companies for unfair business practices, took the federal government to court dozens of times for violating the rights of Washingtonians, beat the NW Detention Center at trial and stopped its abusive practice of paying detained workers just $1/day to run that facility, stood up for pregnant workers whose rights were flouted by their employers, and defended farmworkers who were subjected to wage theft and harassment.

For years, Colleen has volunteered through the statewide Access to Justice Board to advance rules that improve court access, and through the King County Bar Foundation to support pro bono legal service programs and minority law student scholarships.

As a Supreme Court Justice, Colleen is already making an impact– working to ensure that courts are safe and accessible to all, and advocating for the use of technology to improve court access, particularly in Eastern Washington. She regularly speaks to civic and community groups about the importance of state courts and state constitutions in safeguarding our democracy.
Colleen is the proud mother of two daughters who attend public school. She lives with her husband and children in rural King County.

paragraphs: I am Scott Edwards, attorney and longtime advocate for principled, independent judgment. I’m running to serve Washingtonians with fairness, integrity, and respect for the rule of law.
I grew up in Anchorage, Alaska, where my father’s service as Alaska Attorney General and U.S. Attorney rooted the practice of law early in my life.
Over decades of litigation and counseling, I’ve learned that trust in our courts depends on careful reasoning, equal treatment, and a steady commitment to the law.

I am running for the Washington Supreme Court to bring independent judgment to every case—focused on the Washington State Constitution, the statutes, and the people we serve. Outside the courtroom, I’m grateful for family, including time with my granddaughter, which keeps me grounded in what our decisions mean for future generations.
What I will bring to the Washington Supreme Court
Decisions guided by the law and the record — never by politics or pressure.
Clear, principled reasoning that strengthens confidence in our courts.
Respectful process, equal treatment, and an unwavering commitment to due process.
Decades of complex litigation experience and disciplined analysis.
A record of excellence and leadership in the legal profession.
