We must make Capitol Hill a welcoming basin for queer youth arriving from around the nation seeking refuge.
Housing is a human right. Let’s lead the charge with policies that reflect the priorities of the people and get the outcomes we deserve.

Keeping people in their homes is one of the most effective ways to reduce homelessness. Eviction prevention, rental assistance, and mediation cost far less than responding after someone loses housing, and they work. In New York City, right-to-counsel and eviction prevention programs have reduced evictions by more than 30%. A Stay Housed Guarantee provides rapid access to eviction prevention, mediation, financial assistance, and navigation services so temporary setbacks do not lead to housing loss.
Stay Housed Guarantee: When displacement is imminent, the county must provide access to rapid support services, including:
Universal access to eviction prevention support
Mediation and rental negotiation services
Navigation support for seniors and parents on fixed income
One time emergency grants to stabilize families facing displacement
Rental Assistance Funding through CBO partnerships
See the Model: United Way of King County Rental Assistance Program

The “Right to Return” and Reparative Investments: Over decades, the people of District 2 have experienced the impacts of inflation and gentrification, and being systematically priced out of the homes and neighborhoods they love. For communities of color, this is compounded on top of the underlying legacy of racist, exclusionary laws, policies, and covenants that has led to the direct loss of capital for black and brown communities.

A Right to Return policy is evidence-based and grounded in the scale of harm. County research (championed by Executive Zahilay) found that redlining and discriminatory housing practices led to $12 billion to $34 billion in lost wealth for BIPOC households in King County, including $5.4 billion to $15.8 billion lost by Black households alone.
Government must address the impacts of generations of racist and exclusionary policies

Create a pathway for families who were pushed out of historically redlined neighborhoods to return and become homeowners via a Voucher-to-Homeownership Pilot. King County should dedicate funding to expand voucher-to-homeownership pathways so housing assistance can help families build equity, not only pay rent to private landlords. KCHA’s Dream to Keys program already allows eligible voucher holders to use assistance toward a mortgage, but King County should scale this model by pairing vouchers with down payment assistance, homebuyer counseling, Community Land Trust homes, and public land opportunities. The County should also explore a rent-to-own pilot where publicly supported homes are structured so monthly housing assistance helps families move toward ownership while preserving long-term affordability.

Pair homeownership opportunities with down payment assistance, homebuyer counseling, and financial education so first-time buyers have the support they need to successfully purchase and sustain homeownership.

Expand existing partnerships with community based organizations to expand Community Land Trusts and Shared Equity Models to provide technical assistance, financial literacy and counseling for families navigating bureaucratic processes to promote accessible pathways to homeownership.
A temporary property tax cap for the first 5 years of homeownership to promote accessibility to affordable homeownership.

Pool utility taxation for all unincorporated areas so the tax burden is more equitably distributed between a larger population base. This will significantly lower the utility bills for those living in Skyway and other unincorporated areas.

Puget Sound Regional Council projects that the region’s population will grow by another 1 million people by 2035, which leaves King County facing a severe housing shortage, needing tens of thousands of additional homes to meet current and future demand, which is driving rising costs, displacement, and homelessness. By prioritizing public land, social housing, and community-based ownership, we can increase supply in a way that keeps housing affordable in perpetuity, stabilizes communities, and ensures the benefits of growth reach the people who call District 2 home.

A "Transit Oriented Development-First" Land Bank: The moment a new light rail station is announced, land prices spike. We will aggressively landbank properties around future transit stations now . And we must refuse to sell county-owned lands off to the highest bidder. Instead, we should use that land for 100% social and affordable housing, ensuring that transit expansion benefits the existing community.
See the Framework: Seattle Equitable Transit-Oriented Development Strategy

Scaling social housing across King County: King County should be a national leader in building social housing. I support expanding models like House Our Neighbors and working with Seattle’s Social Housing Public Development Authority to deliver permanently affordable, mixed-income housing at scale. This means dedicating County-owned land, aligning future housing levies and funding tools, and ensuring these developments are built with strong labor standards that create union jobs. Social housing must be part of how we meet the scale of this crisis and ensure long-term affordability for working families. We should also prioritize investments in developments that integrate wraparound services such as workforce development & early learning so families have real opportunities for upward economic mobility and long term stability.

TOD Community Roots Bonus: I will introduce a "Density Bonus" program similar to the City’s Roots to Roof program, with a specific focus on historical realities . Developers will get incentives like extra height or density if they commit to a certain number of affordable units when developing within historically redlined neighborhoods.
See the Strategy: Seattle Roots to Roofs Program

Community Land Trusts and radical homeownership: We cannot just build rentals; we must build intergenerational wealth. I will push for greater investments into Community Land Trusts. This takes land out of the speculative market forever and ensures it remains permanently affordable for our families.
See the Model: WA Community Land Trusts Case Studies

Along with articulating a vision for the future, we must have a plan for how to fund it. I’m proud to offer concrete solutions to pay for the housing infrastructure we so desperately need. This includes new revenue sources, promoting efficiencies within current processes, and stronger accountability so every tax dollar is spent towards its intended purpose.
For a more in-depth description of our campaign platform’s vision for progressive funding, please visit the “progressive revenue” subtab on our webpage .

Countywide Housing Levy: I support King County Executive Zahilay’s proposal for a Housing Levy. A recent King County study championed by Executive Zahilay found that King County has $9B for bond capacity, but needs a revenue source to bond against. For King County to stabilize a billion dollar bond, it would need $148m in revenue; through Seattle’s new voter-approved levy, Prop 1A, the Seattle Housing Authority got $130m in 1 year, showing us that $148m is imminently achievable. A housing levy is a great start.

Public Development Authority for economic development: King County should explore standing up its own Public Development Authority to directly develop and manage housing projects. It already has the legislative authority to do so. This could look like liquidating a property that has moved through the county auction process and using that as affordable housing.

Progressive taxation: I will advocate for a bill in the state legislature that would allow King County to impose progressive taxes, such as a modified Business & Occupancy Tax to tax profits of large corporations on their profits instead of revenues, which would lead to more progressive taxation of the ultra wealthy. We must ensure any tax on our businesses does not land on the backs of our small businesses community.

Controlling costs by promoting efficiencies: Some major market drivers of cost are beyond our control such as the hard costs (labor, materials). But soft costs are an area where the county can help. Soft costs include permitting, architect fees, and design fees.

Speed up permits so projects don’t get stuck: Right now, approvals can take months because applications sit in backlogs and bounce between departments. We can improve this by assigning a dedicated full-time staff member to manage the internal review process, track caseloads, and keep permits moving so they don’t stall between departments. Affordable housing and childcare projects should move through a streamlined review process with clear, objective standards and limited discretionary steps. I would also set a target of a five-day turnaround for each stage of review to ensure accountability and keep projects progressing.
Hire enough staff necessary to reduce the backlog. Hire sufficient staffing to eliminate the permitting backlog and ensure timely, predictable review of housing projects.

Public Land for Public Good : Before any County-owned surplus property is sold, King County should require a formal review to determine whether the site can be used for affordable or social housing, ensuring public land is used to meet housing needs before being transferred to private development.

Work on Permitting Efficiency to expand transparency, identify delays, ensure compliance with state deadlines, create a broader fast-track pathway for affordable and social housing, improve coordinated review across departments, and explore pre-approved design standards to accelerate housing delivery at scale.

Accountability: I commend Executive Zahilay for standing up an in-house audit function to ensure that every public dollar is accounted for. As a County Councilmember, I’ll fight for pairing the oversight with teeth, like a suspension trigger when there are ethics issues or underperformance. When money goes missing, we need institutional accountability.
COUNTYWIDE HOMELESSNESS PREVENTION GUARANTEE

It is a moral failure that any person in King County doesn’t have a stable home or guaranteed meal. When people make contact with King County, it should be the turning point where their life changes for the better. The county must make bold commitments and investments to address the immediate needs and support a continuum of care to permanently transform people's lives into a place of self-sufficiency.

Set the Goal of Zero Child Homelessness: Fighting for a better future begins with making the wellbeing of our children a priority. Families with kids experiencing homelessness must be given priority for stabilization.

Guarantee Housing Before Exit for Foster Youth: No young person should leave foster care or juvenile detention without a stable place to go. Today, one in four youth exiting foster care will experience homelessness within four years. King County should ensure that housing is secured before discharge, with dedicated navigation, access to rental assistance and Youth Diversion Infrastructure Project funds, and continued support to ensure young people transition into stable, long-term housing.

Boost funding for Community Based Organizations. Much like during the global pandemic. CBO’s receiving flexible funding can expeditiously meet the unique needs of their diverse community members in a culturally specific and appropriate way. Whether they are people of color, queer and trans youth, or limited english speakers, CBO’s do the hard work of creating shelter and safety.

Invest in Interim Housing options that create the sheer availability of shelter needed to answer the crushing needs of this moment. I support standing up a model similar to the Civic Hotel that gives priority to families with kids, and letting them stay for the duration of the school year or until they are transitioned into stable housing.

Safe Parking: While we build permanent housing, we must invest in immediate safety. I support expanding "Safe Parking" programs and specialized interim housing options for families. We must ensure that a lost lease doesn't lead to a child sleeping on the street or being separated from their parents.
See Current Resources: King County Safe Parking Programs

Continuum of Care Case Workers: Connecting folks to shelter and housing is just the first step . This continuum of care will help families navigate apprenticeship opportunities, workforce re-entry, bureaucratic paperwork, and legal systems to ensure they have the stability to stay housed, compliant, and economically independent.
See the Framework: LCYC Legal Support & Stability Model

Closing the 6-12 month care gap: I am proposing we take the proven model of the Seattle Preschool Program and expand it downward to serve our most vulnerable age group, which is infants from 6 to 12 months old. The Seattle Preschool Program succeeded because it standardized quality and pay. We need to do the same for infant care. The Best Starts for Kids levy allows for capital facility grants. I will push to ensure any surplus revenue is fenced exclusively for infant care capacity. Building out safe spaces for babies is the most expensive part of the system due to safety codes, and that is where public dollars should go.

The 10% Affordability Cap: The current market rate is crushing families. I will fight to expand Best Starts for Kids subsidies to ensure no low-to-moderate income family in King County pays more than 10% of their annual household income on child care. This puts real money back into the pockets of working parents.
See the Data: DCYF Report: Policies to Increase Access & Affordability

The Child Care Navigator: We will launch a child care navigator program, a unified resource that inventories child care providers, from centers to home care providers, so folks know what is available to them in their neighborhood, near their place of employment, or along their commute line. Families can also receive information about current subsidy programs that they can access that are available. There will be a dedicated staff person to support people with inquiries.
See the Model: Port of Seattle Childcare Navigator Program

The Home Care Provider Incubator Program: We will launch a County-backed incubator to help home-based providers navigate the complex maze of licensing and safety standards. This isn't just about regulation; it is an economic development tool to help skilled providers, who are often black or immigrant women, turn their caregiving skills into sustainable, licensed small businesses.This is mission critical to ensuring families have a diversity of local options to choose from, that will provide culturally appropriate care to their loved ones.
See the Assessment: DCYF Report: Addressing Regulatory Barriers
See the Model: Port of Seattle Small Business Accelerator Program

Worker Wage Boost Pilot - Make it permanent: We cannot build high-quality care on the backs of workers earning poverty wages. I will fight to make the BSK Wage Boost Pilot program permanent. Using County funds to directly subsidize higher wages for child care workers will ensure they can afford to live in the communities they serve without raising tuition for parents.
See the Pilot Program: Best Starts for Kids Wage Boost Pilot
The demand for childcare far outpaces the supply of accessible, affordable care. We know that people will use child care near where they live, work, or along their commute line.
King County must conduct a childcare center feasibility study to assess opportunities to develop centers in its jurisdiction. This is an inevitable first step to meet the urgency of demand.
See the studies: Child Care Collaborative Task Force Report; Washington Communities for Children Report

Transit Oriented Development of Child Care: We will identify underutilized parcels owned not just by the County, but by Sound Transit as well. Sound Transit is legally mandated to prioritize community benefits in their Transit-Oriented Development (TOD) projects. We will partner with them to ensure that when a new station opens, it includes rent-free, built-in child care space at the ground level. We can lease these public spaces at one dollar a year to providers who agree to serve low-income families and transit workers. When we lower overhead costs for the business, we can raise wages for the staff.

Density bonuses for child care: KC should also offer density bonuses for new housing and highrise development in its jurisdiction when the first floor to childcare and they can site a dedicated, private outdoor play space for children. Additionally, King County should partner with cities and the Washington Department of Children, Youth, and Families (DCYF) to streamline the overlap between building local codes and operational licenses given by the state.
See the studies: Child Care Collaborative Task Force Report; Washington Communities for Children Report

It is a moral failure that any person in King County doesn’t have a stable home or guaranteed meal. When people making contact with King County, it should be the turning point where their life changes for the better. The county must make bold commitments and investments to address the immediate needs and support a continuum of care to permanently transform peoples lives into a place of self-sufficiency.

Set the Goal of Zero Child Homelessness: Fighting for a better future begins with making the wellbeing of our children a priority. Families with kids experiencing homelessness must be given priority for stabilization.

Boost funding for Community Based Organizations. Much like during the global pandemic. CBO’s receiving flexible funding can expeditiously meet the unique needs of their diverse community members in a culturally specific and appropriate way. Whether they are people of color, queer and trans youth or limited english speakers, CBO’s do the hard work of creating shelter and safety
Invest in Interim Housing options like Civic Hotel, LIHI, and tiny house villages that create the sheer availability of shelter needed to answer the crushing needs of this moment

Safe Parking: While we build permanent housing, we must invest in immediate safety. I support expanding "Safe Parking" programs and specialized interim housing options for families. We must ensure that a lost lease doesn't lead to a child sleeping on the street or being separated from their parents.
See Current Resources: King County Safe Parking Programs

Continuum of Care Case Workers: Connecting folks to shelter and housing is just the first step . This continuum of care will help families navigate apprenticeship opportunities, workforce re-entry, bureaucratic paperwork and legal systems to ensure they have the stability to stay housed, compliant, and economically independent.
See the Framework: LCYC Legal Support & Stability Model

Inflation happens when demand outpaces supply. One of the best tools we have to combat affordability is build, build, build. We need to build more housing and childcare alike, to meet the crushing needs of our communities, and we need to start yesterday.

Fixing the "Rainier Valley Rail Trap": The Rainier Valley is the only segment of our regional light rail system built at street level, leading to higher collision rates than anywhere else. I will demand that Sound Transit invest in grade-separation retrofits or, immediately, "smart" safety gates and AI-based hazard detection at all 28 at-grade crossings. We cannot accept a system where convenience for commuters comes at the cost of safety for our neighbors.
Linkable Source: USDOT: Sound Transit Rainier Valley Safe Project

Restorative Justice for the South End: District 2 bears the scars of past infrastructure decisions. The construction of I-5 tore through redlined neighborhoods creating the very border of the the District. And, the decision to run light rail at street level through the Rainier Valley—unlike anywhere else in the system—created a permanent safety hazard. We are going to fix it.
Rainier Avenue: People Over Pavement: Rainier Avenue is our Main Street, but it is also the most dangerous corridor in the city. We will stop prioritizing through-traffic cars over our own families.
I support aggressively pursuing the RapidRide R Line , which will soon replace the popular Route 7, one of the most popular routes in D2. Timely delivery is an equity issue.
I support installing raised crosswalks, pedestrian grade lighting along Rainier Ave S. If a street design kills people, the design is the problem and we will change it.

HARD NO to adding lanes on Rainier Ave S. to accommodate SOVs. WSDOT is considering adding 2 lanes to Rainier Ave S. near the I-90 off ramps to support projected population growth and SOVs. Absolutely not. Instead, it should be as pedestrian friendly as possible, to accommodate the housing density/residents coming to the area and the opening of Judkins Light Rail Station. Signage, lighting, greenery and a protected bike lane are a better use of funds to develop that segment of Rainier Ave. S., which leads to the Rapid Ride R route.
See WSDOT’s proposal: I-90 Judkins Station Advisory Group Meeting Minutes

Lidding I-5 (LIDDING 1-5): I am fully committed to the vision of lidding I-5. This is not just a park; it is a restorative justice project . We will reclaim that space to heal the "concrete scar". By covering the freeway, we can reconnect our neighborhoods and create continuous green space that actively combats air pollution.
See the Feasibility Study: City of Seattle: I-5 Lid Feasibility Study

Community Assets on the Lid: We won't just plant grass. We will use the new land created by the I-5 lid to build affordable childcare centers and community spaces. We will turn a source of pollution and division into a source of health, connection, and opportunity for our kids.
See the Health Context: King County Community Health Indicators
We operate in a state with the most regressive tax code in the nation, and while the County has limited tools compared to the state legislature, we cannot use that as an excuse for inaction.

Regarding progressive revenue, I will explore establishing a public bank in King County, which would increase lending capacity so that selling bonds isn't an issue (which is the major issue with Executive Zahilay’s workforce housing proposal. A public bank of course could still sell bonds if it wanted to but why would it?) This would allow us to divest in Wall Street where King County currently banks, and dramatically increase financing capacity for housing, childcare, electrification and other new development.

I support maximizing our use of progressive levies , specifically the Crisis Care Centers levy, to ensure we are delivering on mental health services. I will also explore every avenue to implement high-earner excise taxes where legally permissible to fund housing and homelessness prevention. We must stop balancing the budget on the backs of the poor. I will prioritize a participatory budgeting process so that the communities most impacted by cuts are the ones at the table deciding where the money goes.
I will aggressively lobby the state legislature to lift the 1% property tax cap which strangles our ability to fund basic services.

Policing, Courts and Corrections are fundamentally reactive safety mechanisms. When we rely on them exclusively, we stay in a cycle of arrest, release, and rearrest. We need to break this cycle. I am deeply committed to stewarding public resources responsibly, and I want to ensure our public funds go to programs that accomplish their stated purpose. If we fail to do that, then we don’t serve our community, we don’t serve our goals, and we don’t serve our youth. I believe upstream investments are critical to realizing our public safety goals, and that the greatest public safety tool we have is creating access to opportunities.
Our criminal legal system must be re-shaped to maximize progress towards our goals of better outcomes, reduced recidivism, and support for victims .

Diversion that Works: Some diversion programs have demonstrated efficacy, including Law Enforcement Assisted Diversion (LEAD), which has been identified by the auditor as a leader in evaluation and use of data for program improvement. LEAD allows police to shift people away from the criminal system and instead connect people committing low-level offenses to housing, treatment, and case management. The LEAD model addresses the root causes of crime and helps officers resolve situations more effectively, all of which helps reduce repeat offenses. LEAD has won credibility and support across the political spectrum because it offers a framework in which all partners, from police to harm reduction service providers, play the role they’re best suited to play, coordinate, and identify the path most likely to accomplish behavior change in each case. Yet, we have fallen short of scaling this model County-wide, and state-funded efforts to replicate it in some areas of King County have been repeatedly cut.

Ending "Pretextual Stops": Champion a "Traffic Safety for All" ordinance, which would direct the Sheriff’s Office to stop pulling drivers over for non-moving violations (like a single broken taillight or expired tabs). Data shows these stops are disproportionately used against BIPOC drivers and do not improve road safety.

Language Access Settlement Compliance: The most recent DOJ settlement involving King County was announced in February 2024 and focused on language access issues with the King County Sheriff’s Office (KCSO). King County agreed to implement significant changes to improve how the Sheriff’s Office communicates with LEP individuals. Key parts of the agreement include:
Hiring a language access program manager.
Developing interim and final language access directives that prohibit the use of unqualified interpreters (like family members or bystanders).
Creating training for deputies on language access.
Conducting outreach with community members.
Establishing an accessible complaint process.

Body-Worn Camera (BWC) Audits: Now that BWCs are standard, propose a "Random Audit" program where OLEO reviews a percentage of footage not associated with a complaint to ensure deputies are following de-escalation protocols consistently.

Civil Asset Forfeiture Reform: Transparency in how the county seizes property is a major issue. This should be reported publicly by KCSO. Propose a "Zero-Profit" rule where all assets seized during investigations are directed to a survivor services fund to support recovery and stabilization needs of commercial sexual exploitation survivors and other crime victims, rather than back into the Sheriff's budget, removing the financial incentive for seizures.
Empowering the Office of Law Enforcement Oversight (OLEO)

Effective oversight is essential to building public trust in government, especially in systems that hold the power to detain and deprive individuals of their liberty. As someone who was hired by the King County Council to help reboot the Office of Law Enforcement Oversight in 2017, I have seen firsthand how critical independent oversight is to ensuring transparency, accountability, and community confidence in how public safety functions are carried out. I strongly support strengthening OLEO’s independence, resources, and scope so it can fully meet this moment, with proactive oversight, meaningful access to information, and clear public reporting. Accountability is about making our systems stronger, more transparent, and more worthy of the public’s trust.

Full Subpoena Power: Ensure OLEO has the independent legal authority to compel testimony and documents during misconduct investigations without needing to wait for the Sheriff’s internal review to conclude. Give them the authority to audit KCSO to ensure non-compliance with ICE requests for access to information and assistance, and to ensure full compliance with the Keep Washington Working Act.
Community-Guided Framework: Propose a permanent position for South Seattle on the Community Advisory Committee for Law Enforcement Oversight.

Community Oversight of Use-of-Force: Create a Community Task Force specifically for District 2 that meets monthly with the Sheriff to review precinct-level data on use of force and stops and publishes an annual report.

Jailing kids does not work to set them on a better path–and unaccountable, ineffective diversion is a wasted opportunity. Our kids and communities deserve better. Diversion can be done well, and it must be. We must intercede earlier, ensuring healthy places to learn and grow, with access to long-term, professional mentorship. We know that a child jailed before the age of 18 is four times more likely to be incarcerated as an adult. And we also know that after school programs effectively reduce youth involvement with crime by 50%.

When King County runs evidence based, well funded, and accountable programs that address family and social environments, they can shift youth out of the incarceration cycle. We put kids in jail for behaviors that often stem from trauma, ongoing violence, or a lack of support. We must put kids on the path to success. We’ve seen the incarceration system fail to do that time and again. We’ve also seen some county investments in juvenile diversion fall short. But, we must renew our commitment to robust alternatives to incarceration. Any child in a jail cell must be seen as a policy failure. The County should employ national best practices in youth diversion, and deploy skilled community partners in a new accountable, transparent framework. We must give communities flexibility to tailor their response to the needs of each individual child.

Functional Family Probation and Parole: Equip probation officers, many of whom bring strong skills, to engage in family-centered case management and coaching roles using evidence-based models like Functional Family Therapy. Focus supervision on engagement and motivation, identifying family interaction patterns, behavior change strategies, and sustaining positive behaviors in school and community. They’ll conduct structured family engagement and therapy during probation supervision, address family dynamics that contribute to delinquency, and provide 12 to 14 structured sessions over several months focused on behavior change and support. This aligns with what has been proven to be successful at the State of Washington.

Wraparound community supports Require the family-centered case managers to provide wraparound community support services that address root causes of justice involvement. We must connect youth with mental health and trauma care, school re-engagement and tutoring, job training and apprenticeships, substance use treatment, as well as mentorship and after-school programs
Courts: Expanding Diversion and a Restorative Justice Lens
We want involvement in the system to be rare.

Support Pre-Filing Diversion Programs whereby individuals won’t be charged with a crime so long as they complete a workshop. That way, people can avoid the collateral consequences of a criminal record such as housing and employment opportunities.

Establish a Goal of Zero Youth Incarceration: We know that a child jailed before the age of 18 is four times more likely to be incarcerated as an adult. We also know that after school programs effectively reduce youth involvement with crime by 50%. Instead, let’s shift funding toward pre-filing diversion programs, diverting youth to community-led groups for accountability and healing. We must give communities flexibility to tailor their response to the needs of each individual child.

Support Pre-Trial Diversion Programs: Even if we scale up pre-filing diversion through the LEAD framework, sometimes cases that are filed and need judicial oversight can still be effectively and fairly diverted prior to trial, if we have effective alternative options to address the situation that gave rise to the problem. Effective, evidence-based pre-trial diversion options are critical to containing legal system costs at a time of resource scarcity.​​ Some examples include anger management programs, and FIRS which deals with kids who are usually in some sort of crisis (here, families are at their wit’s end, and kids are acting violently towards family. If they’re arrested and released, they’ll go straight back home and nothing has changed. This program helps them get some respite time.)

Crime Survivor Resources: Many crime survivors want to know that they will be made whole (to the extent possible), and that the person who harmed them won't do this to them or others again. Punishment is rarely a primary goal. More attention to survivor safety needs is critical to shift the paradigm in a constructive direction. Physical safety, psychological safety, and economic safety are all top concerns for many survivors. Guaranteed paid time off for dealing with matters related to their case, low-barrier access to mental health services, a repair and recovery fund independent of the progress of a criminal case, all address survivor needs more directly than criminal prosecution.

Fund collateral consequences attorneys, who act as social workers. Clients have very complex criminal and civil legal needs (like a divorce case or facing eviction or foreclosure) and they have mitigation specialists within those offices but not enough, and they don't have enough collateral consequences attorneys, who were there to address OTHER legal system needs instead of just that case, to address the whole person. It’s an investment to address needs around housing, healthcare, civil and criminal law, but can reduce recidivism. They would come into contact at the point of arraignment. “Not enough money”.

Fully funding public defenders - and ensuring no case is filed unnecessarily: Stabilizing the public defense workforce is critical for many reasons–it’s the best way to prevent miscarriages of justice; as well, without adequate defenders, cases that belong in court sometimes must be dismissed. The advent of pervasive body cameras and other video evidence in recent years has vastly increased the time required to investigate even routine cases. The WA Supreme Court recently mandated lower caseload limits for public defenders to address a workforce crisis, and King County has proactively adopted some of these standards. This should be maintained. At the same time, we can’t afford to assign lawyers and court staff to situations that can be better resolved outside of court, which is why redoubling our efforts to scale effective pre-filing diversion pathways (not requiring assignment of lawyers) is so critical.

Set the goal of eliminating court fees for indigent defendants: King County has already eliminated court costs for juveniles - we can go further to ensure that people without the means to pay aren’t carrying an impossible debt burden that makes it much harder to make ends meet, ironically, increasing crime. I’d explore, with Court leaders and other public safety advocates, an approach that eliminates all court fees that are not mandated by state law. The budget cost of attempting to collect these funds is not warranted by the amount we realistically can expect to collect, and meanwhile, unpayable fees are an obstacle to recovery and stabilization.

Leverage technology platforms such as texting programs, video conferencing and bus transit voucher programs and other court reminder mechanisms to reduce failures to appear, warrants, and promote efficiencies in court calendars . Eliminate court fees that drive noncompliance.
Corrections: A Rehabilitation First Approach

When someone leaves jail, we should not set them up to fail. If a new parent leaving a hospital receives coordinated support to help their family succeed, we should offer the same level of care and planning to people returning from incarceration. The goal is simple: ensure that people leaving custody have access to housing, healthcare, and opportunity so they can rebuild their lives and avoid returning to the system.

We also must ensure that there are no perverse incentives to push people further into the legal system than necessary just so they can access superior supportive services by virtue of the fact that they were charged with a crime or booked into jail. A basic principle, as we enhance re-entry supports, should be to ensure that everything available upon leaving jail, prison or the court system is equally available to someone who needs, and likelihood of being referred to the legal system, are identified in the community before they have to come to the attention of our emergency response and enforcement systems.

Strengthen Re-Entry: Successful reentry is one of the most effective tools we have for preventing crime. King County should build a comprehensive reentry ecosystem that ensures individuals leaving custody have:
access to healthcare and behavioral health services
employment and job training opportunities

Family Connection and Physical Contact Research consistently shows that maintaining family bonds reduces recidivism and improves mental health outcomes. Maintaining family relationships is one of the strongest predictors of successful reentry. I support expanded family visitation opportunities, policies allowing physical contact such as hugging family members during visits, and child-friendly visitation spaces

Protect Access to Cultural Groups Inside For so many people, connection to your cultural identity and community is a stabilizing factor. Access to cultural and community groups is strongly associated with improved well being and lower recidivism. King County could guarantee regular access to cultural groups, faith-based services.

Access to Preventative Health Care Sickness inside is an ongoing issue in carceral atmospheres. King County could ensure routine flu vaccinations, COVID vaccination access, screenings for chronic conditions, continuity of medications.

No Private Prisons or For-Profit Incarceration: I oppose privately owned or operated correctional facilities and any model that allows incarceration to become a profit generating enterprise. Public safety is a core government responsibility and should never be delegated to companies whose financial incentives depend on keeping beds full. King County should commit to a clear principle that deprivation of liberty is a public function that must remain publicly accountable .

Scale Violence Intervention Funding & Support Regional Coordination: Fully fund evidence-based community-led violence intervention models, identified by the King County Regional Office of Gun Violence Prevention, to de-escalate conflict before it leads to violence. Regional coordination should be strengthened, particularly with the City of Seattle, as these dynamics move back and forth across jurisdictional lines. And we should consider expanding rapid response teams that provide counseling, case management, and stabilization services after a tragedy to prevent further harm and support healing.

Support participatory budgeting to invest in community-led solutions: King County must support community-based groups doing the hard work in small yet profound ways to promote social bonds between youth and families. Fully fund community-led groups that work on the ground to de-escalate conflict before it leads to violence.

Put young people in the driver’s seat: The most credible messengers to youth are other young people. King County should create youth leadership councils in neighborhoods most impacted by violence so young people can help design prevention strategies, advise policymakers, and lead peer outreach. Provide grants and stipends for youth to run neighborhood projects that promote safety, from organizing events and mentorship to designing outreach campaigns that speak directly to their peers.

Trauma informed response when violence occurs When shootings happen, families and youth need immediate support. When shootings happen, families and youth need immediate support. King County should expand rapid response teams that provide counseling, case management, and stabilization services to prevent further harm. We can maintain focus on youth at Rainier Beach and surrounding neighborhoods. The ongoing violence near Rainier Avenue South and South Henderson Street requires coordinated youth intervention on which the King County Regional Office of Gun Violence Intervention has been providing leadership. I strongly support the ROGVP continuing to partner with the City of Seattle, Rainier Beach High School, community mentors, and youth employment programs to strengthen after school engagement, conflict mediation, safe passage, and pathways to jobs and leadership. This allows young people to engage deeper in our communities and to have a say in what safety looks like for them. Additionally, KC can expand peer mediation and conflict resolution programs in schools that train students to mediate disputes and de-escalate conflicts before they spill into the streets.

Invest in culturally grounded violence prevention: King County should expand partnerships with trusted community organizations serving the East African community , building on the model used by Seattle’s Office of Immigrant and Refugee Affairs. This means funding culturally competent outreach, conflict mediation, and family support programs delivered by organizations that already have trust in Somali, Ethiopian, and Eritrean communities.

Secure storage: Allocate $300,000 for an education campaign on secure storage of firearms in vehicles. 2000 firearms stolen, 400 of which from cars, in the past four years (source: SPD). 40% of guns are stolen from vehicles. We need stronger “secure storage” requirements (could give Washington an A rating).

To be clear, no one is above the law . What we have today is a federal apparatus hiring bad apples for nefarious purposes. They are violating the law in broad daylight, testing the limits of their legal authority. They are going to keep making mistakes. Local citizens must not be afraid to file reports against ICE agents. Local law enforcement must prioritize citizen complaints against ICE to the prosecuting attorneys office. And the PAO should feel empowered to file charges against and prosecute ICE agents when there is a preponderance of evidence against them. When they commit crimes, ICE should be just as afraid that someone's going to come knocking at their door. I want to see our law enforcement apparatus make the first arrest, trial and conviction of an ICE officer for acting outside of the law, whether they are on or off duty.

District 2 is home to the heart of Seattle's LGBTQIA+ community; the second largest (12.9%) queer population in the United States. Capitol Hill has been the geographic and cultural center of the queer community and the movement for civil and human rights for decades. Through the 1970s, 80s, and 90s, Capitol Hill became the center of the city's lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender community, building a vibrant arts and music scene that shaped Seattle's identity. The Wildrose, which opened in 1984, is the oldest lesbian bar in the country. Capitol Hill is where Pride celebrations step off, where community organizations were built, where queer people built chosen families when their families of origin turned them away, and where generations of LGBTQIA+ people found each other and found safety.

That history asks something of anyone who wants to represent this district. District 2 requires a committed, unwavering defender of civil rights with a clear and coherently articulated queer agenda. Champions move not only in rhetoric, but in policies, budget decisions, and the willingness to stand up when it is uncomfortable. I will be that leader.

We are in a moment of coordinated, federal and statewide attacks on queer communities and trans/non-binary individuals in particular. Recent federal actions represent direct attempts to erase the existence of transgender, gender-nonconforming, Two Spirit, and intersex people: defining them out of law, barring them from serving in our armed forces, banning trans girls from competing in athletics, and denying evidence-backed gender-affirming healthcare.

We also carry the grief of Juniper Blessing, a trans 19-year-old University of Washington student violently murdered in the laundry room of her off-campus housing complex on May 10. Her life is a testament; that Trans people deserve to exist, with safety and dignity. And it’s a reminder that Seattle is not exempt from the horrific biases, hatred, threats and disparities lfacing trans individuals. We are still grieving, and grief without action is unacceptable.

Through legal action, equity analyses and commitments, and clear policies and budget investments, King County can make itself a fortress of protection for our LGBTQIA+ community members. That is what I am committed to building.
HOUSING AND ANTI-DISPLACEMENT: KEEPING OUR COMMUNITY HERE

The number of same-sex couples in Capitol Hill's Broadway district has dropped from 5% in 2000 to 1.6%. Gentrification is dismantling a community stronghold that was built over decades. When queer folks are priced out of Capitol Hill, they lose proximity to their affirming community, cultural institutions, and the safety that comes from being surrounded by people who know and accept you.

That’s why my affordability agenda centers queer and trans people, and other vulnerable communities historically pushed to the margins, with a strong emphasis on anti-displacement protections that specifically consider the impact on LGBTQIA+ residents, including:

Tenant protections with real teeth -- just-cause eviction requirements, right-to-counsel for low-income tenants facing eviction, and mediation services that help keep people housed before they are pushed into crisis. Queer and trans tenants face higher rates of housing discrimination, harassment, eviction risk, and hostile housing conditions, especially when race, income, disability, immigration status, or family rejection compound those barriers. King County needs a housing system that will protect people, not one that leaves them to navigate discrimination and displacement alone.
Affordable and social housing with dedicated units in LGBTQIA+ affirming buildings.

Protecting community-owned LGBTQIA+ spaces -- supporting the acquisition and long-term security of LGBTQIA+ community centers, historical sites, cultural spaces, and gathering places through community land trusts and county-backed financing tools. The institutions that anchor this community must not be priced out of existence.

Queer and trans youth are disproportionately represented among young people experiencing homelessness, oftentimes driven by family rejection, discrimination, and instability. As a Councilmember, I will:
Expand dedicated, affirming shelter and transitional housing -- set asides for LGBTQIA+ youth specifically.

Fund tailored wraparound services and workforce development -- connecting people to gender-affirming healthcare navigation, legal support for name and gender marker changes, mental health care that centers queer and trans experience, and pathways into apprenticeships and stable employment.

Invest in mutual aid infrastructure -- Every Wednesday night on Capitol Hill, community organizers are meeting queer and trans youth who need food, supplies, warmth, and stability. King County should fund the organizations doing that work, not make them fight for scraps through competitive grant cycles.

Expand county-level food access -- I support creating a County-level Fresh Bucks program, modeled after Seattle's, to subsidize fresh groceries for people struggling to afford food. Food insecurity is disproportionately felt by LGBTQIA+ youth navigating housing instability, and this is a concrete tool we can deploy now.
BEHAVIORAL HEALTH AND CRISIS RESPONSE: SAFETY WITHOUT HARM

Too many in the queer community, and particularly trans individuals and QTPOC, and people experiencing homelessness -- It is building a behavioral health and crisis response infrastructure. I will push for:

Walk-in crisis clinics in District 2 -- accessible, no-appointment behavioral health services for people in acute distress, designed to serve queer and trans clients with affirming, trauma-informed care.

Far too many people have had traumatic, dangerous, or deadly interactions with law enforcement, including on their own turf in Capitol Hill. There is documented disparities in how police respond to anti-trans vs trans rights demonstrations. Biases in policing, excessive use of force, and harm in the carceral system are all failures of the system. The answer is not simply better policing.

Zero tolerance policy for bias. Use of biased terms or expressions of hateful attitudes will not be tolerated. You cannot serve the community when you lack compassion and recognition of the sanctity of their lives or commitment to their rights. They’ll be terminated and recommended for decertification to the CJTC.

Law enforcement accountability standards . When law enforcement is involved, officers must use correct names and pronouns, respect gender identity, and accurately report and classify crimes against trans and queer people. Misgendering and deadnaming by law enforcement can cause real harm and undermine trust in institutions that are supposed to protect people.

Survivor services for LGBTQIA+ people experiencing violence -- ensuring that domestic violence, sexual assault, and hate crime survivor services are fully accessible to LGBTQIA+ individuals, including those who may be undocumented, unhoused, or afraid to engage with law enforcement.
HEALTHCARE ACCESS: PROTECTING GENDER-AFFIRMING CARE

Federal attacks on gender-affirming healthcare are real and accelerating. King County has jurisdiction over public health infrastructure, and I will use every tool available to protect access to care.

I will work to ensure King County's public health system explicitly includes and funds gender-affirming care, hormone therapy access, affirming mental health services, and abortion access for all people with uteruses. I will oppose any attempt to restrict or defund these services at the county level, and will advocate loudly at the state level to ensure Washington remains a place where trans people can access the care they need to survive and thrive. King County is a place of refuge for LGBTQIA+ people across this country, and without focus and investment, that may not always be true.
Art, creation and anti-gentrification as a catalyst for Social Justice

Art is how communities tell the truth about who we are. It carries our stories, preserves our identity, and helps pass our values to the next generation. In District 2, arts and culture flow free, without gifts, grants or permits. It’s an expressive cornerstone to our pain, resilience, brilliance and soul.
My commitment on the Council is to treat arts funding as essential infrastructure.
That means centering the cultural expressions of our communities in every policy decision, from housing, to transit, to economic development.

When we invest in the arts, we invest in the well being of District 2’s soul.Displacement is not only a housing crisis, it is a cultural crisis. When people are priced out of their communities, their culture and the essence of the neighborhood goes too. Preserving the ability for artists to live and work in D2 is a racial, gender and economic justice issue. Let’s fight for:
anti-displacement protections that explicitly include live-work artist spaces and small cultural venues.

Local Arts Anchors: Support for small, community-based cultural organizations in District 2 to acquire or secure long-term leases for performance, studio, and exhibition space -- preventing the displacement of cultural infrastructure as land values rise.
Permanently affordable makers, studio and rehearsal spaces to protect and curate our creative economy.
Supporting the Creative Economy in District 2

Artists are workers, and the creative economy is a real economy that deserves real investment. Film crews, musicians, graphic designers, game developers, muralists are tangible industries generating real jobs, wages, tax revenue, and adding to our GDP. District 2 has untapped creative economic potential, too often overshadowed by economic development strategies that center downtown Seattle. I believe it has unique and special strengths towards the effort of buoying our creative economy. We can cultivate that through:
workforce development for talented young professionals
small business support for creative entrepreneurs
partnerships between schools and working artists!

Artist-in-Residence Programs: Partner with schools, libraries, community centers, and public housing developments across District 2 to embed working artists in community spaces -- bringing creative opportunity directly to residents, not asking residents to travel to it.

Youth Creative Pipeline: Fund pathways from K-12 arts education to paid creative work -- connecting young people in District 2 to internships, apprenticeships, and mentorships in film, music, visual art, and digital media. Harbor Island Studios should be a key partner in this pipeline.

Creative Small Business Fund: A dedicated micro-grant and technical assistance program for creative entrepreneurs in District 2 -- solo artists, small studios, music venues, and cultural nonprofits that fall below the threshold for traditional economic development programs.

Public Art as Neighborhood Narrative: Fund community-driven public art that reflects District 2 as it really is: its history, its people, its movements, and its culture. Public art should be created with communities, not placed on top of them.
A thriving creative economy in District 2 means local artists can build careers without leaving their communities, the county, or the state.
4Culture for 4 just outcomes: Make the Money Actually Reach Our Communities

4Culture has done important work, and the Doors Open program is a genuine step forward (sending roughly $70 million to 720 organizations in 2025! This is a massive expansion from the $10-15 million annual baseline.) But in my view, scaling programs is only equitable if the money reaches worthy creatives who’ve historically missed out on the opportunities and the fact is, too many grassroots organizations in District 2, especially BIPOC, queer or immigrant-led community organizations, still face structural barriers to accessing public arts funding. The application process is complex, deadlines are unforgiving, and organizations without development staff are routinely left out. As a Councilmember, I will work with 4Culture to:

Expand multilingual technical assistance so artists and organizations in communities with limited English proficiency can access every grant program -- not just via a phone number buried in the guidelines, but through proactive, funded support.
Simplify and streamline applications for smaller, community-based organizations -- reducing the gap between large institutions and emerging grassroots groups.
Increase the geographic floor for funding outside Seattle -- the 25% minimum for organizations outside the City of Seattle is a floor, not a ceiling. District 2 communities deserve a larger share.
Create a dedicated District 2 arts navigator -- a funded position to help small organizations build the capacity to compete.
People doing the work they were hired to do shouldn’t have to wonder whether they’ll ever get paid. Musicians shouldn’t have to become employment lawyers just to collect a check after a performance.
At the County, I’ll advocate for gig economy workers by:

• championing clear prompt-pay standards in County-funded contracts. Any venue, festival, arts organization, or event receiving King County funding should certify that performers are paid within a defined timeframe, such as within 30 days of a performance, regardless of whether they are classified as employees or independent contractors.

• I’ll also convene a roundtable with the Musicians’ Union, artists, venues, arts organizations, and legal advocates to develop standard arts worker contract templates that clearly outline payment timelines, cancellation policies, and dispute resolution processes. Too many performers rely on informal agreements that leave them vulnerable when problems arise.

King County does not control every aspect of employment classification, but it can set expectations and protect workers. If we value the gig workers, we should make sure they can count on being paid for the work they’ve already done.

pages.title: Meet Toshiko Hasegawa | Rooted in King County District 2 — Toshiko Hasegawa for King County Council, D2
paragraphs: My family has lived in our community for generations.
The house I’m raising my two young children in today is the same home on Beacon Hill my grandparents bought after they were released from Camp Minidoka, an American concentration camp.
It’s where they rebuilt their lives after losing everything and raised my father. It’s where he and my mother raised my sister and me.
And now, it’s where my kids are growing up, attending the same school their grandfather once did.
Today, the ability to afford to put down roots is out of reach for too many people in our community.

Staying rooted here has never been easy. Like so many families in the South End, we’ve lived through redlining, gentrification, and affordability crises that have pushed people out of the neighborhoods they love.
Remaining in place took sacrifice, advocacy, and an entire community looking out for one another.
That’s the legacy I come from. It’s also the responsibility I carry forward.
I was raised in a union household, where standing up for working people wasn’t an abstract value, it was daily life.

My dad was a labor organizer and Secretary-Treasurer of Teamsters Local 174. My mom is a mental health professional at King County and a proud member of SEIU 775. From them, I learned that real change doesn’t happen alone. It happens when people stand together and demand better.

I’m the proud product of the community that raised me: civil rights advocates who show it’s not just standing up for each other, but standing up with each other - centering people impacted the most and empowering them to use their own voice. We lift one another up, so all of us may rise.
That belief has guided my entire career, and is what brought me to public service.

Today, I serve as Port of Seattle Commissioner, and am proud to be the first woman of Asian ancestry elected to the Port in its over 110-year history, including most recently as Port Commission President.
Since I took office, we’ve transformed a relatively unrecognizable and unknown public institution into a powerhouse for progressive policy, delivering victories for our communities across the region.
Leadership isn’t about power. It’s about responsibility.
Championed expanded access to childcare and transit for airport workers
Ended the pink tax by providing free period products across Port facilities , including the airport
Advanced pay equity for non-represented workers and improved working conditions for union members
Launched the Teal New Deal as Port Commission President; Advancing Seattle as a clean energy manufacturing and supply chain hub
Strengthened local jobs while helping transform industries globally and sustain the workforce for the next 50 years.
Together, at the Port of Seattle, we’ve …
• prioritized unprecedented investments in job training and career pathways for youth, women, LGBTQIA2S+, indigenous, immigrant, refugee and people of color.
• protected North SeaTac Park from development.
• created pathways to grants for cities and communities who’ve never before accessed direct funds from the Port for community improvement.
• invested millions into community engagement and outreach, to begin building transparency and trust with communities that have too often been excluded from decision-making.
• delivered major capital projects to promote clean energy and sustainability in maritime and aviation.
Yes! We can dream big, fight hard, and do BIG things. This is the sense of urgency and the energy I am going to bring to the County Council.
If it’s possible at the Port, it’s possible at King County.
I worked there for years, including as staff to King County Councilmember Jeanne Kohl-Welles, where I supported work on the Law and Justice Committee.

During that time I was appointed by Governor Inslee to the State Task Force on Deadly Force in Community Policing, where I helped advance reforms that became the foundation for Initiative 940, a landmark change to Washington’s police accountability laws.

I directly supported survivors of police violence, as well as families who lost loved ones to deadly force, hired by the County Council to help reboot the County’s Office of Law Enforcement Oversight, which serves as checks and balances to the King County Sheriff’s Office. I listened to their grief, their anger, and their need for answers.
I learned how deeply systems can fail people, and how much accountability, compassion, and transparency matter in moments of crisis.

Before running and serving two-terms as a Port Commissioner, I advised Governor Inslee, his administration legislature, and all other state agencies on policies, programs and laws that impact historically excluded and underserved communities as Executive Director of the Washington State Commission on Asian Pacific American Affairs, a cabinet-level agency at the State of Washington.
Accountability, transparency, and compassion matter.
Everything I’ve done comes back to one question: how do we make government work for everybody?
People just want to be able to set down roots and thrive in the places they love. They want to live dignified, secure lives in healthy, safe and thriving neighborhoods.
I’m raising my two beautiful children in the same family home my grandparents rebuilt their lives in after the camps, because I believe community is worth fighting for.
I believe affordability, accountability, and justice aren’t separate issues; they’re deeply connected.
And I believe leadership should always be rooted in lived experience, humility, and a commitment to leaving things better for the next generation.
Generation by generation, counting on community has been the key.
This is who I am. I would be honored to earn your support.

pages.title: Re-Elect Jorge Barón to King County Council District 4
paragraphs: Re-Elect Jorge L. Barón for King County Council, District 4

pages.title: Vision — Elect Jorge Baron - King County Council District 4
paragraphs: My vision for King County is grounded in the value that our success as a community depends on the well-being of every one of our neighbors. And my approach to policy-making is centered on the concept that those most directly impacted by public policies should be involved in the shaping of those policies.

There are two overarching issues that inform how approach all policy areas. First, racial justice. I recognize that so many of the challenges we face as a county–and as a society–are driven by the ongoing impact of systemic racism. I believe it is essential to use a racial justice lens when evaluating policies in all these issue areas.

Second, I believe that we will not be able to make sufficient progress in any of these issue areas if we do not address the way that county services are funded. It is essential that we generate new urgency to the work with state legislators to develop progressive sources of revenue that will support the investments necessary to tackle the challenges in all of these areas.
People are not 'vulnerable' or 'voiceless'; they are powerful, courageous agents of change, in their own lives, the lives of their families, and of their communities.

Our national political landscape has changed significantly since I was first elected to the King County Council in 2023. At the time, a second Trump Administration was a daunting possibility, but now it’s a reality that is threatening the safety and well-being of so many, especially our immigrant and transgender neighbors. It is a reality that threatens state and local governments with depriving them of funding if they don’t succumb to the pressures of the federal administration. It is a reality that sees masked federal agents violating the constitutional rights–and even taking the lives–of people in our communities.

Particularly at a time like this, I believe it is crucial to have leaders in state and local government who will be uncompromising in defending and advancing our community’s values in the face of an increasingly chaotic and authoritarian federal administration. This is an important part of the work I have been doing on the county council: strengthening our county’s policies to protect immigrant communities; working to protect our health and human services infrastructure from the impacts of cruel federal funding cuts; and standing up for our transgender community members.

Continuing to stand up for our community’s values is one of the primary reasons I am running for re-election to the county council. I have spent most of my professional career advancing and defending human rights and I will continue to be a fierce advocate of those values on the council if given the opportunity to serve.

I’m deeply committed to promoting public safety in King County through a thoughtful and community-centered approach. I recognize the importance of a holistic approach to public safety that goes beyond traditional law enforcement measures. I believe in investing in preventative strategies, such as community-based programs, youth development initiatives, and mental health services, to address the underlying causes of crime and reduce recidivism. I also believe in upholding the health and safety of our first responders.

During my first term on the council, I served as chair of the Law and Justice committtee. In that role, I have worked to ensure that the King County Sheriff’s Office and the Department of Adult and Juvenile Detention prioritize transparency and accountability. I support measures to strengthen law enforcement oversight, enhance training in de-escalation techniques, and promote unbiased policing practices. My approach to this issue has been informed by my work as a member of the Joint Legislative Task Force on the Use of Deadly Force in Community Policing. Furthermore, I understand the need to address systemic inequalities within the criminal legal system. I’m dedicated to implementing reforms that reduce racial disparities in policing, sentencing, and incarceration. I have worked and will continue to work to eliminate discriminatory practices and promote fairness and equity at every level of the criminal legal system.

I am deeply thankful for the leadership of Washington State on gun safety - particularly for Representative Liz Berry - and I know we must do more at the county level. Lockdown drills have been a routine fixture of my children’s school lives and all three of my kids have been outspoken advocates for gun safety. My middle daughter in particular has led walk-outs, mobilized her peers, spoken to the media, and engaged legislators to secure mental health resources for our public schools and ban assault weapons. I will continue to partner with young people and advocate for accelerated progress in addressing the public health crisis of gun violence. It is untenable that gun violence is the leading cause of death for children and youth in our country, and also disproportionately impacts communities of color.

I am committed to continuing to work collaboratively with community leaders, law enforcement agencies, first responders, social service providers, and stakeholders to achieve these goals and ensure that public safety is a shared priority and responsibility.
We must address the crisis of homelessness in King County with urgency, centering the experiences and needs of our unhoused neighbors.

A comprehensive approach to solving homelessness combines short-term emergency measures with long-term strategies. Immediate shelter and support services are crucial to providing stability and dignity to individuals experiencing homelessness, and we must increase investments in affordable housing because safe and stable housing is the most effective solution to ending homelessness in the long-term. Addressing the root causes of homelessness also require expanding access to mental health services, substance use treatment, and increasing tenant protections.

During my first term on the county council, I have served on the Governing Board of the King County Regional Homeless Authority (KCRHA). I have prioritized streamlining the governing structure of the agency and ensuring that it is able to carry out its mission. I have also worked to protect funding for homelessness services, particularly in light of federal funding cuts.
Access to safe, affordable housing is a fundamental human right and essential for building strong and equitable communities.

We must take a comprehensive and inclusive approach to tackling the housing crisis. I will continue to advocate for the development of affordable housing options that cater to the diverse needs of King County residents, including low-income families, seniors, and individuals experiencing homelessness.

Housing affordability is interconnected with other social and economic factors. I’m committed to fostering partnerships with community organizations, local businesses, and government agencies to create innovative solutions and increase affordable housing stock in King County.

I understand the significance of equitable development and the need to address historical disparities. I will prioritize policies that promote equitable distribution of housing resources, reduce segregation, and combat housing discrimination.

I’m dedicated to promoting housing stability and ensuring that every resident of King County has access to safe, affordable, and dignified housing. Through collaborative efforts and bold initiatives, I will work to create sustainable and inclusive communities where everyone can thrive.

As a member of the King County Council, I am committed to improving transportation and transit in our region. I understand that a well-functioning transportation system is essential for the economic vitality, livability, and accessibility of our communities.

I believe in investing in a comprehensive and multimodal transportation network that serves the needs of all residents. This includes prioritizing the expansion of public transit options to provide reliable and efficient transportation choices for commuters, students, and residents throughout King County.

During my first term on the King County Council, I served as chair of the Regional Transit Committee and advocated for increased funding and resources to improve and expand our public transit and active transportation infrastructure. I have also worked to ensure that our public transit system is accessible, affordable, and convenient for all, including those with disabilities and those living in low-income communities.

I also recognize that safety on our public transit system and especially on our Metro buses is critical: if people do not feel safe riding the bus, we will not have an effective transit system. I served as part of the King County Transit Safety Task Force and will continue to advocate for the implementation of its recommendations.

By championing comprehensive transportation solutions, investing in public transit, promoting sustainable modes of transportation, addressing transportation equity, and prioritizing safety, I will continue to work to create a transportation system that enhances the quality of life for all residents of King County and supports our region's continued growth and prosperity.

The district my family calls home is a vibrant hub for the arts with many important arts and cultural institutions. A thriving, resourced, and diverse arts community is a core component of a strong King County.

I am proud of my family’s involvement in the arts. Growing up, I saw my father using music and arts as an avenue to bring peace to Colombia as our country navigated internal conflict. I learned from him the importance of cultivating and uplifting local talent, as he worked to bring Colombian artists national and international attention. After college, I worked in the film industry before my interest in civil rights drove me to attend law school. Now, I see the impact and importance of strong arts, music, and theater in our public schools through my three children. My middle daughter trained at the Seattle Children’s Theater, and the experience has led her to wish to pursue a college degree in theater. I’m grateful to the arts community in Seattle for the opportunities it has provided my family, and I will continue to be a strong advocate for the arts and culture community on the King County Council.

We must ensure that arts and cultural programs are open to all communities across the county. I will continue to work to develop policies and initiatives that promote diversity, equity, and inclusion within the arts community. As a county, we have an exciting opportunity to address historical disparities in funding and representation.

We must foster climate resilience to ensure a sustainable future for King County for generations to come. Climate change is here, and I am dedicated to implementing comprehensive strategies that address the intersectional nature of our climate crisis.

I also recognize that the climate crisis is disproportionately impacting communities of color, who are bearing the brunt of the public health impacts from wildfires, flooding and extreme heat. I will therefore continue to approach this issue as one of climate justice, prioritizing the mitigation of impacts of the crisis on marginalized communities.

I am committed to stewarding the abundant natural resources of the Puget Sound region through conservation and restoration, protecting biodiversity and ensuring sustainable land use practices throughout King County.

pages.title: Meet Jorge — Elect Jorge Baron - King County Council District 4
paragraphs: Jorge L. Barón's formative experiences as an immigrant greatly shaped his path as a civil rights leader. Jorge arrived in the United States from Bogotá, Colombia at the age of 13 and did not speak English, which led to bullying in school. He also had to assist his mom in raising his two younger brothers while she worked often late hours. Those experiences instilled in him a deep appreciation for hard work and resilience.

Despite initially not speaking English, Jorge's dedication and the support of an exceptional ESL teacher enabled him to overcome language barriers and excel academically. This experience fostered his love for this country and a profound understanding of the power of government. Jorge attended Duke University, propelled by his commitment to education and his desire to make a positive impact. After graduating from Duke, he worked in the film industry as an assistant director. He decided to leave the industry to pursue a career in law and helping people left behind in society. This led him to Yale Law School where he refined his passion for justice and met his wife, Tyler.

Throughout his career as a civil rights leader and Executive Director of the Northwest Immigrant Rights Project (NWIRP) for 15 years, Jorge fought tirelessly for what is right and for the safety of individuals and families. He dedicated decades to being a frontline human rights defender, advocating for keeping families together and providing safety to those fleeing violence. Notably, Jorge was a key local leader in responding to the first Trump Administration's policies, including the Muslim Ban, and worked diligently to prevent unjust deportations.

Jorge was elected to the King County Council in November 2023 and began serving in this new role in January 2024. During his time on the council, Jorge has focused on issues that residents of District 4 have asked him to prioritize: ensuring our criminal and civil legal systems are operating effectively and fairly so we can enhance community safety; stabilizing and strengthening our homelessness response system so we can reduce the number of people living unhoused in our region; and protecting our public health clinics and investing in our county hospital, Harborview Medical Center, so we can preserve access to health care. More recently, Jorge has also focused on protecting the county and its residents from misguided policies and unlawful actions from the Trump Administration. For the first two years of his term, Jorge served as chair of the Law and Justice Committee and now serves as chair of the Committee of the Whole. As a sign of the respect he has earned from his colleagues, Jorge was unanimously selected as a vice-chair of the council after only two years of service on the body.

Jorge's leadership and commitment to upholding justice and equality have been recognized through numerous interviews, articles, and awards. Community leaders have praised his efforts in defending civil rights. Now Governor Bob Ferguson, for example, credits Jorge as the driving force behind the establishment of the civil rights division in the Attorney General's office.
Motivated by his experiences and the desire to improve the lives of marginalized communities, Jorge ran for office in 2023 to continue his work and strengthen the county's critical safety net.

Beyond his work, Jorge also has personal interests and hobbies including a deep love for nature, as well as a lifelong love of fútbol (soccer). Additionally, he finds solace in the Pacific Northwest wilderness through activities like backpacking, hiking, and snowshoeing, often sharing these experiences with his wife and children. He is a proud husband to Tyler, and father to Isabella, Luna, and Luca.
