Teresa’s track record on King County Council proves she’ll put the people of our region first. We are proud to endorse Teresa for King County Council District 8!”

“ MLK Labor is proud to endorse King County Councilmember Teresa Mosqueda for re‑election. As someone who rose directly from the ranks of the labor movement, she has never lost sight of our values. Throughout her service in public office, Councilmember Mosqueda has been steadfast in her commitment to working people and their rights on the job. She consistently centers the well‑being of working families and sets a standard for leadership across our region. Unions appreciate her work fighting for fair pay, enforcement of labor standards, and the essential public services that working families depend on.”

With your support, I will continue to be the champion for residents of District 8 in King County by providing the infrastructure that allows every person to achieve economic security and improve population health. Learn more about my King County Council re-election priorities:
Public Health: community health, healthy youth, healthy workforce
Build Housing: workforce housing, supportive housing, green housing
Working Family Stability: healthcare, childcare, transit, living-wage jobs

pages.title: A Healthy, Housed and Resilient King County - Teresa Mosqueda
paragraphs: I am running for King County Council District 8 to improve the opportunity for local families to be healthy, housed, and resilient. We can do this by investing in greater behavioral health and public health support, addressing displacement and expanding housing that make it possible for people to stay stably housed, and investing in what working families and small businesses need: affordable childcare, accessible transit, and good job opportunities.

With your support, I have delivered on policy and made significant investments to support small businesses, provide cash assistance for workers, pass grants for childcare expansion, rental assistance for working families and small landlords, cash relief for immigrants and refugees, and food security for King County families. With your support, I will continue to be that champion for District 8 in King County to create a more equitable and healthy economy and community for all by providing the infrastructure that allows every person to achieve economic security and improve population health.

The importance and the vulnerability of the public health system is on full display since the pandemic hit our region. This includes vulnerabilities in our systems due to gaps in resources and services for behavioral health as we see more people with compounding health crises experiencing homelessness and a lack of places to care for them. My priorities are to:

Increase funding and support for Public Health Seattle/King County to have a stable workforce and adequate resources necessary to address our compounding health crises today and the possible public health emergencies of the future.

Address gun, youth, and interpersonal violence as the public health crisis they are by expanding gun awareness programming and money for dispute resolution programming to educate youth on the severe risks and dangerous consequences of having a gun at school, coupled with direct funding to community based programming for cultural and linguistically appropriate services.

Increase access to care by investing in behavioral health services and workers, support human service providers who care for those who are experiencing homelessness or living in supportive housing by creating wage parity and creating career ladders into public health service.

These investments are more important than ever, as we see the shadow pandemic of isolation and depression compound the public health crisis of addiction and the looming global pandemic. I will bring my commitment to creating a healthy community for all as the central pillar of my service to King County residents.

While we have made massive investments in creating additional housing in King County, it’s just not enough to serve the population who work in the county , let alone the number of people who are coming to our region. While we have made massive investments in creating additional housing in King County, it’s just not enough to serve the population who work in the county , let alone… We need additional housing options, as well as holistic services to care for vulnerable individuals so they can stay housed and healthy. King County has the ability to invest in both the capital infrastructure needed to build housing and the workforce needed to keep folks stably housed. My priorities are to:

Address displacement and increase workforce housing across District 8. From Vashon Island to Tukwila and north to throughout West Seattle and First Hill, employers and workers have told me that they need workforce housing in this district. Teachers, nurses, construction workers – workers of all kinds – are getting priced out and pushed out of our region. When we invest in building more workforce housing, it creates more opportunity for workers and business owners to have greater opportunity and stability.
Support and grow the “supportive housing” workforce that provides care to vulnerable community members are being re-housed so people stay housed and healthy.

Create incentives to build more green, lasting and affordable housing throughout our region in partnership with local jurisdictions and communities to promote density, greenspace, trees, and community cohesion as part of the effort to combat climate change.

The lack of housing across our region has caused the cost of a home to skyrocket for working families across King County, resulting in displacement for working families and especially among communities of color. I’m committed to working with local jurisdictions and prioritizing funding to expand the opportunity for first time home ownership, building affordable housing options across our region, and addressing the root causes of displacement.

Engaging in economic opportunities that support small businesses or create good union jobs creates stability and prosperity, especially for women, people of color, lower wage workers, which in turn helps address the gender and racial exclusion from good living wage jobs in our region. My priorities are:

Expand accessible and affordable childcare in our county by supporting workforce pay, career pipelines and creating the infrastructure needed to deliver childcare service, which in turn support workers and small businesses.

Provide accessible transit around our region continuing to push for more cost efficient and sufficient Sound Transit service in SODO and West Seattle, support rider safety and workforce needs on Metro busses, and advance a Transportation Benefit District for King County to invest in much needed road repairs in unincorporated King County, like White Center and Vashon Island.

Continue to promote good living wage jobs for all by investing in job-training, union apprenticeships, and Community Workforce Agreement requirements. These investments support workers and our local economy by ensuring the wealth that is being generated is shared – allowing more spending in local small businesses and thus economic growth.

The diverse needs of neighbors across District 8 require someone who will be a champion, a work horse, a listener and an organizer, and an action taker who will serve in partnership with the local leaders and community members from White Center to Burien and Tukwila, from Vashon Island through the Duwamish Valley to South Park and Georgetown, to the Chinatown International District, First Hill and Pike Place Market area. I will deliver on the vision of a healthy economy and community throughout this diverse District with a focus on improving the public’s health, housing, and worker & small businesses support necessary to create opportunity for all.

pages.title: About - Teresa Mosqueda
paragraphs: In the heart of the Puget Sound here in King County’s District 8, nestled in West Seattle, is my home. My husband and I are raising our daughter in a community surrounded by working families, play areas and parks, nearby public beaches, bustling small businesses, bike lanes and trails, community centers and childcare, and multiple lines of transit. As a Progressive Labor Democrat , this type of diverse, welcoming neighborhood is my hope for every resident of our region. As your District 8 King County Councilmember, that vision has fueled the policy goals I have championed to expand and improve the health and economic opportunity for all.

Throughout my career, I have brought together diverse coalitions to pass impactful policy by being principled and inclusive. By uniting labor, business, housing, transit and environmental advocates, I was able to pass meaningful and lasting policies that have earned the public’s support, and buoyed our local economy. I was named one of Seattle’s Most Influential People 2018 for my dedication to acting with urgency on critical legislation immediately upon coming into office. I am proud to have receive the Local Progress 2019 Ady Barkan Progressive Champion Award, and in 2020, and earned national attention by leading the passage of progressive revenue to invest in housing, economic resilience, green new deal investments and equitable development.

Working to eradicate the root causes of poverty and improve community health has been the focus of the work throughout my career. While on King County Council, serving as the Health, Housing and Human Services Committee Chair and the regional Board of Health Chair, I actively worked to generate and pass legislation to strengthen community resilience, health and opportunity. Recognizing that our population health improves when we invest in the social determinants of health, I have fought for and expanded worker protections, the ability to create affordable and multi-family housing, and expanded funding for critical hospital services and public health food inspections, among other policy wins.

On the S eattle City Coun cil , I have doubled the investments in affordable housing, improved worker standards and protections for domestic workers and hotel workers, ensured sick leave for drivers, and supported small business opportunities especially for women and people of color. Prior to getting elected twice to serve the residents of Seattle, I served over half-a-million union workers in our state while working at Washington State Labor Council, AFL-CIO for almost a decade. In this role, I advocated for progressive state legislation to improve labor standards, protect immigrant rights, create healthy and safer workplaces, and promote health care for all. In this role I also helped lead the state-wide passage of I-1433 to provide paid sick leave and increase the minimum wage for all.

At the Children’s Alliance, I led the coalition efforts to implement Apple Health for Kids to ensure every child in our state had health insurance, and advanced nutrition and early learning policies to create a healthy start in life for all kids. I was appointed by Governor Inslee twice to serve terms on the Affordable Care Act (ACA) Exchange Board, where I fought to ensure health coverage that was promised under Obamacare was delivered. While working at the Washington State Department of Health as the legislative coordinator for the Community and Family Health Division, I completed my Master’s Degree in Public Administration. But my roots in community health start right here in District 8, where after graduating from UW, I worked at SeaMar Community Health Centers in South Park serving Latino seniors with food security, housing assistance, healthcare and social interaction programs.

I grew up in the Puget Sound, a third-generation Mexican-American, daughter of educators and policy wonks who fought for social justice and against oppression. As a Chicana, I am proud of what I have been able to do to create greater opportunity and equity for marginalized communities and workers while in office. But ther e is much more work to be accomplished to share our region’s prosperity and create more accessible, affordable, safe communities for families across southwest King County. With your continued support, I would love the honor of continuing to create more healthy, equitable, affordable and accessible communities for all by serving you on King County Council, District 8.

pages.title: DUDA FOR KING COUNTY COUNCIL
paragraphs: A practical Democrat focused on outcomes, accountability, and making King County work better for the people who live here.
“Ask yourself honestly: is our region better off than it was nine years ago?”

Everyone I talk with in our district wants the same things: safe streets, good schools, treatment for those who are suffering, clean air and water, an affordable place to raise a family or start a business, and a government responsive to its community.

My campaign is about improving our outcomes. That means public safety with real accountability, compassionate paths to recovery, more housing, better transit, and a government that measures success by results, not spending.
Real consequences for dealers and traffickers. Real competence to keep our streets safe.
1- Fix the intake system. Properly staff jail medical intake so arrests do not routinely turn into failed bookings or hours-long hospital waits.
2 - Take trafficking seriously. Target pimps and traffickers while giving victims housing, services, and a path to clear their records.
3 - Restore consequences. Use diversion where appropriate, but escalate consequences for chronic and organized offenders.
Protect communities → Restore consequences → Rebuild trust
Compassion means helping people recover. Accountability means expecting change and working toward independence.
1 - Treatment when people need it. Expand public capacity and utilize private treatment beds when necessary.
2 - Intervene earlier. Create stabilization centers and fix the broken jail medical-intake process.
3 - Build sober housing. Give people in recovery somewhere safe to live away from active drug use and dealing.
Stabilize → Treat → Recover → Rebuild Independence
If we're going to invest billions in transit, we should build around it, protect it, and make it work for everyone.
1- Make transit safer and fairer. Accessible fare gates paired with reduced and free fares for people who qualify.
2 -Build more housing near light rail. Allow substantially more density within several blocks of stations.
3 - Create complete neighborhoods. Make room for groceries, childcare, and everyday needs around transit.
More Housing → Safer Transit → Higher Ridership → Better Value
04 - ACCOUNTABILITY & MEASURABLE OUTCOMES
Set measurable goals. Publish the results. Scale what works. Change what doesn't. Strengthen audits and contract oversight before failures become crises.
Stabilize → Treat → Recover → Rebuild Independence
1 - Fast-track permitting Clear timelines and one accountable point of contact.
2 - Protect industrial land Keep the space, power, freight and infrastructure needed to build.
3 - Build the workforce Train machinists, technicians, engineers and skilled trades.
4 - Become a proving ground Use measurable pilots to let local companies solve public problems.
King County should be the best place in America to build the technologies of the future.
Build it here → Grow it here → Create family-wage jobs here
If you believe government should be ambitious about helping people and equally serious about measuring results, join the campaign.

pages.title: Home — DUDA FOR KING COUNTY COUNCIL
paragraphs: My opponent has been in elected office for 9 years. During her time, open-air drug markets have grown exponetiailly in the CID, trafficking flourished on Aurora, businesses left our region, and hundreds of millions of dollars were spent
Compassion means protecting people from harm. Accountability means enforcing reasonable rules.

pages.title: Public Safety — DUDA FOR KING COUNTY COUNCIL
paragraphs: Public safety depends on a basic social contract: people should be able to walk through their neighborhood, run a business, or raise a family without being routinely subjected to violence, theft, or open drug activity. They should also be able to feel safe while doing so.
In many ways, we are far too lenient on crimes with real impact, and too punitive for many others.

A society that allows disorder and unfairness in the criminal justice system creates distrust and skepticism. The healthiest communities don’t experience this, but it’s all too common on parts of our region. Here are tangible actions and priorities to address this.
Police officers should not spend hours in hospital rooms because the jail cannot safely process someone they have already arrested.
Police officers should not spend hours in hospital waiting rooms because the jail cannot safely process someone they have already arrested.
Today, medical declines can turn otherwise valid arrests into hours-long hospital trips, taking officers off the street and sometimes resulting in the individual never being booked at all.
Properly staff jail medical intake so the jail can safely accept people with common medical and substance-use issues.
Create clear medical-intake standards so officers, hospitals, and jail staff know when hospital care is actually necessary.
Use stabilization facilities when appropriate for people who need short-term observation or treatment rather than an emergency room.
Track medical declines and failed bookings so the public can see how often they happen, why they happen, and what happens afterward.
An arrest should not become meaningless because different parts of government cannot coordinate.
2 — Serious crimes of exploitation warrant serious action.
Our region should have far less tolerance for the people who profit from exploitation, both via sex trafficking and drug dealing. our failure to act this way is the biggest stain on our region.
For those who exploit the vulnerable, like pimps and fentanyl dealers, law enforcement should treat these as the most serious crimes, and our judicial system should have no leeway here.
For their victims, we should meet them with treatment, safe housing, and services and depending on their needs.
Aggressively pursue pimps, dealers, and organized exploitation.
Provide victims with safe housing and immediate services so leaving a trafficker does not mean becoming homeless.
Connect victims with treatment, counseling, employment, and legal assistance.
Create meaningful pathways to clear criminal records associated with exploitation when victims successfully exit trafficking and cooperate with appropriate services or investigations.
The objective should be straightforward: make life much harder for traffickers, much easier for victims to escape them, and much safer for victims to testify against them.
Diversion can work. Treatment can work. Second chances matter.

We have a system currently that aims to be compassionate through diversion, but a system without escalation eventually stops being compassionate—to victims, neighborhoods, businesses, and even to people cycling endlessly through the criminal justice system without meaningful intervention.
King County should use a graduated approach:
First intervene with diversion, treatment, or other alternatives when circumstances warrant it.
Set clear expectations and measurable requirements for diversion programs rather than treating participation itself as success.
Escalate consequences for repeated offenses when previous interventions have failed.
Focus enforcement on chronic and organized offenders responsible for disproportionate harm.
Create pathways to expungement after genuine rehabilitation so accountability does not become a permanent barrier to employment and stability.
The principle is generous opportunities to change, paired with real accountability when those opportunities are repeatedly rejected.
4 — Prevent violence before it becomes a lifetime pattern.
Public safety cannot begin only after someone commits a serious crime.
For young people at risk of becoming involved in gangs or gun violence, King County should combine focused enforcement with strong alternatives:
Expand youth sports, mentorship, employment, and after-school opportunities in neighborhoods experiencing persistent violence.
Intervene earlier with young people repeatedly involved in serious offenses.
Coordinate schools, families, community organizations, law enforcement, and behavioral-health providers around the small number of individuals at greatest risk.
Advocate for state laws that allow meaningful intervention before repeated serious offenses escalate into shootings or homicide.
Accountability and prevention are not opposing ideas. The best public-safety systems do both.
A stronger public-safety system also requires public confidence in the people enforcing the law.
We should recruit, train, and retain excellent officers, compensate them competitively, and expect professionalism in return.
Competitive staffing and compensation so agencies can attract strong candidates.
High standards for conduct and training.
Clear performance expectations and transparent accountability.
Better coordination between law enforcement, courts, treatment providers, prosecutors, and corrections so officers are not repeatedly asked to solve failures elsewhere in the system.
We should expect a lot from law enforcement—and give them a functioning system in which to do their jobs.
Protect communities → Intervene early → Restore consequences → Reward rehabilitation → Rebuild trust
Public safety does not require choosing between compassion and accountability.
A functioning system should provide people every reasonable opportunity to get back on their feet—and protect the community when they refuse.

pages.title: Treatment and Recovery — DUDA FOR KING COUNTY COUNCIL
paragraphs: Our region has spent enormous sums addressing homelessness, yet the number of people living outside remains far too high. One reason is that we too often talk about homelessness as if it has a single cause.
Someone who loses a job, faces an unexpected medical bill, or experiences another short-term financial crisis needs help quickly getting back on their feet. We should provide that help.
But someone living outside while struggling with severe addiction needs something different: intervention, treatment, recovery support, and ultimately a pathway back toward independence.

Failing to distinguish the difference between these situations has led us to spend more while accepting outcomes that should be unacceptable—for people suffering from addiction and for the communities around them.
Our goal should be clear: help people get healthy, regain stability and autonomy, and move toward independent lives whenever possible.
We don't have enough treatment capacity.
For too many people experiencing serious addiction, treatment isn't readily available when the moment for intervention arrives.
Our region spends heavily on homelessness services and subsidized housing, but dedicates far less capacity to the treatment and recovery services necessary to help people leave addiction behind.
Housing matters, but for someone suffering from severe addiction, housing alone is not treatment.
Expand public capacity and use private treatment beds when necessary.
King County should have enough treatment capacity so that someone who is ready, or required, to enter treatment does not have to wait weeks for a bed.
Expand public treatment capacity , particularly residential and intensive treatment.
Contract with qualified private providers when public beds are unavailable.
Shift resources toward recovery when existing homelessness programs consistently fail to produce better outcomes.
Measure success based on whether people stabilize, complete treatment, remain in recovery, and ultimately move toward greater independence.
Treatment should be available when the opportunity for recovery exists—not weeks or months later.
Our current system too often cycles people between the street, emergency rooms, jail, shelters, and service providers without creating a meaningful point of intervention.
One example is our broken jail medical-intake process.

When police arrest someone who reports recently ingesting drugs or presents certain medical concerns, officers may have to take that person to a hospital rather than directly to jail. That can consume hours of police time while still doing little to address the underlying addiction.
We need a better option between doing nothing and relying on either an emergency room or jail.
Create stabilization centers and fix jail medical intake.
King County should develop stabilization facilities where law enforcement, outreach teams, and other responders can bring people experiencing serious addiction or behavioral-health crises.
Immediate medical assessment and stabilization.
Withdrawal management and connection to treatment.
A safe alternative to unnecessary emergency-room stays.
Direct pathways into residential treatment when appropriate.
Coordination with law enforcement when someone has been arrested or presents a public-safety risk.
At the same time, we should ensure the King County Jail has the medical staffing and protocols necessary to safely accept people who can appropriately be booked there.
The goal is simple: intervene sooner, stabilize people faster, and connect them directly to treatment instead of sending them back through the same revolving door.
Know Who Needs Help—and What's Available
Effective intervention also requires much better information.

King County should maintain a privacy-protected, real-time by-name system that allows authorized providers to understand who is repeatedly interacting with homelessness, behavioral-health, emergency, and justice systems.
We should also maintain real-time information about available shelter, stabilization, detox, and treatment beds.
Keep people from falling through the cracks.
Better understand each person's needs and history.
Match people with an available bed faster.
Hold publicly funded organizations accountable for results.

We live in one of the world's leading technology regions. There is no reason our response to one of our greatest humanitarian crises should operate with fragmented information and incomplete visibility into available resources.
Recovery shouldn't mean returning to active drug use.
Low-barrier housing can play an important role in getting people off the street. But it should not be the only housing model we provide.
Someone who has completed treatment or is actively pursuing recovery should not have to return to an environment where drugs are readily available or dealing is tolerated.
That undermines recovery and makes independence harder to achieve.
Create substantially more sober recovery housing.
King County should ensure that people pursuing recovery have somewhere safe to live.
Create dedicated sober housing throughout the county-funded housing system.
Increase sober capacity each year based on demand.
Enforce clear rules against drug dealing in publicly funded housing.
Provide recovery-oriented services and peer support.
Help residents progress from treatment to recovery housing and eventually toward independent living whenever possible.
Housing should support recovery—not make recovery harder.
Diversion can be an effective alternative to incarceration, particularly for someone's first encounters with the justice system.
But diversion without meaningful accountability cannot become an endless cycle.

Addiction itself should not be treated as a moral failing or simply as a criminal problem. But addiction can contribute to theft, disorder, drug dealing, and other crimes that directly affect the surrounding community.
We need a system that is generous on the front end but accountable when repeated interventions fail.

For repeated drug-related offenses, after earlier opportunities for diversion and voluntary treatment, the justice system should be able to require participation in treatment as an alternative to incarceration, subject to appropriate legal safeguards and individualized assessment.
Diversion first. Treatment whenever possible. Accountability when repeated interventions fail.
We shouldn't abandon people to addiction, and we shouldn't ask communities to endlessly absorb the consequences of untreated addiction.
This is not about punishing people who are struggling.
It is about refusing to accept permanent addiction, permanent homelessness, or permanent dependence as the best outcome we can offer.
Identifies → Intervenes → Treats → Stabilizes → Supports Recovery → Builds Independence
That is more compassionate for people suffering from addiction, more respectful of our communities, and a better use of public resources.

pages.title: Housing & Transit — DUDA FOR KING COUNTY COUNCIL
paragraphs: King County and our region are investing billions of dollars in transit. We should make sure those investments produce more than just trains and stations.

They should help us build more housing, create safer and more reliable transit, and support neighborhoods where people can get to work, school, groceries, childcare, and everyday needs without having to rely on a car.
TOO MANY RIDERS AREN’T PAYING — AND THE SYSTEM ISN’T WORKING AS WELL AS IT SHOULD
Sound Transit has struggled with fare compliance even while offering reduced and subsidized fares for people who need them.
It undermines basic fairness. Riders who pay should not feel like following the rules is optional.
It reduces revenue at a time when Sound Transit faces enormous financial pressure to deliver the transit system voters were promised.
Open stations make it harder to manage behavior and maintain safe, orderly platforms and trains.
It weakens public trust in a system taxpayers are spending billions of dollars to build.
A compassionate transit system should make sure people can afford to ride.
An accountable transit system should also expect people to pay when they can.
ACCESSIBLE FARE GATES + AFFORDABLE FARES
Install modern, accessible fare gates at Link stations while expanding reduced and free fare programs for riders who qualify.
If you can afford the fare, you should pay it. If you can’t, we should make sure cost isn’t the reason you can’t ride.
Other transit systems, including BART in the Bay Area, are increasingly using modern fare gates to reduce fare evasion and improve station conditions.
King County and Sound Transit should pair:
Accessible fare gates that work for people with disabilities, luggage, bikes, and strollers.
Reduced and free fares for low-income riders and others who qualify.
Clear expectations and consistent enforcement instead of a system where the rules frequently feel optional.
Clean, safe stations and vehicles that people want to use.
The goal is to make transit affordable enough that everyone can use it — and orderly enough that everyone wants to.
OUR ZONING DOESN’T MATCH THE SCALE OF OUR TRANSIT INVESTMENT
The areas within walking distance of frequent, high-capacity transit should be among the easiest places in the region to build substantially more housing.
We are spending billions of dollars building light rail, but in too many places we still treat the land around stations as though nothing fundamental has changed.
Our current approach is often too timid:
We under-build around some of our most valuable public investments.
Development requirements make projects difficult to finance, meaning less housing actually gets built.
We push housing growth farther into surrounding neighborhoods because we don't allow enough density immediately around transit.
We miss the opportunity to create neighborhoods where daily trips can happen without a car.
Allow significantly more housing within several blocks of major light-rail stations — including buildings of roughly 15–20 stories where appropriate.
We should be ambitious about building housing where our infrastructure can support it.
Thousands of additional homes in places with excellent transit access.
More opportunities for people to live with one car or no car at all, resulting in less congestion on our streets
A larger customer base supporting transit ridership and nearby businesses.
More housing supply without placing the same development pressure on every surrounding residential block.
More property and sales-tax revenue generated from the infrastructure we've already paid to build.
We have made a generational investment in light rail and our zoning should reflect it.
If we're going to build more homes near transit, we should also make those areas excellent places to live.
That means creating space for the things families and residents need every day:
Too often, we talk about housing and transportation as separate policies, but they’re not.
A family that can walk to childcare, take light rail to work, and pick up groceries on the way home has a fundamentally different transportation burden than a family that needs a car for every trip.
That can mean lower household costs, less traffic, higher transit ridership, and stronger neighborhood businesses.
We shouldn't simply build apartments next to stations.
We should build complete neighborhoods around them.
This is how we get more value from the billions we're already investing:
Create neighborhoods where people can meet more of their daily needs close to home.
And make our enormous transportation investments work harder for the people paying for them.
MORE HOUSING. SAFER TRANSIT. BETTER NEIGHBORHOODS.
This is possible with the right political will.

pages.title: Accountability — DUDA FOR KING COUNTY COUNCIL
paragraphs: Good government isn’t measured by how much we spend.
We have an accountability problem in our region.
Too often, elected leaders point to how much money we spend as evidence of how seriously we are taking a problem. But the more important question is: What are we getting for it?

Are fewer people homeless? Are more people recovering from addiction? Is transit safer and more reliable? Are projects being delivered on time? Are taxpayers receiving more services for every dollar we spend?
I believe in robust public services. I believe government can, and should, help people who need it. But believing in strong public services also means demanding that those services actually work.
Fiscal responsibility and liberal government are not opposites. In fact, without accountability, waste ultimately means fewer services, higher taxes, and less public trust.
WE WAIT TOO LONG TO DEMAND ACCOUNTABILITY
The stories across our region have become far too familiar.
Problems emerge. Warning signs are ignored. Budgets continue to grow. Years pass. And only after a failure becomes impossible to overlook do elected leaders demand reform.

Problems at the King County Regional Homelessness Authority became apparent years ago. Concerns about financial controls, contracting, governance, and basic organizational management continued to mount.
Yet meaningful intervention came only after the problems became a public crisis.
Whatever one thinks of the original promise of regional homelessness coordination, oversight should have happened before dysfunction became entrenched—not after.

My opponent was Budget Chair, and after the state found in 2022 that KCRHA lacked financial controls, she could have done something, and didn’t. Over $700M were spent in the years afterward and the issues only grew.
King County’s Department of Community and Human Services faced serious concerns about contracting and financial oversight, including fraud allegations and whistleblower complaints.

An audit later found an enormous gap between the county's own expectations for contract monitoring and what was actually occurring. The fixes were not brought by my opponent, who Chairs the committee with oversight over DCHS, and the issues raised in the audit were downplayed by her.
That matters because DCHS oversees billions of dollars in services for some of the most vulnerable people in our community.
Compassion without oversight doesn't protect vulnerable people. It puts the services they depend on at risk.
Sound Transit demonstrates the same problem on an even larger scale.

Major projects have repeatedly faced escalating costs, delays, and changing timelines. ST3 was sold to voters with one set of expectations; today, the price and delivery schedule look dramatically different. Our $54B package is now $148B, and doesn’t include a line to Ballard.
These aren't engineering problems, but rather they are accountability problems.

When taxpayers authorize major public investments, government has an obligation to clearly explain what is changing, why it is changing, who is responsible, and what is being done differently as a result.
Each of these examples reflects both a process failure and a leadership failure .
Audits matter. Reports matter. New policies matter.
But accountability cannot simply mean reacting after something has already gone wrong.
The job of elected officials is to ask difficult questions before the headlines appear:
Are programs achieving the outcomes promised?
Who is responsible when goals are repeatedly missed?
When warning signs appear, leaders should intervene early instead of waiting years for a crisis.
And when oversight repeatedly fails, we shouldn't automatically assume the same leadership that allowed the problem to grow is best positioned to fix it.
King County needs leaders willing to challenge institutions they support, demand answers from agencies they fund, and act before problems become crises.
There is an even bigger structural problem underneath these individual failures:
Our budget process is primarily designed around how much we spend—not what that spending accomplishes.
Ask a few basic questions about almost any major government program:
How much does it cost per person served?
What measurable outcome are we trying to change?
What does success look like one year from now?
What evidence tells us the program is working?
Too often, those questions do not have clear answers.
That makes real oversight nearly impossible.
If we cannot clearly define what success looks like before spending the money, it becomes very difficult to determine afterward whether taxpayers received what they paid for.
We need to replace the current cycle with:
Define the problem → Set the outcome → Fund the solution → Measure the result → Improve or scale
AN OUTCOME STATEMENT FOR EVERY MAJOR PROGRAM
Every King County program receiving more than $1 million annually should be required to publish a simple, public Outcome Statement .
What specific outcome are we trying to change?
What are we paying per person served or per outcome achieved?
What evidence suggests this approach will work?
Who is directly responsible for delivering the result?
Which populations and communities benefit?
What should taxpayers expect to see after Year 1?
What should taxpayers expect to see after Year 2?
These shouldn't be buried in 200-page budget documents.
They should be published in a simple public dashboard anyone can understand.
Measuring outcomes means very little if nothing changes when programs succeed or fail.
So the budget process should create real consequences.
If a major program cannot establish a measurable baseline, clear goals, and an accountable leader, 25% of its funding should be withheld until it can.
Government should not spend millions of dollars without being able to explain what taxpayers are purchasing.
Missing a target once does not automatically mean a program is bad.
Government deals with difficult problems, and responsible experimentation requires allowing programs to learn and improve.
But repeated failure should have consequences.
If a program materially misses its targets, it should receive a corrective-action period to demonstrate improvement.
If it still cannot produce results, funding should shrink, leadership should change, or the program should be redesigned.
Accountability isn't only about cutting things.
It's also about identifying what works and doing more of it.
If a treatment program produces better recovery outcomes, expand it.
If a homelessness intervention moves people into stable housing more effectively, scale it.
If a transit investment improves ridership and reliability, invest more.
The purpose of accountability isn't smaller government. It's better government.
Outcome-based budgeting should be paired with stronger auditing and contract monitoring.
Strengthen independent performance and financial audits.
Require agencies to respond publicly to major audit findings.
Track whether corrective actions are actually completed.
Increase contract-monitoring requirements for large service providers.
Publish performance information for major contractors.
Flag programs with repeated cost overruns or missed outcomes for Council review.
Give auditors the resources and independence necessary to identify problems early.
Audits should function as an early-warning system , not an autopsy after something has already failed.
The debate over government too often gets reduced to two choices:

If we reduce waste, improve contracting, catch problems sooner, and direct money toward programs that demonstrate results, we can provide more effective services without constantly asking residents to pay more.
That matters in a region where families are already struggling with housing costs, utilities, transportation, childcare, and taxes.
Every dollar wasted is a dollar that cannot go toward treatment, transit, housing, public safety, parks, or other services residents depend on.
Being responsible with public money isn't separate from providing strong public services. It's how we protect them.
Set measurable goals. Publish the results. Scale what works. Change what doesn't.
That's how we restore trust in government—and make every public dollar work harder for the people it is supposed to serve.

pages.title: Home - Elect Jan Trasen for District Court Judge
paragraphs: “As an experienced Administrative Law Judge, Judge Pro Tem, and public defender with decades of experience, I will improve access to justice and work for better outcomes for all court participants and the community.

I have dedicated my career to fairness, equal justice, and ensuring our courts work for everyone. I will bring my skills and temperament to the King County District Court to interpret the law, apply it to the facts, and ensure that all parties are treated fairly.”

Experience that spans the justice system —trial, appellate, administrative, and judicial perspectives. Courtroom compassion backed by fairness —a record of treating every party with respect while upholding the law. Community‑minded solutions —embracing mental‑health and substance‑use treatment options that reduce recidivism and make our neighborhoods safer.
Jan has spent her life turning empathy into action. With your support, she will keep doing exactly that—from the District Court bench—on behalf of every resident of King County.
Administrative Law Judge – Washington State Office of Administrative Hearings
Judge Pro Tem, King County District Court & Edmonds Municipal Court
Washington Appellate Project – Appellate practice in the Court of Appeals and Washington Supreme Court
Legal Aid Society- Trial practice in New York City trial courts
Cardozo Society Judicial Evaluation Committee Member
Ruby Room & National Charity League Board Member
Former Teach for America public school teacher

pages.title: About Jan - Elect Jan Trasen for District Court Judge
paragraphs: Jan Trasen is an Administrative Law Judge, Judge Pro Tem, and former public defender with decades of experience spanning multiple areas of practice.

Jan has spent her career standing up for fairness—first as a public defender, now from the bench. Jan also serves Washington families statewide as an Administrative Law Judge in the Office of Administrative Hearings Child & Family Care Division. There, she conducts hearings and issues final orders on cases that directly affect children’s safety, family stability, and access to critical services and medical care.

As a Judge Pro Tem for King County District Court and Edmonds Municipal Court, Jan presides over jury trials, arraignments, civil‑protection orders, and small‑claims matters, guiding every case with empathy, efficiency, and an unwavering respect for all who enter her courtroom.

Before taking the bench as an ALJ, Jan spent 26 years as a public defender —16 with the Washington Appellate Project and 10 with the Legal Aid Society—arguing before the Washington State Supreme Court and Court of Appeals and handling serious felony, misdemeanor, and juvenile cases. Her advocacy in criminal defense, dependency, Indian Child Welfare Act proceedings, and civil‑commitment matters helped expand access to justice for thousands of Washingtonians.

Jan’s dedication to public service began long before law school: she was part of Teach For America’s inaugural corps, teaching in an underserved Los Angeles middle school and mentoring students who still turn to her three decades later.

When not working or spending time with her two daughters, Jan is active in the community, serving on the Board of Directors of The Ruby Room , a Renton non-profit organization that supports low-income and foster-involved youth. She has also served on her local boards of the National Charity League and Lawyers Helping Hungry Children . Committed to cultivating the next generation of legal talent, Jan volunteers as a judge for mock‑trial and moot‑court competitions at the University of Washington and served on the Cardozo Society’s Judicial Evaluation Committee .

From the classroom to the courtroom, Jan Trasen has earned a reputation for balanced judgment, deep community roots, and a tireless commitment to justice—values she will bring to the District Court every single day.

pages.title: Bianca Tse | Judge | King County District Court
paragraphs: Justice for all through thoughtfulness, safety, and empathy.

Before a fair decision can be made, there must be time to listen. There are two sides to every story, and a good listener hears what others miss. A thoughtful judge will not judge a book by its cover or make decisions based on assumptions. Instead, the court should remain balanced and even-minded, carefully weighing the facts, listening to all sides, and taking the time to get it right. Every person who enters the courtroom deserves to be heard, respected, and treated fairly. That is thoughtful justice: balanced and fair.
16+ years of protecting the community as a King County Deputy Prosecuting Attorney , handling criminal cases ranging from misdemeanors to serious felonies, including homicide.
Served as a Judge Pro Tem since 2021 , presiding over criminal and civil matters in King County District Court and Eastside municipal courts.
Managed high-volume court calendars while giving careful and fair consideration to each case.
Leads Tse & Associates P.S. , providing legal services in civil litigation, real estate, business, and estate planning.

Everyone deserves to feel safe in their home, at work, and in their community. Safety begins long before a case reaches the courtroom, with strong communities, good policies, and the people who respond when something goes wrong. The courtroom is an important part of that process, where accountability can help prevent the same problems from happening again. That means treating the cause, not just the symptoms, and looking for thoughtful alternatives when they can make our communities stronger. A safe community protects the most vulnerable, offers a path forward, and practices compassionate, holistic accountability.
Tried dozens of cases before juries and judges, building extensive courtroom and trial experience.
Provided training to law enforcement on search and seizure issues and legal updates, supporting the proper application of the law.
Presided over evidentiary hearings and jury trials, bringing extensive criminal trial experience to the courtroom.
Successfully negotiated numerous legal disputes , helping clients reach favorable resolutions.

Walking a mile in someone else’s shoes means taking the time to understand what they may be carrying with them. Every person who enters a courtroom has a story, and understanding that story helps a judge make better, more thoughtful decisions. Whether seeking justice, facing accountability, or simply trying to move forward, every person deserves the same dignity we would hope for ourselves. Seeing the person, not just the case, reminds us that empathy costs nothing but can mean everything. Empathy does not mean lowering standards or excusing actions. It means building trust in the process while creating a path toward accountability, healing, and a better future.
Served as a court-appointed Guardian ad Litem for vulnerable children, investigating family circumstances and representing the child’s best interests.
Provided bilingual legal services, helping clients overcome language barriers and access legal advice.
Served families in need through KidVantage, helping support children from low-income families with basic necessities.
Supported young people in her community, including more than a decade as a Girl Scout troop co-leader and volunteering in Bellevue schools.
"Bianca would bring fairness, integrity and intelligence to the court. As a person of color, she would reflect the diversity of the community appearing in her court . . ."

My story began in Hong Kong. When I was 6 years old, the Tse Family (Pronounced "Say") came to the United States in search of a new life. We put down roots in King County, and I came to learn what so many immigrant families know well: nothing is handed to you. You work hard, help your family, and never forget where you came from. That belief has guided me in my life. I attended the University of Washington and later Tulane Law School. It was there, while working with people facing discrimination who could not always afford legal help, that I found my calling. I wanted to stand up in the courtroom and help people find their voice.

After law school, I came back home to King County and spent more than 16 years as a Deputy Prosecuting Attorney protecting the community. Handling everything from DUI and property crimes to robbery, assault, and homicide cases. I tried cases before juries and spent years learning that every case is more than a file. Behind every case are real people whose lives have been completely changed by what happens in the courtroom. Since 2021, I have served as a Judge Pro Tem across King County and the Eastside. My promise is simple: justice for all through thoughtful, safe, and empathetic leadership.

Today, I am a mother of two Bellevue school graduates and lead Tse & Associates, helping families, businesses, and members of our diverse community navigate the legal system. I am proud to provide bilingual legal services to help people who might otherwise struggle to be heard. When I am not practicing law, I give back by supporting families in need through non-profit boards and youth organizations across the Eastside.
From a young immigrant finding a new home to serving the community as a Judge Pro Tem, my journey has always been about one thing: Justice for all.
Endorsed by over 50+ trusted leaders in every corner of the Eastside.
Fmr. Associate Justice, Washington Supreme Court
State Representative 41st Legislative District
Presiding Judge, King County District Court, East Division
State Representative 48th Legislative District
Matthew York, Judge, King County District Court, South Division
"Bianca has the experience and judgment to make an outstanding judge ."
Building trust in the process while creating a path toward a better future.
Have a Question for Bianca? Email info@biancaforjudge.org

pages.title: Home - Re-Elect Judge Peck
paragraphs: Thank you for taking the time to visit my website. I appreciate your interest in learning about my background and my record of pursuing and providing justice for the citizens of King County each day.

I was honored to be unanimously appointed to be a King County District Court Judge by the King County Council in December of 2019. I was then elected to this position in the fall of 2020 and re-elected in 2022. Prior to my appointment, I served as a pro tem judge, or fill in judge, in the King County District Court system for 29 years.

I practiced as a trial lawyer in King County from 1983 to 2019. As an attorney in private practice, I represented over 200 individuals in employment discrimination cases. I also represented individuals in civil rights matters and federal criminal proceedings.

As a judge, I value transparency, integrity and fairness. It’s my goal that each litigant that appears before me is entitled to understand their rights and the implications of any legal decisions they make. Throughout my legal career, I’ve worked to ensure that all individuals receive equal protection under the law, while also valuing the court system’s role in preserving public safety.

My legal accomplishments include: successfully pursuing a case through the U.S. Supreme Court to uphold free speech rights; chairing the Washington State Bar Association’s Civil Rights Committee; and serving as a board member to the Washington Community Action Network for more than three decades.

I have been honored to be endorsed by more than 100 current and retired judges including unanimous endorsement by all other King County District Court Judges. Seven Justices of the Washington State Supreme Court have endorsed my candidacy, including the Chief Justice.
I look forward to meeting you and to discuss my values and experience. Please feel free to reach out with any questions, thoughts or concerns at judgekevinpeck@gmail.com .

pages.title: Home - Denice Gagner for King County District Court Position 6
paragraphs: Thank you for taking the time to read about why I am running for election in 2026 to be a King County District Court Judge.

I am a lifelong resident of Washington State and have lived and worked in King County for thirty years. Both my legal and life experiences have uniquely qualified me to serve as a District Court Judge in these challenging times, and I hope to earn your vote.

I’ve spent my entire legal career working in critical roles that serve the King County Court system: as a victim advocate supporting domestic violence and sexual assault victims, as a prosecutor, public defender, criminal defense attorney, and civil litigator. And since 2022, elected judges across King County have asked me to serve as a Judge Pro Tem in their courts. This balanced experience is one of the reasons I have gained such broad support for my campaign to become an elected District Court Judge.

People from our communities come to the District Court seeking fairness, hope, and resolution. I am running for District Court Judge because I believe every person – no matter their background or their story – deserves to be treated with respect, dignity, and humanity. I will work every day to uphold the law with integrity, while also recognizing the role that equity, rehabilitation and accountability to the community play in a just legal system. My own life experiences have prepared me well to connect with those who come before the Court dealing with issues around addiction, untreated mental health issues, and family challenges. I invite you to read more about my background here . I will bring both empathy and accountability to this role.

I have worked hard for the last 18 years to earn the respect of attorneys, judges, clients, and the community at large. I am eager to continue my career in public service with my election to the District Court bench. Between now and November 2026, I will be travelling throughout East King County to connect with as many voters as possible. I hope to earn your vote. Thank you.

pages.title: About Denice - Denice Gagner for King County District Court Position 6
paragraphs: Denice Gagner brings a uniquely balanced combination of legal and life experiences to the King County District Court bench.
She has distinguished herself as a prosecutor, as a criminal defense attorney, civil litigator, as a victim advocate, and now as a Judge Pro Tem.

For several years beginning in 2001, Denice managed a heavy caseload of sexual assault and domestic violence cases as a victim advocate for the King County Prosecutor’s Office. There, she learned first-hand the heavy toll these cases take on families and children.

After earning her law degree at the University of Washington in 2007, Denice began her career as a prosecutor for the City of Seattle, handling a demanding trial caseload for six years. In 2012, she opened her own law office, earning respect as both a criminal defense attorney and a civil litigator. She now brings her diverse expertise to those facing mental health challenges, addiction struggles, and various forms of injury and trauma. For the past three years, she has also been much in demand as a Judge Pro Tem, serving regularly in nearly all of the King County District Courts, as well as several municipal courts across the county.

Life experiences, which can be important to the perspective of a judge, have also been instrumental in Denice’s preparation for her judicial role. Growing up with very modest means on the far outskirts of a small Eastern Washington town, she witnessed family struggles with addiction and the death of a parent at a young age. These experiences have greatly enhanced her ability to connect with those who now appear before her in court.

Denice has been an active member of the Redmond community, serving on the City’s Planning Commission and as President of a PTA. She and her husband, a Microsoft developer, have two children, ages 11 and 13.

pages.title: Home - Elect for Judge Heather Barker
paragraphs: Fair and thoughtful justice builds stronger communities.

As a Judge Pro Tem in King County District Court since 2022, I have seen firsthand how this court impacts the daily lives of the people we serve. District Court handles the cases that most directly affect our community—from misdemeanors such as theft, trespass, and assault to protection orders, infractions, and small claims disputes.

I bring both judicial and real-world community experience to this role. I am the founder and owner of Northwest Community Law, PLLC, a small firm focused on civil matters affecting local families, neighbors, and small businesses.

I am deeply rooted in the Southeast Division. I was born and raised in Kent and now live in Renton, where I am raising my family. This is my community. Our court needs a judge who listens carefully, treats everyone with dignity, and applies the law fairly and thoughtfully. I am committed to protecting public safety while strengthening the well-being of the community we call home.

pages.title: About Heather Barker - Elect for Judge Heather Barker
paragraphs: Heather Barker , a native of Southeast King County, brings to our District Court her own broad experience with the challenges faced by working families and the struggles of owning and managing a small business. Heather’s care for the community, respect for all its members, and deep understanding of life’s challenges makes her the kind of judge we deserve.

Soon after graduating from Kentwood High School, Heather headed for sunny southern California in search of some sun where she bought and ran a small coffee shop and worked as a waitress, learning her aptitude for interacting with a great variety of people. After graduating with honors from Cal State Long Beach in 2005, Heather came “home” to Washington State and worked in residential real estate development for three years until the recession forced her to look for a new career – so her path to the bench began, starting with attending law school at Seattle University.

After earning her law degree in 2013, Heather eventually opened her own solo law firm – Northwest Community Law – practicing property law. In 2022, she began serving as a Judge Pro Tem. Heather presides over both civil and criminal calendars and is honored to be one of two Judges Pro Tem who preside over Mental Health and Veterans Courts.

Service to the community has also been a priority for Heather, and she has participated for more than a decade in the First Responder Will Clinic, a pro bono clinic that drafts estate plans for our fire fighters, police officers, and emergency medical technicians.

Now living in Renton with her husband, a Boeing senior manager and Army reservist of twenty years, and daughters Ella (age 11) and Signe (age 8), Heather is mostly found cheering on her girls at soccer and basketball games when not working. She also enjoys the coast and surfing vacations with her family.

pages.title: About Andrea | Friends of Andrea Jarmon
paragraphs: Judge Jarmon with her mom and mentor, the late Julie Zarelli, a long time educator in the Seattle Public School system.

Judge Andrea Samonica Jarmon was born in Macon, Georgia - red dirt and country roads. She came to Washington as a teenager after her birth mother divorced her father, ending their long abusive relationship. Unfortunately, like many victims of domestic violence, her mother's next partner was also abusive. ​Like many of our homeless youth today, as a youth, Judge Jarmon had to seek safety and shelter through public transportation, the generosity of strangers, and foster homes. She was aided by the resources of group homes like those provided by Friends of Youth and United Indian's Labateya. Along her path she met several incredible women who inspired and encouraged her to move beyond her circumstances. Among those women was the late Julie Zarelli (Ms. Zee), a Seattle high school counselor who became not only a friend to her, but also a life coach, mentor, and the woman that she would come to call mother. Not only was Ms. Zee instrumental in Judge Jarmon's completion of high school, but she guided Judge Jarmon through undergraduate and law school. Judge Jarmon speaks often how how Ms. Zee modeled for Judge Jarmon in both philosophy and practice what it means to care about people, to create opportunities for others, and to serve with no other purpose than to advance good in the world. That is precisely why those have been the values that Judge Jarmon has carried with her throughout her education and throughout her legal career.
“Against the odds, single mother makes progress towards dreams.” Seattle Post Intelligencer, February 16, 1997. (Featured in news article as Andrea S. Harris)
Attorney Andrea S. Jarmon and her daughter Zipporah J. Jarmon volunteering at the King County Bar Association's neighborhood legal clinic. Judge Jarmon volunteered from 2012 to 2021.

Judge Jarmon has worked as an Assistant City Attorney in the Criminal Division of the Seattle City Attorney's Office; as a City Prosecutor for the City of Auburn; and as an Assistant Attorney General for the Washington State Attorney General's Officer, where she began in the Medicaid Fraud Control Unit, prosecuting the financial exploitation and physical abuse of Medicaid patients and then worked in the Sexually Violent Predator and L&I Units. She has also practiced in the criminal field as a Defense Attorney representing individuals accused of crimes at the misdemeanor and felony level. ​She operated a private law office, where she represented parents and children in dependency and termination proceedings; practiced family law, and supported paralegal students in training with externship opportunities. Prior to election to the King County Bench in November of 2022, Judge Jarmon worked as an Appeals Judge with the Board of Industrial Insurance Appeals, where she presided over proceedings involving workers compensation and employee injury cases. Valuing the educational experience she had as a running start student at Seattle Central, she taught at Tacoma Community College and Green River Community College.
In 2015, Attorney Andrea S. Jarmon was appointed to the Washington State Bar Associations Board of Governors.

Having personally experienced the vulnerability and challenges of navigating the complicated court systems without a lawyer, Judge Jarmon understands the importance of making sure that each person who comes before the Court is given an opportunity to be heard; have the process respectfully explained; and to be treated with fairness and dignity. Judge Jarmon believes it is important for a judicial officer to be prepared, patient, compassionate, and sincere and should strive to issue decisions that are grounded in the law, with a focus on equity, access, and justice. Her own life experiences have shaped her belief that our courts must be accessible, accountable, trauma-informed, and human-centered. As your judge, Judge Jarmon has reduced her calendar dockets to allow for more meaningful hearings, streamlined pre-trial hearing calendars, expanded the Court’s community engagement efforts, and created civic engagement programs to help introduce young people to careers in the law.

"I had gotten a no seat belt ticket a few months back. I appreciate you dismissing the fine and I am so touched by your kind words. I was having a rough day today mentally and your words were just what I needed. Cancer is a scary thing but knowing that even a stranger can be so kind has lifted my spirits."
Because people who access the Court must sometimes come with children, Judge Jarmon created an area in the courtroom for children to play quietly.
Presenting at the Black Law Student Association and Seattle University's Access to Justice Institute's Social Justice Monday.
Participating in a Gratitude Award Ceremony to honor community leaders and social justice agents.
Judge Jarmon with newly sworn in Attorney Ayoub Ahmed.
Judge Jarmon pictured with participants and attendees at the 2024 Justice Charles Z. Smith Youth and Law Forum.
Sharing her personal journey as a survivor of violence at ELAP's 2026 Breakfast for Justice. Watch here: youtu.be/VuZiwgoitYE.
Judge Jarmon swearing in Representative Osman Salahuddin at a Community Swearing In Ceremony.
Judge Jarmon with the King County District Court booth at MHS Day of Dignity 2026.
Modeling Possibilities organized by Judge Wiggs and Judge Jarmon, and sponsored by the Ummah Bar Association.

pages.title: Home
paragraphs: "With Experience, Integrity, and Respect for the Rule of Law, I remain committed to serving the People of King County fairly and impartially."

Judge Fa'amomoi Masaniai, Jr. has dedicated more than 30 years to serving the people of Washington and American Samoa through the justice system. His career reflects a commitment to fairness, integrity, and public service, from courtroom clerk to prosecutor, defense attorney, and ultimately Judge.

pages.title: About
paragraphs: Equal Justice to All is extremely important. Anyone can realistically navigate the legal system now. With technology advancing in the court system, the access to interpreter services has expanded. Zoom has allowed individuals to appear from remote locations without fear of missing their court dates. This advancement has also benefited disabled people by providing them access to court without struggling to travel to court.

Taking into account marginalized communities, I am committed to show fairness toward groups historically treated unequally in the system including racial minorities, immigrants, LGBTQ+ people, low-income defendants, and individuals with mental illness.
Due Process, Fair Trials, Equal Protection, and Protection from Discrimination are the foundation in which I run my courtroom. All are treated the same.
Judicial accountability and transparency

I take my time in explaining each sentence I give in hopes that the individual understands the terms so they may be successful. It also provides a pathway for redemption for those who appear in court. This also reduces recidivism and in many ways restores trust in the Courts.
I believe in Rehabilitation versus pure punishment, but I won't hesitate in protecting the citizens if Rehabilitation fails by incarcerating those who consistently offend the law.

Starting my journey in 1994 as a volunteer and working almost every position in the courtroom has provided me a unique and different experience than most judges. Understanding the hard work and dedication a clerk has with the split second thinking most attorneys utilize while maintaining trust from the public is a delicate balancing act. My 32 years in this field has equipped me with the necessary experience to be successful and to inspire trust in the community.
Fair and Impartial Application of the Law

Being a judge requires a balance of being transparent and accountable to voters while also protecting judicial ethics, fairness, and independence. It also means listening to the people who appear before you and relying on your experience in the law to make fair and impartial rulings.
Each person is worth more than the worst thing they have done.
Understanding Local Courts and Community Concerns

Having served in Federal, State, District and Municipal Courts, I have come to appreciate the community concerns for local business, local governments, and citizens. I am earnestly trying to reduce case backlogs, protecting victims’ rights and hearing their voices at times of sentencing, ensuring fairness for defendants, improving access to treatment/diversion programs, and supporting veterans or mental health courts while maintaining courtroom transparency and professionalism.

pages.title: Meet Judge Fa'amomoi Masaniai
paragraphs: Judge Masaniai, Jr.'s journey in the legal profession began in 1994 as a volunteer with the Tukwila Municipal Court. His dedication quickly earned him a full-time position in 1995 as an in-court bailiff and court clerk, providing him with firsthand experience in the daily administration of justice.
In 1999, he entered Washington's prestigious APR Rule 6 Law Clerk Program, gaining practical legal training while working at Stewart Beall & MacNichols, P.S.
By 2001, he became a Rule 9 Legal Intern, where he successfully tried and won his first fifteen jury trials.
After completing the Rule 6 Program in 2003, he passed the Washington State Bar Exam in 2004 and became a licensed attorney.
In 2006, Judge Masaniai, Jr. accepted a position as an Assistant Attorney General in American Samoa, prosecuting Domestic Violence and Sexual Assault cases.
His work expanded in 2009 when he was appointed Independent Prosecutor, handling complex cases involving government corruption, white collar crime, and human trafficking.
Judge Masaniai, Jr. returned to Washington in 2012, practicing law in both federal and state courts, representing clients in bankruptcy, mediation, and civil litigation.
In 2014, he returned to public defense in the City of Shoreline.
Judge Masaniai, Jr.'s judicial experience continued to grow
2014: Served as a Pro Tem Judge in the City of Seattle.
2015: Appointed Pro Tem Commissioner for the Juvenile Division of King County Superior Court.
2018: Appointed Pro Tem Judge for King County District Court.
2019: Served as Pro Tem Judge in Des Moines, SeaTac, Renton, Issaquah, and Puyallup.
In 2021, the King County Council unanimously appointed Judge Masaniai, Jr. to the King County District Court bench.
This appointment marked two historic milestones:
The first Samoan Judge appointed to the bench in Washington State.
Believed to be the first graduate of Washington's APR Rule 6 Program to become a judge.
The voters reaffirmed their confidence in his leadership by electing him to a full term in 2022.

Since 2023, Judge Masaniai, Jr. has served in the King County District Court's Regional Mental Health Court and Regional Veterans Court, helping connect individuals with treatment, accountability, and resources while promoting safer communities.
Judge Masaniai, Jr. has served on numerous judicial committees dedicated to improving Washington's courts, including:
King County District Court Law Day Committee
King County District Court Budget Committee
Former member of the King County District Court Security Committee
Former member of the King County District Court Probation Committee

Judge Masaniai, Jr. married his lovely wife, Polu, in 2008. Together they have built a strong family and are proud parents of three children. Their children are ages Seventeen (17), Sixteen (16), and Twelve (12).
His commitment to family, community, and public service continues to guide his work on the bench every day.

pages.title: Harry Steinmetz for Judge
paragraphs: CANDIDATE FOR KING COUNTY DISTRICT COURT JUDGE, SOUTHWEST DIVISION, POSITION 4

Harry S. Steinmetz is a seasoned attorney, former judge, and dedicated public servant with more than three decades of legal and community leadership experience. He is running for King County District Court to bring integrity, fairness, and a deep understanding of the law to the bench.

Over a 36-year legal career, Harry has built a broad and balanced background across multiple areas of the justice system. He has served as a criminal defense attorney, representing individuals facing serious charges and ensuring their constitutional rights were protected. He has also worked as a Deputy Prosecuting Attorney, giving him insight into the responsibilities of the state in pursuing justice. This dual perspective has shaped his commitment to fairness and impartial decision-making.

Harry’s judicial experience includes serving as an Administrative Law Judge with the Washington State Board of Industrial Insurance Appeals, where he presided over hearings, managed complex caseloads, and issued well-reasoned decisions in workers’ compensation cases. He has also served as a Judge Pro Tem, further demonstrating his readiness to serve on the bench with professionalism and sound judgment.

In addition to his legal career, Harry has a strong record of public service. As Deputy Mayor and City Councilmember for Des Moines, he worked on public safety, municipal budgeting, and long-term policy planning. His time in elected office strengthened his understanding of how legal decisions affect communities, families, and local government.

Harry also brings experience from working behind the scenes in government, including serving as an Investigator for the Commission on Judicial Conduct and as a Staff Attorney to the Washington State Senate Judiciary Committee. These roles gave him valuable insight into judicial ethics, accountability, and the legislative process.
A graduate of Santa Clara University School of Law, Harry has remained committed to the legal profession through bar association involvement and ongoing professional development.

Harry is running for King County District Court because he believes the court plays a critical role in everyday life. From traffic infractions and misdemeanors to civil disputes and protection orders, District Court is often the public’s first interaction with the justice system. Harry is committed to ensuring that every person who enters the courtroom is treated with dignity, respect, and fairness.

His campaign is grounded in the belief that justice requires both legal expertise and an understanding of the real-world impact of judicial decisions. With experience on both sides of the courtroom, on the bench, and in elected office, Harry Steinmetz is prepared to serve the people of King County with integrity, accountability, and sound judgment.
