JUDICIAL ACCOUNTABILITY MATTERS. IN THIS ELECTION YOU HAVE A CHOICE.
Judges must be held to the highest standards of integrity, professionalism, and respect.

In April 2026, the Washington State Commission on Judicial Conduct publicly reprimanded my opponent, Judge Fa’amomoi Masaniai, after he stipulated violations of the Code of Judicial Conduct involving his conduct towards a court clerk.​
https://www.cjc.state.wa.us/materials/activity/public_actions/2026/12896StipFinal.pdf

Judge Masaniai agreed that he violated Cannon 1, Rule 1.1 and 1.2 requiring a judge to act in a manner that promotes public confidence in the independence, integrity and impartially of the judiciary. He agreed he violated Rule 2.3(B) prohibiting judges from engaging in harassment and Rule 2.8(B) requiring judges to maintain appropriate courtroom decorum and be patient, dignified and courteous to all persons with whom they deal in their official capacity. The Commission ordered remedial training focused on sexual harassment and gender dynamics.
All communities in southwest King County agree sexual harassment in the workplace is unacceptable behavior.

pages.title: Home - Merfeld for Judge
paragraphs: The role of a judge requires more than knowledge of the law. It requires judgment, humility, curiosity, and an understanding of the community you serve.

That is the kind of judge I want to be. I’m running for King County District Court because I believe judges should listen and learn—both inside the courtroom and in the community. At a time when trust in our institutions is fragile and many people feel increasingly disconnected from one another, that kind of engagement matters. By understanding the problems that bring people into court and working with the community to address them, the court can help tackle underlying issues in ways that lead to lasting change. When we do that, we build trust, strengthen accountability, resolve conflict, promote rehabilitation, and make our communities safer.
Noel has worked as a prosecutor, public defender, and a dependency attorney — giving him a full picture of how our legal system works, and where it can do better.
Noel lives in White Center and has dedicated his career to serving the people of this region, including those who too often go underserved.
Noel believes every case is a problem to be solved — not just a verdict to be reached. He’ll bring that mindset to the bench every day.

pages.title: Values - Merfeld for Judge
paragraphs: District Court touches people’s lives in immediate, profound ways. The judge who sits on that bench makes decisions that affect families, victims, defendants, litigants, and entire communities. Noel Merfeld approaches that responsibility with a clear set of values.
Noel believes courts are most effective when they understand, engage with, and earn the trust of the communities they serve. For a judge, that means:

Listening, learning, and building trust. Judges should spend time in the community, listening to people and learning about their experiences and the challenges they face. This helps judges better understand the people and problems that come before the court while building trust in the justice system. Building trust encourages people to participate in the justice system and turn to the courts when they need help.

Strengthening community partnerships. Judges should engage with community organizations and treatment providers to strengthen existing partnerships and identify new opportunities for collaboration. Many of the problems that bring people to court require help the court itself cannot provide. Community organizations and treatment providers can offer treatment and support that help people make meaningful changes and successfully reintegrate into the community.

Valuing community perspectives in the courtroom. Judges should recognize the value of perspectives from families and others who know and support the people before the court, while ensuring those perspectives are heard in ways appropriate to the case. Their input can provide important context and help judges make better-informed decisions.

Reinforcing community standards and accountability. Communities can support the work of the court by reinforcing shared expectations of responsibility, respect for others, and lawful behavior, while encouraging those who have caused harm to make meaningful changes.

When someone commits a crime, it is rarely an isolated event. It is the result of a unique set of life experiences, circumstances, and often, systemic failures. Noel believes that understanding this context doesn’t excuse harm — it helps address it more effectively. He brings emotional intelligence and genuine empathy to the bench, not to soften accountability, but to make it more meaningful. Research shows that defendants are more likely to accept a sentence as fair — and more likely to reflect on their own behavior — when they feel truly heard by the judge who imposed it.

Noel believes judges should be compassionate, but not permissive or naive. Accountability and punishment are not the same thing. Punishment is imposed by the court; accountability must ultimately come from the individual. It means recognizing the harm caused by your actions, accepting responsibility, and taking meaningful steps to ensure that harm is not repeated. That can include engaging in appropriate treatment and paying restitution to those who were harmed. Noel believes true accountability should always be the goal. His community-oriented approach is rooted in the belief that people are more likely to take accountability when courts engage with the families, treatment providers, and communities that can support meaningful change. When people genuinely take accountability and change their behavior, the entire community is safer.

But not everyone is willing to accept responsibility or make the changes necessary to stop causing harm. Some continue to offend and put others at risk. Noel will not hesitate to impose jail when the facts of an individual case show that it is necessary to protect the public or achieve a just result. There is nothing compassionate about allowing someone to repeatedly harm others without meaningful consequences. The rule of law matters, and our community members deserve to feel safe and secure.

Court’s can be overwhelming, especially for people without lawyers. Judges must remain neutral and cannot give legal advice or favor one side over another. But they can clearly explain court procedures, use language people can understand, and ask appropriate questions to make sure they have the information necessary to make an informed decision.

Courts should also look for practical ways to make the legal system easier to navigate. Noel supports expanding assistance for people representing themselves, including considering the use of court facilitators who can help people identify the right forms, understand filing requirements, and complete the procedural steps necessary to move their cases forward.

A fair justice system should not depend on how much money someone has or how familiar they are with the legal system. Everyone who comes to court should have a meaningful opportunity to present their case, be heard, and receive a fair decision.

As someone who has practiced in therapeutic courts as both a prosecutor and public defender, Noel has seen firsthand how these programs can promote genuine accountability and rehabilitation, reduce recidivism, and improve public safety.

King County District Court operates several important therapeutic courts, including Community Court, Mental Health Court, and Veterans Court. These programs play a vital role in addressing the underlying issues that bring people into the justice system and strengthening connections between the courts and the community.

We must continue investing in the approaches that work while remaining willing to improve and refine those that do not. The community partnerships that make these courts successful must be strengthened, and more people who could benefit from therapeutic court programs should have access to them.

Noel has seen firsthand the devastating impact the fentanyl epidemic is having on individuals, families, and communities — damage that will continue to affect future generations. As a public defender, he represented clients who died from fentanyl overdoses while their cases were pending. As a dependency attorney, he has represented children whose parents struggled with fentanyl addiction, including some who lost their lives to overdose.

The Court must approach this crisis with urgency while recognizing the limits of its role. Courts can make information about treatment and recovery services readily available and foster an environment that values close collaboration with treatment providers and community organizations. Noel understands that for someone struggling with fentanyl addiction, delays can have devastating consequences, and the court should be a constructive partner in the broader community response.

The justice system has a particular responsibility to protect those who are most vulnerable to violence, abuse, and exploitation. Noel’s experience as a prosecutor, public defender, and child attorney has given him firsthand insight into the challenges vulnerable people face and the consequences when they lack adequate protection.

Understanding vulnerability. Youth, disability, mental illness, addiction, and economic instability can increase vulnerability to abuse and exploitation. Those who lack the ability to protect themselves or depend on others for basic needs can be especially susceptible to manipulation and control. As a child attorney, Noel has represented teenage girls without adequate parental protection who were particularly vulnerable to sexual violence, trafficking, and abusive relationships.

Recognizing interconnected forms of abuse. Intimate-partner violence, child abuse, and animal abuse are often part of the same pattern of power and control. Abusers may threaten or harm children and pets as a means of controlling an intimate partner. Evidence of one form of abuse should make the court attentive to the possibility of others. When appropriate, protection orders should protect children and pets even when they are not the direct victims of abuse.

Recognizing trafficking and exploitation. Trafficking and sexual exploitation can involve overlapping patterns of grooming, coercion, manipulation, and violence. Information presented to the court may reveal signs of exploitation that are not immediately obvious. Judges should be attentive to these indicators and consider appropriate protections when the circumstances warrant.

Using the court’s authority effectively. Protecting vulnerable people requires judges to understand the relationships and circumstances involved in each case, ask appropriate questions, and make informed decisions. Judges should also expect the parties to provide the information necessary for the court to understand the risks involved. The court should use its authority thoughtfully and effectively to protect those who are most at risk of harm.

People deserve to feel safe and secure where they live. Property crime, dangerous driving, street racing, illegal fireworks, and other conduct that threatens safety or repeatedly disrupts a neighborhood can leave people feeling unsafe and undermine confidence in the rule of law. Noel believes courts should take these concerns seriously and respond appropriately to the circumstances of each case.

Noel understands both the importance and the inherent limitations of the judicial role. The challenges facing our communities — addiction, homelessness, mental illness, and poverty — will not be solved by any single judge. Judges are not policymakers, and there are important limits on the role judges may play in advocating for policy change. Meaningful progress requires collaboration between courts, service providers, policymakers, and the broader community.

At the same time, judges remain important and influential stakeholders within the justice system. A judge who is thoughtful, committed, creative, and deeply connected to the community can make a meaningful difference — case by case, person by person. That is the kind of judge Noel intends to be.

pages.title: About - Merfeld for Judge
paragraphs: Noel Merfeld has spent his legal career prosecuting criminal cases, defending the accused, and advocating for children and families — all in service of building a justice system that works for people and strengthens our communities.

Born in Seattle and raised in Bellingham, Noel earned his B.A. in Interdisciplinary Social Sciences from UW-Seattle. He went on to earn his J.D. from UW School of Law. While in law school, he served as a Rule 9 intern with the Skagit County Prosecutor’s Office.

After graduating, Noel began his legal career as a prosecutor with the Okanogan County Prosecutor’s Office. He later transitioned to criminal defense, spending several years as a contract public defender in Okanogan County. During this time, he lived near many of his clients in a small rural community and gained a firsthand understanding of the challenges surrounding addiction, mental health, and poverty. He also saw firsthand how access to the resources and community support systems can genuinely change lives.

After returning to Western Washington, Noel joined the firm Feldman & Lee in Lynnwood, where he practiced criminal defense in Lynnwood Municipal Court and Snohomish County District Court. During the COVID-19 pandemic, he continued public defense work in Okanogan County while living in White Center.

Most recently, Noel has represented children and families navigating dependency proceedings — filing motions, conducting bench trials, and advocating for young people during some of the most difficult moments of their lives.

Through each chapter of his career, Noel has seen both the strengths and shortcomings of our justice system firsthand. As a judge, he will work to make our courts more responsive, more community-oriented, and more focused on solving problems.
While many judicial candidates have seen the courtroom from one angle, Noel has seen it from nearly every one.
As a prosecutor, he worked closely with law enforcement, built relationships with victims, and engaged directly with issues of public safety, quality of life, and protecting the vulnerable.

As a public defender, Noel stood beside clients during some of the worst moments of their lives, fighting to protect their constitutional rights and ensure meaningful access to justice. He also helped connect clients with the treatment, services, and community support systems they needed to rebuild stability in their lives

As a dependency attorney, Noel has represented children across a wide range of settings, including court proceedings, school meetings, and protection order cases, ensuring that vulnerable young people have a strong voice and meaningful advocacy.
This is the experience that matters for a judge who will handle the full range of cases that come before the Court every day.

pages.title: Renee Walls for Judge | King County, Position #5
paragraphs: A conscientious and careful arbiter, Renee brings a deep understanding of how judicial decisions affect individuals, families, and the broader community.
Through community leadership, pro bono work, and youth advocacy, Renee has dedicated her career to serving others both inside and outside of the courtroom.
With more than two decades of experience as a prosecutor and judicial officer, Renee brings the knowledge, judgment, and experience our community deserves in a judge.
With your support, Renee will continue serving our community – with a commitment to fairness, a dedication to justice, and uncompromising integrity.

pages.title: Renee Walls for Judge | King County, Position #5
paragraphs: Renee Walls was born in South Korea and adopted by an immigrant mother from the Philippines and a farmer from rural Minnesota. Through them she learned the value of hard work, a dedication to education and learning, and a deep commitment to public service. Since the inception of her career, these tenets have informed Renee’s approach to public service and leadership.
Renee has served the King County community as a prosecutor and judicial officer. Her experience includes 26 years as a Prosecuting Attorney and 17 years as a Judge Pro Tempore.

Serving in both prosecutorial and judicial roles has allowed Renee to develop a broad lens through which she views justice. This vantage point encompasses more than the rule of law – it’s about people, families, and the extraordinary impact our courts have on our community.
We need and deserve a judge who possesses the legal acumen, demonstrated judicial temperament, and relevant experience necessary to perform the functions and duties of a judicial officer.
Renee is uniquely qualified to address the challenges facing our justice system, understand the evolving needs of our community, and make the difficult decisions required of a judge.

With decades of legal practice behind her, we know Renee can serve because she has served. As District Court Judge she will continue to serve with the accumulated knowledge, the gained experience, and the proven integrity our community deserves.

pages.title: Retain Judge Bardi Martin
paragraphs: KING COUNTY DISTRICT COURT POSITION #1 | WEST ELECTORAL DISTRICT

Judge Bardi Martin brings proven courtroom experience, steady judgment, and a lifelong commitment to King County to the District Court bench. Unanimously appointed by the King County Council to serve as a District Court Judge, he is a graduate of the University of Washington and Seattle University School of Law and has built his career in the courts and communities he now serves.

Judge Martin began his legal career in King County courtrooms as a public defender, protecting the constitutional rights of people who could not afford counsel. He later built a successful Seattle law practice representing individuals and small businesses in civil and criminal matters. Before his appointment to the bench, he also served as a judge pro tempore, gaining valuable experience from both sides of the courtroom.

Today, Judge Martin presides over criminal calendars, protection orders, small claims, civil cases, and community court. He brings broad courtroom experience, careful preparation, and deep respect for the people who come before the court. His courtroom is organized, respectful, and clear: he listens carefully, explains rulings plainly, applies the law fairly, and treats every person with dignity.

Judge Martin believes courts earn public trust through fairness, transparency, and accountability. Public safety and equal justice are not competing values - they depend on each other. Safe communities require courts that work, courts that listen, and courts that people can trust.

pages.title: About | Retain Judge Bardi Martin
paragraphs: ABOUT Judge Bardi Martin RAISED IN SERVICE • GROUNDED in king county
Before Bardi Martin was a judge, he was a musician.

For years, he lived a life far removed from the courtroom—playing bass, writing and recording music, performing for audiences, and touring as a member of Seattle’s Candlebox. He remains a songwriter and musician today.

As a member of Candlebox, Bardi co-wrote and recorded music including “Far Behind,” one of the band’s best-known songs. But his connection to music goes beyond the songs themselves. Over the years, he has continued to perform, including at benefit shows supporting charitable causes and community organizations.
For Bardi, music offered an education that has stayed with him.

A bass player may not always be the most prominent voice in a song, but the bass provides rhythm, structure, and foundation. Playing well means paying attention—not only to your own part, but to everyone around you. It requires preparation, timing, discipline, collaboration, and knowing when to lead and when to support.
Those lessons have a natural connection to the courtroom.

As a judge, Bardi listens to people from very different circumstances and perspectives. Each person who enters a courtroom has a story and deserves to be heard. The responsibility of a judge is to listen carefully, apply the law, weigh the facts, and treat everyone who comes before the court with fairness and respect.
The stage and the courtroom may seem like very different worlds. For Bardi, however, some of the most important lessons traveled with him.
Music taught him to prepare. To pay attention. To work with others. To understand his role within something larger than himself. And perhaps most importantly, to listen.
That part of his story didn’t end when he left the stage.
It became part of who he brought with him to the bench.

pages.title: Home | Nilu Jenks For Seattle City Council
paragraphs: By submitting your phone number you are agreeing to receive up to 2 text message(s) per day Nilu Jenks For Seattle City Council.

A first-generation Iranian-American, Nilu has directly benefited from the freedoms this country provides. Having experienced marginalization firsthand, she is deeply motivated to protect those freedoms and to help realize the nation’s democratic ideals for the benefit of all communities. Her values, deeply rooted in community and sustainability, have informed her lifelong commitment to equity, civic engagement, and public service.

Blue, democratically controlled cities like Seattle need to show they can deliver and meet people’s needs. Seattle has become increasingly unaffordable, harder on kids and their families, tougher to find food and pharmacies near your home, and has not exemplified the leadership that cities with immense resources like ours should provide.​.
From protecting immigrants to improving democracy, it's time for leadership that shows concrete, community-driven results for all of our Seattle neighbors.

pages.title: Platform | Nilu Jenks For Seattle City Council
paragraphs: Building 1,000 New Units of Affordable Housing For Working Families Seattle cannot solve its housing crisis without bold, district-level leadership. As a City Councilmember, Nilu Jenks will champion the creation of 1,000 new units of affordable housing in her district. If every district City Councilmember made the same commitment, Seattle would add 7,000 units of affordable housing citywide, a meaningful step toward meeting the scale of the crisis. Expanding affordable housing would help stabilize rents, keep working families in their neighborhoods, and prevent more people from being pushed into homelessness. Nilu believes housing is a human necessity, not a luxury, and that the City must use every tool available, public land, zoning flexibility, and partnerships with nonprofit developers – to deliver housing that people can truly afford. By building more homes for people at all income levels, especially middle-class and working families, Seattle can reduce displacement, strengthen communities, and move closer to ending homelessness.

Fixing the Food Desert As a Lake City resident, Nilu has directly experienced the devastating impact of the closure of the Fred Meyer on Lake City Way. Entire neighborhoods were left without a reliable place to buy affordable, healthy food or pick up prescription medications, especially harming seniors, working families, and people without easy access to transportation. Nilu is committed to fixing these growing food deserts by supporting local grocery stores, community-owned food co-ops, and expanding farmers markets, including extending hours to evenings and weekends, so working families can access them. Food access is a public health issue, and no Seattle resident should have to travel miles for fresh produce.

Implementing Ranked Choice Voting Nilu Jenks brings unmatched expertise on voting reform as the Political and Partnerships Director of FairVote Washington. She will ensure Seattle successfully implements Ranked Choice Voting in 2027, strengthening democracy and giving voters more meaningful choices. Ranked Choice Voting encourages positive campaigns, reduces vote-splitting, and ensures elected leaders have broad community support. Nilu will focus on voter education, community outreach, and a smooth implementation so all Seattle voters, especially those historically excluded from the political process, can participate with confidence. The new District 5 councilmember must work every day to make government more accountable and responsive to neighbors’ needs and be accessible and listen to all residents. Nilu would have weekly drop-in office hours in District 5, so she can hear directly from her neighbors about local community needs.

Creating a Child-Friendly City Raising a family in Seattle is getting harder. Housing costs continue to rise, child care is increasingly expensive and difficult to find, and too many neighborhoods lack safe, welcoming spaces for children. Nilu believes Seattle must become a child-friendly city again. That means investing in affordable child care, improving walkability, increasing park safety, and designing public spaces with kids and families in mind - including teenagers! This includes expanding free child public transit to all students in Seattle, including college and university students. As a mother of two, Nilu understands these challenges firsthand and will be a strong advocate for families, ensuring Seattle is a city where children can thrive and parents are supported. North Seattle remains the last area of the city without a complete sidewalk network, creating serious safety risks for pedestrians, children, seniors, and disabled residents. This is unacceptable. Nilu will make sidewalk construction a top priority, especially in District 5. Safe sidewalks are essential for walkability, public safety, climate goals, and access to schools, transit, and local businesses. Every resident deserves safe streets, and Nilu will push to ensure North Seattle finally gets the infrastructure it has been denied for far too long.

Protecting Immigrants The federal government is increasingly disregarding due process and constitutional protections, tearing at the fabric of our local economy and social trust. As a City Councilmember, Nilu will fight for robust sanctuary policies that ensure local resources are never used to support federal mass deportation efforts. Nilu will strengthen legal defense funds, expand pathways to safety, and ensure that every person – regardless of documentation status – can go to medical appointments, attend school, and go to work without fear. Seattle’s strength lies in its solidarity, and Nilu will fight to ensure our city remains a place where belonging is a right, not a privilege. Safe, Healthy Communities For All Every neighbor in District 5 wants the same things: to walk home feeling safe, to know the right help will show up when they call 911, and to live in a city that cares for people in crisis. Nilu believes Seattle needs to be both serious and smart about safety — focused on what actually works. That means investing upstream in housing, mental health, and youth so fewer crises happen in the first place. It means a fully funded CARE Department responding 24/7 to behavioral health calls, working in true partnership with SPD and Fire Response so every call gets the right responder. As Councilmember, Nilu will fight for 24/7 co-responder domestic violence teams with culturally matched advocates for immigrant and refugee survivors. She will champion sustained funding for crime victims, support restorative justice approaches that pair accountability with compassion, and invest in trauma-informed services for survivors of trafficking and adults in sex work who want a way out — including housing, treatment, and job training. Gun violence is a public health crisis, and Nilu will treat it like one. She will invest in community violence intervention programs that send trusted messengers to interrupt retaliation cycles, expand hospital-based intervention so survivors get connected to support before leaving the ER, and champion safe storage and school partnerships to keep guns out of young people's hands. Nilu will stand with City Attorney Erika Evans to build a community court that connects people to treatment and housing, reducing repeat offenses through real accountability. She will also defend the independence of Seattle's police accountability bodies — the CPC, OPA, and OIG — so accountability has real teeth. Safe, healthy communities are built, not promised. pages.title: About | Nilu Jenks For Seattle City Council
paragraphs: Nilu Jenks is the Political and Partnerships Director at FairVote Washington, and she is a dedicated community advocate committed to building a more representative, inclusive, and participatory democracy. In her role at FairVote Washington, she works with community partners, advocates, and policymakers to advance voting reforms that strengthen accountability and ensure every voter has a meaningful voice.

As a first-generation Iranian-American, Nilu has directly benefited from the freedoms this country provides. Having experienced marginalization firsthand, she is deeply motivated to protect those freedoms and to help realize the nation’s democratic ideals for the benefit of all communities. Her lived experience informs her lifelong commitment to equity, civic engagement, and public service. As a resident of North Seattle with deep ties to her community, she is committed to making Seattle more affordable, safer, and more responsive to the needs of everyday residents. Her lived experience drives her belief that our democracy works best when every voice is heard and valued. In 2023, Nilu ran for Seattle City Council District 5, bringing a people-centered vision focused on strengthening democracy, improving public safety through community-based solutions, expanding housing affordability, and supporting working families. While the campaign did not result in a win, it energized voters and elevated critical conversations about representation, inclusion, sustainability, and the role of local government in creating safer, more equitable communities.

Nilu has a strong record of grassroots and education-focused advocacy. As a board member of Roosevelt Alumni for Racial Equity (RARE), she co-wrote a racial equity curriculum that is being facilitated after school by the Urban League of Metropolitan Seattle at Roosevelt and Garfield High Schools. She has served as PTA Advocacy Chair at John Rogers Elementary School and as a Learning Coach for English Language Learner students at Mercer Middle School.
A mother of two, Nilu has invested her energy in improving local schools and ensuring the success of all children, and she has been a consistent advocate for families.

After the devastating Parkland shootings, Nilu partnered with Gun by Gun and the San Mateo County Sheriff’s Office in CA to help implement the nation’s largest gun buyback program, reinforcing her belief that local governments achieve better outcomes through direct community engagement. Following the Uvalde tragedy, she shared her experience with King County leaders to support ongoing efforts toward responsible, community-driven gun safety initiatives.
Nilu graduated from Wellesley College with a degree in Economics and Spanish.

pages.title: priorities - Julie Kang for Seattle City Council – District 5
paragraphs: Compassion and safety go hand in hand. District 5 faces complex public safety concerns, including gun violence, trafficking, the fentanyl crisis, and repeat small business break-ins along key corridors.

These challenges are deeply connected to housing instability, behavioral health gaps, and systemic failure. We cannot allow vulnerable people to languish in encampments, nor can we allow families to feel unsafe in their own neighborhoods. True compassion means intervening, not accepting the status quo.
Building back Seattle Police Department staffing levels and moving forward with a second police precinct in District 5.
Using every tool in our tool box to bring pimps and johns to justice, including the Stay Out of Area Prostitution (SOAP) zone along Aurora Ave. N.
Improving our homelessness response by requiring more coordination between the city and housing and public health service providers to finally move the needle on one of our greatest challenges.
Expanding access to on-demand substance use disorder treatment so that our unhoused neighbors can get onto a path of recovery.
Ensuring that our parks and other public spaces are safe and accessible to all.
Focusing immediate attention and resources where District 5 needs them most, including shutting down open air drug markets that prey on the vulnerable and threaten neighborhood safety.

The rising cost of housing, groceries, utilities, and childcare is squeezing working families, seniors, and small business owners. Even union and double-income households are struggling to keep up. The city must acknowledge the heavy financial burden it imposes on its own residents and local businesses through rising taxes, red tape, and inadequate basic services. Whether it’s a local shop owner repeatedly paying out-of-pocket to replace broken storefront windows, another regressive sales tax hike, or a homeowner facing an expensive, months-long permitting process just to remodel their kitchen, the current system is actively undermining affordability instead of supporting the people.
Affordability is not a luxury; it’s the foundation of a healthy city.

Everyone deserves a safe, stable place to live, and growth should strengthen neighborhoods. District 5 is growing quickly, but housing, sidewalks, transit, and public infrastructure have not kept pace. Rising rents and limited options are pushing families, workers, and seniors out.
I support density that brings vibrancy and local business activity, alongside mixed-income housing so neighborhoods remain inclusive. To achieve this, I will advocate for:
Fixing our broken permitting system. That starts with shortening the permit review process – because time adds money to projects, driving up the cost of housing and inhibiting economic opportunity.

Moving away from the Mandatory Housing Affordability (MHA) framework, which is a tax on desperately needed housing. Instead, we should direct more Payroll Expense Tax (“JumpStart”) revenue to fund affordable housing.

Protecting and expanding our urban tree canopy so that increased housing also means greener, healthier, and more climate-resilient neighborhoods. Trees should never be the reason we can’t expand housing supply, but the neighborhoods we build should be greener than what they replace.
Matching housing growth with basic public infrastructure like completing North Seattle’s missing sidewalk network and expanding transit access, especially for east to west connectivity.

Diversity makes cities stronger and more vibrant – and this includes our immigrant community. Right now immigrants face unprecedented challenges from federal actions, and we must come together to keep our community safe.

Our city must maintain its status as a Sanctuary City and not allow federal immigration attacks to separate families or unjustly harm people living in our communities. As an immigrant myself, I know that our local economy relies on the contributions of our immigrant neighbors.

I will fight for intentional action that strengthens current programs, protects workers of all identities and visa statuses, and ensures that immigrant owned small businesses have the support they need to thrive.

District 5 needs accountable, experienced leadership. District 5 has too often received inconsistent attention and fewer resources, despite clear needs. District 5 deserves a councilmember who brings practical problem-solving experience in education, finance, and community work.
A leader who uses data and lived experience to guide decisions.
Being a consistent advocate so District 5 gets its fair share of investments.

District 5 deserves leadership that shows up every time and focuses on the basics that make our neighborhoods work. These priorities reflect a simple belief that Seattle is strongest when people can afford to live here, feel safe in their neighborhoods, and trust that their city sees them. District 5 deserves nothing less.

pages.title: Retain Judge McDowall
paragraphs: “I am proud to serve my community from the Seattle Municipal Court bench. I am running to continue the work we’ve started—to bring an innovative and collaborative approach to advancing court reforms and eliminating barriers to justice.”

Judge Cat McDowall is running for re-election to continue her service on the Seattle Municipal Court—bringing deep legal experience, thoughtful judgment, and a commitment to fairness, dignity, and equal access to justice.

Judge McDowall began serving as a Judge Pro Tempore in 2013, presiding in Seattle Municipal Court, King County District Court, and King County Superior Court (Juvenile Division). As a Pro Tem Judge, she handled a wide range of cases and served in specialty courts, including Mental Health Court, Community Court, and Veterans Court, strengthening her ability to navigate complex cases with care and sound judgment.

pages.title: About 5 — Retain Judge McDowall
paragraphs: In 2020, she was appointed as a full-time Judge on the Seattle Municipal Court.

Since joining the bench, Judge McDowall has earned the respect of attorneys, colleagues, and court staff for her preparation, diligence, and collaborative leadership. She has played an active role in court reform efforts, including:
Advancing equity-focused reforms to reduce bias in court processes
Helping modernize court operations and improve access to justice
Working collaboratively with judges, staff, and stakeholders to strengthen public trust in the courts
Her work reflects a careful balance of legal rigor, practical experience, and compassion.

Judge McDowall believes that courts must work for everyone—not just those who understand the legal system or can afford representation. Throughout her career, she has focused on making the justice system more accessible, transparent, and fair for the people who rely on it.

As a judge, she works to ensure that everyone who enters her courtroom is treated with dignity and respect, and that court proceedings are clear and understandable. She prioritizes plain language from the bench, careful explanation of rights and procedures, and thoughtful consideration of the circumstances people bring into the courtroom.

Judge McDowall has also supported efforts within the court to modernize systems, improve access to information, and strengthen specialty courts that address underlying issues such as mental health, substance use, and veterans’ needs. These approaches help connect people to resources while maintaining accountability under the law.
Her commitment to access to justice reflects a simple principle: the legal system should serve the public—and it should be understandable, fair, and accessible to everyone.

In 1997, Judge McDowall moved to Seattle to join the King County Prosecuting Attorney’s Office, where she served for more than a decade, ultimately as a Senior Deputy Prosecuting Attorney. She prosecuted misdemeanor and felony cases at every level of Washington’s court system and handled complex appellate matters, including two cases before the Washington State Supreme Court.

During this time, she developed a deep understanding of how legal systems affect real people—and saw firsthand the inequities embedded in the criminal justice system. That experience shaped her commitment to fairness, integrity, and respect for everyone who enters a courtroom.
Outside the courtroom, Judge McDowall has long been engaged in community service—especially efforts that support children, families, and equity.

She was a founding member of the Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion Committee at Our Lady of Fatima Parish School, working with parents, educators, and administrators to promote inclusive policies and curriculum. She volunteered for more than a decade as a Religious Education Catechist, teaching first-grade students, and has been an active supporter of women’s and children’s charities through Magnolia Moms.

Judge McDowall also served on the Board of Directors of Magnolia Little League, leading the softball division from 2013–2017. Under her leadership, participation nearly tripled. In recognition of that work, she was named Little League International Softball Volunteer of the Year.
Judge McDowall has lived in Seattle since 1997. She and her husband are raising four children here and remain deeply connected to the community she serves.

pages.title: Gabe Rothstein for Judge
paragraphs: ROTHSTEIN 2026 • SEATTLE MUNICIPAL COURT
Courtrooms only work when judges listen.
Gabe has spent over twenty years as a public defender and two years as a pro tem judge. He's running for Seattle Municipal Court.

For more than twenty years, Gabe Rothstein has spent his career standing beside people during some of the hardest moments of their lives. Since becoming a Public Defender in 2005, he has served in nearly every job a trial-level defender can hold: misdemeanors, felonies, drug treatment court, misdemeanor supervisor, lead of the juvenile court unit, and now the civil commitment unit.

Over the course of his career Gabe has tried more than seventy cases to verdict. He Chairs the Washington State Bar's Character and Fitness Board, which vets people seeking admission to practice law in Washington. He sits on the Board of Holman Recovery Center, an inpatient treatment facility in Arlington. He also takes after-hours calls on the statewide Youth Access to Counsel Line, so that kids who've been arrested have a lawyer on the phone before they're questioned.
For Gabe, the work has never been about titles. It has always been about people. Listening carefully, earning trust, and helping others navigate a system that can feel overwhelming.

Since 2024, Gabe has served as a judge pro tempore in multiple District Courts in King County including Seattle, Burien, Redmond, Kent, and Shoreline as well as Everett Municipal Court. He has presided over numerous Court Calendars including Small Claims Trials and Pretrials, Vehicle Impound Hearings, Contested Hearings, Criminal Calendars, and Jail Calendars.

These experiences have reinforced what Gabe has learned over two decades in court rooms: a judge can be patient, decisive, and clear at the same time. Every person who walks into a courtroom deserves to leave understanding what happened, why it happened, and that they were heard by the court.
That belief is why Gabe is running for Seattle Municipal Court.

Twenty years defending people in Washington courtrooms and two on the bench as a pro tem judge have taught Gabe what a fair courtroom looks like in practice. He has seen the difference a thoughtful judge can make and how people react when they don't feel rushed, ignored, or confused. These are the values Gabe will bring to Seattle Municipal Court.

Gabe has spent more than two decades watching how a courtroom changes when a judge slows down, listens carefully, and explains what's happening. Even when the outcome is difficult, people deserve to understand the process and know they were treated with dignity and respect.

Everyone deserves to be heard. The victim who waited months for a hearing. The defendant who is unsophisticated in the system. The pro se litigant in small claims trying to argue a case without a lawyer.
That's the floor for any courtroom Gabe runs.

Too often people remain in jail simply because they cannot afford bail. When that happens, pressure builds quickly, jobs are lost, families are disrupted, and people often plead guilty just to go home. As Gabe wrote in his judicial application, that "is simply not justice."

Gabe believes that release decisions should turn on what they're supposed to turn on: whether somebody is likely to come back to court, and whether they pose a danger. Not whether they have sufficient resources to afford bail.

Many cases that come through Seattle Municipal Court are connected to substance abuse, mental health challenges, or both. Gabe has seen firsthand how treatment can create better outcomes, not only for the person struggling, but for victims, families and the broader community.

Through his work as a Treatment Court Attorney and his work with Holman Recovery Center, Gabe understands that accountability and treatment are not opposing ideas. When treatment becomes part of the solution, fewer people return to court and few victims are harmed.
As Gabe often says, "the opposite of addiction is connection."

Gabe has lost clients who were victims of violence. One was only 16 years old. He knows what it costs a family when somebody gets hurt, and he knows that victims need the same things everyone in court needs: a judge who listens carefully, treats everyone fairly, and moves cases forward without unnecessary delay.
A courtroom should be a place where people feel respected, where decisions are clear, and where justice is delivered with both accountability and humanity.
That is the kind of Judge that Gabe Rothstein strives to be.

pages.title: About Shantrice Anderson - Anderson for Judge
paragraphs: Shantrice began her legal career as a public defender, representing individuals facing misdemeanor, juvenile, felony, and appellate cases. She has substantial trial experience and has worked with specialty courts, including the Veterans’ Court and drug court. Her commitment to justice is informed by firsthand experience advocating for people at their most vulnerable.

Today, Shantrice practices civil law and serves as a Pro Tem Judge and Pro Tem Magistrate in Seattle Municipal Court, where she presides over a wide range of proceedings, including Mental Health Court. She is known for her preparation, fairness, and respectful courtroom demeanor.
Honoring a Mentor: Judge David Armstrong

Shantrice Anderson’s commitment to public service and the law was shaped early by the guidance of David Herbert Armstrong, a Washington Court of Appeals Judge who encouraged her to pursue a career in law. Judge Armstrong was the first Judge that Shantrice had ever met, and immediately began what would be a 20-year mentorship.

Judge Armstrong believed deeply in the responsibility of the legal profession to serve the public with integrity, humility, and fairness. He recognized Shantrice’s potential early on and consistently encouraged her to see the law not only as a profession, but as a calling grounded in service and justice. Judge Armstrong’s guidance shaped Shantrice’s choice to pursue a Philosophy Degree at Gonzaga University. As a proud father of a Gonzaga graduate, Judge Armstrong encouraged Shantrice to pursue a Major that fostered critical thinking and an ability to see the actions of one person both in a microcosm and how that effect can be felt in a larger sense.

A couple of years prior to his passing, Judge Armstrong, himself, entrusted Shantrice with his gavel—a meaningful symbol of his confidence in her character, judgment, and commitment to the values he embodied throughout his career. That gavel is reflected in Shantrice’s campaign logo as a reminder of the responsibility judges carry and the legacy of fairness and integrity she strives to uphold.

Shantrice carries Judge Armstrong’s mentorship with her every day on the bench, approaching each case with preparation, respect for the rule of law, and a deep understanding of the human impact of judicial decisions. She carries his legacy every day in her civil career, as well, analyzing and referencing his many authored-opinions.

pages.title: Home - Shadid for Seattle
paragraphs: The criminal legal system needs judges who are willing to find better ways to address low level non-violent crime in our community. Doing things the way we have always done – arresting and incarcerating repeatedly – can only be expected to produce the same results.

For 12 years, I have worked hard to find real solutions to help lift people out of crime and protect our community. I have revitalized Seattle’s Mental Health Court and created a new Community Court. I believe that our community is safer when people are closely connected to the social safety net and can receive housing, mental health, and drug addiction treatment – but they must also have intense case management to ensure accountability and a positive path to healthier lives.

I believe that this is the way forward for Seattle, but there is much more work to be done. I look forward to another four years as a Seattle Municipal Court Judge, and between now and November, I hope to hear from voters who love Seattle as much as my family and I do. Tell me about your vision for this great city.
I hope you will take a few moments to read about the work I have done so far and what remains to be done. Thank you for the trust you have placed in me.
